The building is made of Jerusalem stone, and the women's section is on the gallery floor.

Milan's old central station of 1864, a through station, lacked the tracks and space for the traffic that followed the Simplon Tunnel's opening in 1906. On 28 April that year King Victor Emmanuel III laid the cornerstone of a replacement, before any design had been picked. The decisive competition came in 1912 and went to Ulisse Stacchini, whose entry bore the Latin title "In Motu Vita", "Life in Motion". He revised it repeatedly, mostly to calm the city government's worries about cost; its style was called an eclectic "Assyrian-Lombard" mix. The main changes were new kinds of platform and Alberto Fava's great steel canopies, 341 metres long and covering 66,500 square metres. Opened in 1931, the terminus at the north end of central Milan is Europe's largest station by volume and Italy's second busiest, after Roma Termini.

The artist Henri Matisse devised the plan for this chapel in Vence, which was built and fitted out from 1947 to 1951; Auguste Perret is also credited. Matisse began at 77 and spent over four years shaping the building, its stained glass, wall paintings and ceramics, the liturgical furniture and even the priests' vestments. Several of his original works are inside, and he counted it as his finest achievement. On a hillside, it is entered by going down a flight of steps and turning right. The plan is an L, its longer arm straight ahead of the door, with the altar angled where the arms meet. It is 15 metres by 6. Casual visitors are divided about the plain white outside, but some rank the chapel among the great religious buildings of the 20th century.

The abstract expressionist Clyfford Still, who died in 1980, willed his whole collection to any American city ready to found a permanent museum solely for its care and display. The museum holds 3,125 of his works, 93 percent of all he made, plus his complete archives. In 2006 the newly formed museum secured a plot in Denver's Civic Center Cultural Complex, beside Daniel Libeskind's Hamilton Building for the city's art museum, then being built. The board gave the design to Brad Cloepfil's firm, Allied Works Architecture. Work began in December 2009, and the building, of 28,500 square feet, opened to the public on 18 November 2011, showing one artist alone. It has nine galleries, an art studio, painting storage and a conservation lab that visitors can see into, archive displays, two outdoor terraces and a green forecourt.

The old temple at this Mexico City shrine kept sinking and had become unsafe as pilgrim numbers grew, so from 1974 to 1976 a new basilica was built to house the Virgin's image and admit more people. Pedro Ramírez Vázquez was one of the six architects who designed it, among them Friar Gabriel Chávez de la Mora and José Luis Benlliure Galán. The interior is round and stands without columns in the way, so the image is visible from every point; moving walkways under the altar give a better view. The engineer Manuel González Flores set it on 344 control piles to avoid the settling seen nearby. Over the seven front doors, an open chapel recalling 16th-century atriums lets mass be said for those in the atrium. Some twenty million pilgrims visit each year, about nine million around 12 December.

The Iranian architect Kamran Diba, a cousin of the empress, designed this museum using elements of the traditional buildings of Persian desert towns such as Yazd and Kashan, and he worked with Nader Ardalan, also an architect, while designing it. It opened in 1977 beside Farah Park, which took the name Laleh Park once the Islamic revolution came. Most of it is underground: a round ramp winds downward with galleries opening off it, a layout likened to a buried version of New York's Guggenheim Museum. The gardens hold sculpture by Western artists including Ernst, Giacometti, Magritte and Moore. After the 1979 revolution the Western collection went into storage in the vault, and it was 1999 before an exhibition of Western art was held again, with works by Warhol, Hockney, Rauschenberg and Lichtenstein.

Risto Šekerinski designed this brutalist residential tower in Belgrade, begun in 1960 and finished in 1963. It stands at 9 Mija Kovačević Street, beside the Faculty of Orthodox Theology of the University of Belgrade, and rises close to the Pančevo Bridge, which links Serbia proper with Vojvodina. Its nickname comes from the triangular shapes worked into its design. Inside, the building is circular, served by two lifts, and it has triangular terraces. The tower was conceived as housing for Belgrade university, and in 1969 it had 104 connections installed. When it was built, the design received an award for its architecture.

This convention centre in Hanoi is the work of the firm Gerkan, Marg and Partners, with Meinhard von Gerkan and Nikolaus Goetze as its designers. In April 2004 four schemes were put forward, and 31 Vietnamese architects on the jury chose theirs without a single dissent; it was titled "Surfing the East Sea". Its forms draw on Hạ Long Bay in Quảng Ninh Province, which is listed as a World Heritage Site. A steel roof shaped like a wave runs over the building and climbs to 53.25 metres (174.7 ft) above the main meeting hall. The main structure measures 215.25 metres long and 113.5 metres wide. Solar panels provide back-up power. The centre was inaugurated on 15 October 2006.

The Shoji Ueda Museum of Photography, in Hōki, Tottori, Japan, is given over entirely to one photographer, Shoji Ueda: it both exhibits his work and keeps it as an archive. The museum was founded in 1995, and the architect Shin Takamatsu designed its building. In it, solid volumes are set against voids, which are cut into the mass as scaled incisions, and the relationship between solids and voids serves to frame Mount Daisen. More than 12,000 works by Ueda make up the collection.

This railway terminus in Mumbai (Bombay) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Frederick William Stevens, a British engineer and architect, designed it in a lavish Indo Gothic style, working from a first scheme by Axel Haig. The old Bori Bunder station had been altered several times up to the 1870s and was cleared after 1877 to make way. Work on the new building, just south of the old one, started in 1878 and ended in 1887, Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee year; the public could use it from 20 May 1888. Of its 18 platforms, seven serve suburban lines and 11 long-distance trains, and it houses the head offices of the Central Railway zone. Its name changed again in 2017 to Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (code CSMT), in which "Maharaj" means great king or emperor.

Pier Luigi Nervi designed this reinforced concrete hall, seating 6,300, completed in 1971. Named after Pope St. Paul VI, it stands on land the Knights of Columbus gave. Only part lies in Vatican City; most is in Rome, and that Italian portion is treated as extraterritorial ground of the Holy See. The pope uses it instead of St. Peter's Square for his Wednesday morning General Audience. Pericle Fazzini's La Resurrezione (The Resurrection), an 80-tonne sculpture in a bronze and copper alloy, dominates the hall. In May 2007 it was announced that 2,400 solar panels would cover the roof, enough to power the building's heating, cooling and lighting all year. The German maker SolarWorld donated the $1.5 million system, which began working on 26 November 2008 and won that year's European Solar Prize for solar architecture and urban development.

This London hall is the practical half of a memorial to the Prince Consort; the ornamental half is the Albert Memorial, due north in Kensington Gardens and now cut off from the hall by Kensington Gore. Its designers were two Royal Engineers, Captain Francis Fowke and Henry Y. D. Scott, both civil engineers, and Lucas Brothers built it. Ancient amphitheatres strongly shaped their ideas, and they also knew Gottfried Semper's thinking from his time at the South Kensington Museum. The walls are mostly Fareham Red brick, trimmed with terracotta blocks from Gibbs and Canning of Tamworth. Rowland Mason Ordish designed the glazed wrought-iron dome. When its temporary supports came out after it was assembled in place, only volunteers stayed on site in case it fell. The hall opened on 29 March 1871 and seats 5,272.

Tulsa's city officials wanted an arena that would become an architectural landmark, and they turned to César Pelli, who had designed Malaysia's Petronas Towers. The result was the flagship of Tulsa County's long-range plan, Vision 2025. Matrix Architects Engineers Planners, a Tulsa firm, was architect and engineer of record, and Odell Associates are also credited. Pelli drew on Native American, art deco and contemporary themes from the city and used swirling circles inside and out. A glass wall 103 feet high and 600 feet long, of 1,600 panels at 350 pounds each, wraps the arena, climbing as it goes and leaning at five degrees. Zahner made and fitted 33,000 stainless steel panels that carry the upward spiral on around the building. Inside, grand staircases from the main lobby curve around part of the arena, following the same movement.

Residents of Nowa Huta formed a parish as early as 1952 and pressed for a church, but the Communist government refused both permits and land. A site was finally secured in 1965, thanks, it is said, to Karol Wojtyła, then metropolitan bishop and later Pope John Paul II. Wojciech Pietrzyk designed it that year; work began in 1967. Because of political limits, volunteers did most of the building without state help, and it was completed in 1977 as the first new church in Nowa Huta. A large sloping roof and a 70-metre mast shaped as a crowned cross refer to Noah's Ark. It is considered a good example of Polish late modernism and is read as a nod to Le Corbusier's Ronchamp chapel of ten years earlier. Under 1980s martial law it became a hub of anti-communist resistance.

Aino and Alvar Aalto won the 1927 competition for this public library with an entry called "W.W.W.". It was built from 1927 to 1935, when the city, then Viipuri, was Finnish; it is now in Russia. The first scheme was Nordic Classicism, drawing on Asplund's library in Stockholm, but in five years of work, 1928 to 1933, it became wholly modernist. The central reading and lending hall is a stepped, sunken well spread over several levels. Deep round skylights spread daylight evenly over the desks without glare, and in the auditorium a wavy timber ceiling carries sound across the room. It was Finland's first public library with a separate children's wing and open shelves. After decades of post-war neglect, a twenty-year international restoration ended in 2013, putting the building and its original fittings back into public use.

This 50-metre bronze statue stands on one of the twin hills called the Collines des Mamelles, outside Dakar, facing the Atlantic from the Ouakam suburb. Pierre Goudiaby Atepa, a Senegalese architect, designed it from an idea of President Abdoulaye Wade, and the North Korean firm Mansudae Overseas Projects built it. A man, woman and child reach skyward: he carries the child on his arm and holds the woman by the waist, an image of Africa rising out of the earth towards the light. Standing for African rebirth, it draws on the vision of Senegal's first president, Léopold Sédar Senghor. Work on the 100-metre hill began in 2006 and on the statue, Africa's tallest, in 2008. After a much-delayed unveiling in 2010, critics worldwide judged it poorly, and local imams called the human figure idolatrous and the half-clothed bodies immodest.

Harry Seidler & Associates designed this building for the Commonwealth government; design and construction ran from 1970 to 1974, and it was originally planned as offices for federal trade agencies. Its structure is precast, prestressed concrete, and radically simple: everything repeats just three parts, façade beams 26 metres long, floor beams or "planks" 16 metres long, and column pieces of 1.5 metres. Seven wings hold 50,000 square metres of offices around two courtyards. It is named after Sir Edmund Barton, Australia's first Prime Minister and one of the first judges of its High Court. Later changes include cladding fitted under the exposed first-floor planks, which improves its thermal performance but has been criticised for hiding the original design. A refurbishment also caused concern for its heritage value and for public access to its central open spaces and artworks.

The Slovenian architect Vladimir Šubic designed this Ljubljana tower for the Pension Institute, which financed it. Building started on 19 April 1931, and when it opened on 21 February 1933 no building in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was taller, and only eight high-rises in Europe were. Its style blends neoclassical and art deco. The tower uses the three-part model for tall buildings pioneered by Louis Sullivan: a base that engages the street and passers-by, a uniform shaft, and a crown, finished with a round colonnade and flagpole added later. Karst marble lines the entrance lobby. Two quick lifts carry visitors up to the café, and a slower one serves the flats. It was the first building to rise above the Baroque outline of the city's bell towers, and some residents, fearing for the skyline, called it a "freak".

Hermann Eggert and Gustav Halmhuber designed this castle-like town hall in the eclectic style of the Wilhelm II era; it took 12 years to build and opened on 20 June 1913. It sits just beyond Hanover's historic centre, inside the 10-hectare Maschpark. It cost 10 million marks and stands on 6,026 beech piles. Bombing raids in World War II damaged it, and in 1946 the state of Lower Saxony was proclaimed in its 38-metre-high hall. The ground floor shows four city models. The dome and its viewing platform reach 97.73 metres. Its lift follows the dome's parabolic curve, something no other lift in the world does, climbing a 50-metre shaft at up to 17 degrees to the gallery, from where the Harz mountains can be seen on clear days.

Backing the Humboldtian ideal of education, King Frederick William III of Prussia had Karl Friedrich Schinkel plan a public museum for the royal art. Plans existed by 1822/23; building ran from 1825 to 1830. The crown prince, later Frederick William IV, shaped it with his drafts, wanting a design steeped in Classical antiquity. Around the Lustgarten, the palace (south) stood for worldly power, the arsenal (west) for military might and the cathedral (east) for divine authority. The museum, on the north side and built to educate the people, stood for science, art and the confident middle class. On the garden front, a plain hall of columns in grand style was to give the building character. Considered a major work of German Neoclassicism, it was first the Königliches Museum and became the Altes Museum in 1845, after the Neues Museum's completion.

Chamberlin, Powell and Bon, whose first project was the Golden Lane Estate just to the north, designed this London estate. It was built between 1965 and 1976 across a 35-acre site, but unlike Golden Lane it was not social housing. Its flats show how widely British building of the 1960s and 1970s let concrete be the visible face of a building. Cars and people are kept completely apart across the whole area, a principle called "slab urbanism". This works through "highwalks", walkways of different widths and shapes, usually one to three storeys above the ground. The main buildings rise as high as seven floors over a podium that joins every facility in the Barbican and gives walkers a route above the street. The terrace blocks are arranged around a lake and green squares.

Boston City Hall was first proposed in 1956 within the Government Center development, after decades of attempts to replace Old City Hall. Securing land and money took about five years, and in 1962 Kallmann McKinnell & Knowles (KMK) won a two-phase design competition; Campbell, Aldrich & Nulty shared the design, and LeMessurier Consultants engineered it. Its nine stories form three tiers that follow the interior's divisions. Public areas fill the first four floors, elected officials the fifth, and agencies closed to the public the sixth to ninth. Brick clads the lower part and concrete the upper, and the doors are on the three lowest levels. Projecting hoods frame the fifth-floor windows, and the top floors push outward around a central fourth-story courtyard. Some interiors pair concrete walls with a coffered concrete ceiling carried on Vierendeel trusses.

Frank Gehry designed this Chicago footbridge, with Skidmore, Owings and Merrill as structural engineers, and it opened on July 16, 2004, with the rest of Millennium Park. Crossing Columbus Drive, it joins Millennium Park to Maggie Daley Park, which used to be called Daley Bicentennial Plaza. Its namesake, energy firm BP, gave $5 million toward it, and it was the first Gehry bridge to be finished. Its curves have led people to call it snakelike. A concealed box girder rests on a concrete base, and hardwood boards cover the deck. Stainless steel parapets stand in for handrails. The bridge runs 935 feet (285 m), and its sloped stretches rise at five percent, keeping it barrier free and accessible. Its sheet metal work has earned awards, and it was built to bear heavy loads without strain from its own weight.

A law of 1909 finally required a direct connection, and a year later Victor Horta was commissioned to design the Central Station complex. The early plans came with a large urban redevelopment: in the 1920s land was bought and over 1,000 buildings were knocked down. World War II slowed construction once again. In 1947, after Horta's death, a team headed by Maxime Brunfaut took charge of the work; his father, the architect Fernand Brunfaut, presided over the National Bureau of the North–South connection. Brunfaut completed the building to Horta's plans but extended them, adding a new line to Brussels Airport in suburban Zaventem and several pedestrian passages underground. The station opened on 4 October 1952, close to half a century after the law. Three island platforms serve its six tracks.

Cairo International Stadium is a multi-use venue built to Olympic standard, with seats for 75,000 and no standing areas. Its architect was the German Werner March, who had designed Berlin's Olympic Stadium between 1934 and 1936, while ACE Moharram Bakhoum handled the engineering and oversaw construction. Almost every major Egyptian match is played here. The ground staged several games of the 2009 FIFA U-20 World Cup, among them both semifinals, the match for third place and the final, in which Brazil met Ghana, and it was one of the venues of the 2019 Africa Cup of Nations. It stands in Nasr City, with Cairo International Airport roughly 10 km to the east and downtown about as far away, and line 3 of the underground has its own Cairo stadium station to serve it.

Sevilla Tower, by César Pelli, was begun in March 2008 and finished in 2015. It is the tallest building in Seville and in all of Andalusia, and ranks eighth in height across Spain. Its site is La Cartuja, the area that hosted Seville's Universal Exposition from April to October 1992. The brief called for a building that would become a fresh icon for Seville and would "preferably" gather its volume into one high-rise. Pelli's tower sits between two podium buildings of four stories, likewise by him. Their curved edges shape a plaza that opens north and south and tightens in the middle, making a shopping street scaled to people on foot. The U.S. Green Building Council awarded the project LEED Gold.

Capital Gate, designed by RMJM and finished in 2011, is among the tallest buildings in Abu Dhabi and leans 18° to the west, over three times the tilt of the Leaning Tower of Pisa. It rests on 490 piles drilled 30 meters (98 ft) into the ground that resist strong winds, gravity and the seismic pressures caused by the lean. The core was pre-cambered, built with a slight tilt the other way; as each floor and the diagonal grid went in, their weight pulled the core slowly upright. Because of the lean, two diagrids were needed: an outer one sets the tower's form, and an inner one ties into the central core through eight one-off pin-jointed members. The outer grid takes the floor loads, and the inner grid passes them to the core, so the floors need no columns.

Nîmes in southern France keeps both a contemporary art museum and its municipal library in the Carré d'Art. British architect Norman Foster's design was chosen, and the building opened in May 1993. It came out of a project to refurbish the square around the Maison carrée, a Roman temple from the very start of the 1st century AD that survives in perfect condition, and it faces that temple, giving it a new setting. Glass, concrete and steel make up the structure. Of its nine storeys, half are sunk deep below ground, so the building stays low in sympathy with the scale of its neighbours. Archive storage and a cinema occupy the lower levels.

Rafael Moneo's project in Cartagena centres on the Roman theatre, built between 5 and 1 BCE for some 6,000 spectators. After over a decade of excavation he won the restoration in 2003, and consolidated the ruins with archaeologists Sebastián Ramallo and Elena Ruiz and restorer Isabel García-Galán. He sought to tie the theatre to nearby buildings, above all the Old Cathedral (Santa María la Vieja), which partly sits over the seating; remains of an earlier Roman house survive inside the museum. The Romans built the theatre near the port, far from the unhealthy lagoon, with the stands in a north-facing hillside sheltered from easterly winds and the axis aimed at the winter solstice sunrise. The area had become one of the old town's most run-down corners, and the theatre's recovery drives the regeneration of a large part of the city.

OMA designed the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing, with Rem Koolhaas and Ole Scheeren in charge and Cecil Balmond of Arup doing the complex engineering. OMA won the contract on 1 January 2002 after an international competition. Rather than a conventional tower, the main block is a loop of six sections, some horizontal and some vertical, with 473,000 m2 (5,090,000 sq ft) of floor space, giving the facade an irregular grid around an open centre. The loop is meant to stand for collectivity, communication, continuity and integration. Building it is seen as a structural challenge, not least because the site is in a seismic zone; the two towers were joined in the early morning, once their steel had cooled to one temperature. Work started on 1 June 2004 and the facade was done in January 2008.

Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza Vieira, born in Matosinhos in 1933, designed the Galician Centre of Contemporary Art. No city beyond Portugal other than Santiago de Compostela has two buildings by him; the second here is the university's Faculty of Journalism. The design began taking shape in 1988 and was presented in 1992, and building work ended between 1993 and 1994. Its three floors hold an entrance porch, an auditorium, a café, a library, offices and exhibition halls. Visitors can walk out onto the terrace, which looks across the old quarter's rooftops and the Convent of San Domingos de Bonaval. The centre was founded in 1993 with an anthological show of Maruja Mallo's work, and since late 1994 it has kept a steady programme, which began with the exhibition Itínere. Camiño e camiñantes.

Mario Botta's church in Mogno, built from 1994 to 1996, replaced a church of 1636 that an avalanche flattened on 25 April 1986. The Swiss architect used stone from the surrounding valleys, gneiss such as Beola from the Riveo quarries and white marble from the Peccia valley, plus an iron frame and glass for the roof. The plan is an ellipse, topped by a tilted circle of glass. In long section, the key element is a rampant arch, which Botta meant to recall the old church's arch, which had shielded part of the village from the avalanche that buried and wrecked the earlier building. Two bells dating from 1746 are all that was recovered. Inside, the fittings are spare: two rows of wooden benches lined up with an altar made of just two blocks of white marble.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed the Avery Coonley House in the Prairie style, and it was built in 1908–1909. It belongs to an estate of 10 acres (4.0 ha) that also includes a carriage house and a cottage for the gardener, both by Wright, while the landscape architect Jens Jensen shaped the grounds with raised and sunken gardens. The house rises two stories, built as a stuccoed frame resting on a flat concrete foundation. Its ground floor, treated like a basement, holds the entrance hall, a playroom and storage. Upstairs, rooms form a U and are grouped by use, the first zoned plan in Wright's work. The house has long drawn praise, and Wright judged it his most successful design of that period. In the 1950s the single home was split into two: 300 Scottswood Road and 281 Bloomingbank Road.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this Phoenix house for David, his son, and Gladys, his daughter-in-law, working in an organic style; it was built between 1950 and 1952. The main house is a curving concrete structure lifted on seven piers and reached by a spiral ramp. It bends through 270 degrees around an inner courtyard, with the kitchen at the northeast, the living room southwest and the bedrooms southeast. Concrete blocks and mahogany boards make up its 2,553 square feet (237.2 m2), which hold three bedrooms and four bathrooms. Circles and other geometric shapes recur inside, and Wright also designed furnishings for it, a carpet among them. The main house is on the National Register of Historic Places, and by the 2010s it was one of four surviving Wright buildings in Phoenix and nine in Arizona.

Tel Aviv has no bigger concert hall than Heichal HaTarbut, the home of the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra. Dov Karmi, Ze'ev Rechter and Yaakov Rechter designed it, and it opened on Habima Square in October 1957 under its first name, the Fredric R. Mann Auditorium. Leonard Bernstein conducted the opening concert, played by the Israel Philharmonic with Arthur Rubinstein as piano soloist. From 2011 to 2013 the hall was renovated under the supervision of the Israeli architect Ofer Kolker, and Yasuhisa Toyota, from Japan, designed its new acoustics. When it reopened in 2013 it took the name Charles Bronfman Auditorium, after Charles Bronfman, the Canadian-American businessman and donor.

Uruguayan architect Mauricio Cravotto designed Montevideo's municipal palace on the former English Cemetery, land the state had bought years before, meaning to house the executive and the judiciary there. Work began in 1935 and the building opened on July 16, 1941, though it departs from Cravotto's 1929 model. His tower was to reach 114 m and become the city's tallest, but for financial reasons it stopped at 78 m, second only to the Palacio Salvo. The side wings, the concourse below ground and the garage were added later. Its place on 18 de Julio Avenue, along the crest of a long ridge, makes it seem grander than its height alone would. A bronze copy of Michelangelo's David stands before the main entrance, and an outside elevator at the back lifts the public to a city observatory on floor 22.

Lluís Domènech i Montaner designed the Palau de la Música Catalana in the Catalan modernista style, and it went up from 1905 to 1908 for the Orfeó Català, a choir formed in 1891 that was a leading force in the cultural movement later called the Renaixença. As is usual in Catalan modernism, curves win over straight lines, moving forms over static ones, and rich floral and organic ornament is used lavishly. Yet the design also pays close attention to function and uses the newest materials of the early 20th century, such as steel framing. The hall seats about 2,200 and is Europe's only auditorium lit solely by daylight during the day, through stained-glass walls on two sides and a skylight by Antoni Rigalt whose inverted golden dome, ringed in blue, stands for the sun and sky.

Rafael Viñoly's 20 Fenchurch Street cost over £200 million and has a top-heavy shape that seems to swell up and out, which earned it the nickname "The Walkie-Talkie" after the handset it is said to resemble. First proposed at almost 200 m (656 ft), the design was cut down over worries about its visual effect on St Paul's Cathedral and the Tower of London. It has 38 storeys and stands 160 m (525 ft). Above the entrance floor are 34 office floors, served by fourteen double-deck lifts. A garden fills the top three floors, reached by two express lifts, with a viewing area, a terrace, a bar and two restaurants. The developer called this 'sky garden' London's highest public park, though whether it is truly a park, or truly public given its access limits, has been debated.

Building work on Abdeen Palace began in 1863 and ran for ten years, and its official opening came in 1874. It was raised under Ismail Pasha to serve as Egypt's official seat of government, taking over from the Citadel of Cairo, the centre of government since the Middle Ages, and it also hosted official events and ceremonies. Léon Rousseau, a French architect, designed it on a site of 24 feddans, working with many decorators from Egypt, Italy, France and elsewhere in Europe. Joseph Urban added a new wing in 1891, and in 1921 Sultan Fuad I created the palace garden on 20 feddans. The palace holds 500 rooms. Its lower floors house four museums: the Arms, Silver, Royal Family and Presidential Gifts museums.

Santiago Calatrava designed the Alamillo Bridge in Seville, built between 1989 and 1992. Its structural idea goes back to his 1986 sculpture 'Running Torso', where tilted stacked marble cubes are held in balance by a taut wire. A single straight tower of steel shell, filled with reinforced concrete, leans backward and balances a 200 m span through thirteen pairs of cables. Because the tower is heavy enough to offset the deck, no back stays are needed; its weight does the job of one set of stay cables. Steel wings cantilever from a hexagonal spine to carry three traffic lanes each side, and the spine's top, lifted 1.6 metres (5 feet) above the road, forms a footway and cycle lane between them. A stairway inside the tower climbs to a lookout at its top.

Alden B. Dow's home and studio in Midland went up between 1937 and 1940. His work with blocks started after his 1931 graduation from Columbia's School of Architecture and eight months as an apprentice at Taliesin in 1933. Together with Robert Goodall, a draftsman for Frank Lloyd Wright, he devised the "Unit Block", patented in 1935: a rhomboid block, mostly square-faced, made in 16 sizes from the cinder Dow had seen heaped outside The Dow Chemical Company's furnaces. Building materials stay visible throughout the house, and Dow used the blocks for walls, terraces and decorative touches such as the stepping stones across the pond on the grounds. Besides two drafting rooms, the studio had a reception area with an entry, and a sunken conference room lying below water level. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1989.

Designed in April 1931 by Albert Frey and A. Lawrence Kocher as a case study, the Aluminaire House rises three stories and was assembled in ten days from donated materials; no earlier all-metal house was built in the United States. Roughly cubic, it has five rooms in 1,200 square feet (110 m2) and stands on six columns. Corrugated metal sheets over waterproof paper wrap a frame of two-inch steel angles, while fabric-covered thin insulation board lines the inside. After its early exhibitions the architect Wallace K. Harrison paid $1,000 for it, dismantled it and rebuilt it on his Long Island estate as the core of a large complex. In desert Palm Springs, the museum added air conditioning and weatherproofing.

Angkor Wat rose between 1113 and 1150 CE as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, built in Khmer king Suryavarman II's reign, on a 162.6-hectare (401.8-acre) site inside Angkor, the medieval capital. Unlike most Angkorian temples, it faces west. It combines the temple mountain, the empire's usual form for state temples, with a later layout of concentric galleries: three rectangular galleries, each higher than the one before, climb to a central tower. The whole represents Mount Meru, the gods' home in Hindu mythology; its central quincunx of towers stands for its five peaks, and the walls and moat for the ranges and ocean around it. Lay people could enter only the lowest level. Its main tower lines up with the morning sun at the spring equinox. Most visible parts are Kulen sandstone; laterite forms the outer wall and hidden structure.

Robert G. Boughey & Associates designed the Bangkok Art and Culture Centre, a home for contemporary art in the Siam area of the Thai capital. After many delays it opened on 29 July 2008. Among the aims of its design were to honour Thai architecture and culture and to bring in daylight in a controlled way. Its spaces were made tall to hold art, and the central atrium acts as the building's emblem and sets the character of the interior around it. The centre also contains an art library, bookshops, craft shops, cafes and commercial galleries. It is meant as a place for cultural exchange, giving Bangkok a working base in the international art world. Visitor numbers climbed from 300,000 in its first year to 1.7 million in 2017.

Bishop Edward King Chapel serves both Ripon College Cuddesdon, a theological college of the Church of England near Oxford, and a community of Anglican nuns (the Communities of St John Baptist and the Good Shepherd). Its dedication honours Edward King, who led Cuddesdon Theological College as Principal from 1863 to 1873 and was Bishop of Lincoln from 1885 to 1910. The design came out of an architectural competition run by RIBA Competitions, which chose an elliptical building by Niall McLaughlin Architects. In 2013 the chapel made the Stirling Prize shortlist and finished runner-up, and it was also shortlisted for the EU Prize for Contemporary Architecture.

Thom Mayne of Morphosis designed this headquarters on South Main Street, downtown Los Angeles, for Caltrans (California's Department of Transportation) and the city's transportation department. It cost $165 million and opened on 24 September 2004; its futuristic, environmentally friendly design is credited with earning Mayne the Pritzker Prize in 2005. The 13-story building fills the block bounded by First, Main, Second and Los Angeles streets, with 716,200 gross square feet of offices plus underground parking for 1,142 cars. Features include a public plaza honouring Eli and Edythe Broad; Motordom, a light installation four stories tall; a third-floor conference room with a glass floor; Code: Survey, 168 glass art panels each a foot square; a four-story "100" house number; and Ten Past Five O'clock on the fourth floor. The History Channel's Modern Marvels followed its design and construction over four episodes.

From the start, Canary Wharf station was planned as the Jubilee Line Extension's showpiece, and Sir Norman Foster won the design contract in 1990. In a drained dock arm, a Tarmac Construction and Bachy UK joint venture used plain cut and cover to dig a huge pit, 24 metres (78 ft) deep and 265 metres (869 ft) long. Foster built on his earlier work for the Bilbao Metro, known as "Fosteritos". The main reason for the size was forecast demand of up to 50,000 passengers a day. It opened on 17 September 1999, and three extra entrances in 2004 raised capacity. The vast interior draws comparisons with a cathedral and has even hosted a wedding. In a 2013 YouGov poll it was voted London's "Most Loved" tube station and called comfortable and inviting despite its immense volume.

Mark Hemel and Barbara Kuit, Dutch architects at Information Based Architecture, designed the Canton Tower together with Arup, the London-headquartered consultancy in design, engineering and business. The team won an international competition in 2004 against many large offices from around the world. Ground was broken in 2005, it topped out in 2009 and opened on 29 September 2010, ahead of that year's Asian Games. Its twisted hyperboloid form matches the Russian Empire patent No. 1896 of 12 March 1899, granted to the engineer and architect Vladimir Shukhov, and its structure resembles Shukhov's 1910 Adziogol Lighthouse in Ukraine's Dnepr delta. Around its waist runs a 180-metre (590 ft) outdoor skywalk, where visitors can climb the tower. Outdoor gardens sit within the structure, and a big outdoor viewing deck crowns it at just over 452 metres (1,483 ft).

Rem Koolhaas of the Office for Metropolitan Architecture won the international architecture tender that launched Casa da Música in 1999. The building was meant to mark 2001, the festive year when Porto was European Capital of Culture, and it was the first in Portugal conceived from the start purely for music, for public performance as well as training and creative work. AFA Arup Group Limited of London and Afassociados of Porto engineered it, on a site where trams were once staged. Building ran over schedule across the next four years and cost 100 million euros; it opened in 2005. Its 1,300-seat main auditorium is filled with daylight, and no other concert hall anywhere has two walls made wholly of glass. Thirteen large surfaces there, from 22 by 15 to 65 by 8 metres, carry a gold leaf woodgrain pattern.

The present Cathedral Church of Christ in Lagos was designed by the architect Bagan Benjamin, and work on it started on 1 November 1924. Edward, Prince of Wales (afterwards King Edward VIII), laid the foundation stone on 21 April 1925, and the building was finished in 1946. Its popular name is Cathedral Church of Christ Marina. No cathedral of the Anglican Church of Nigeria is older. It also holds the largest organ in the country. Early in the 21st century the English firm Harrison & Harrison renewed the whole instrument and rebuilt its console; it has 64 stops spread over four manuals and a pedalboard.

Skidmore, Owings and Merrill designed Cayan Tower in Dubai; the client was Cayan Real Estate Investment and Development. Known as Infinity Tower before opening, it is a 75-story skyscraper rising 306 metres (1,004 ft). Its twist comes from rotating every floor by 1.2 degrees about a cylindrical core that holds the elevators and services. When it opened on 10 June 2013, it was the tallest high-rise in the world with a 90-degree twist. A dynamic analysis studied how the tower might perform in wind, earthquakes and other dynamic loading. To keep direct sun out of the apartments, metal panels in a titanium colour, set on concrete columns cast in place, work with repeated staggered screens. Work halted for eighteen months after the wall holding back the Dubai Marina broke on 7 February 2007 and flooded the foundation site.

George Marsh of R. Seifert and Partners designed Centre Point, with Pell Frischmann as engineers, and Wimpey Construction built it between 1963 and 1966 for £5.5 million. A 34-storey tower is joined at first-floor level to a 9-storey block to the east holding maisonettes, shops, offices and retail units. The 117 m (385 ft) tower, with 27,180 m2 of floor space, stands where a gallows once did, over the former route of St Giles High Street, which was rerouted to make room. Portcrete Limited cast its precast segments in fine concrete with crushed Portland stone on the Isle of Portland, Dorset, before lorries took them to London. The building sat empty until 1975, except for a brief occupation by housing activists in 1974, and in 2015 its offices became flats. Nikolaus Pevsner called it "coarse in the extreme".

In Bengaluru, Chowdiah Memorial Hall serves as a cultural centre for music, theatre and competitions. Designed by S. N. Murthy, it took seven years to build, costing ₹36 lakh (US$37,000), and reached completion on 14 November 1980. The auditorium is shaped like an enormous seven-stringed violin, down to its strings, keys, bridge and bow. Inside, chandeliers light a marble foyer. A low-lying site in Gayatri Park Extension was picked so that the whole hall could be seen from a raised viewpoint. The city corporation granted the academy a 99-year lease on the land.

The Cité des Sciences et de l'Industrie in Paris reuses an abattoir's sales hall, left unfinished in 1973, whose vast steel trusses frame the building. Architect Adrien Fainsilber and the engineers Rice Francis Ritchie (RFR) designed the conversion, commissioned on 15 September 1980. François Mitterrand opened it on 13 March 1986, timed to the Giotto space probe's encounter with Halley's Comet. On the park side, a "bioclimatic façade" is led by Les Serres, three greenhouses, each 32 metres high and wide and 8 metres deep. Their glass fronts were the first structural glass walls built with neither framing nor supporting fins. Some five million people come each year to attractions that include a planetarium, the Argonaute submarine, an aquarium, the IMAX theatre La Géode and areas for children and teenagers.

Jorge Manjarres, Germán Samper, Aníbal Saldarriaga and Raúl Fajardo designed the Coltejer Building in Medellín, the city where Colombia's era of skyscraper building began in the 1960s. Making room for it meant pulling down Edificio Gonzalo Mejía, an art nouveau building that housed the Junín Theatre and the Hotel Europa. Finished in 1972 and 175 metres (574 ft) tall, it was then the tallest building in South America. As of 2016 it was still the tallest in Medellín and ranked tenth in Colombia. Its form is said to recall the needle of a sewing machine, a nod to the textile company that gave it its name.

Ivan Nikolaev designed this constructivist landmark in Moscow's Donskoy District for 2,000 students; built in 1929–1931, it stayed in use as a dormitory until 1996. The brief set a modest ceiling on cost and a building volume of 50 cubic metres per student. Nikolaev's main rule was to keep three things apart: shared study space, public services (cafeteria, showers, storage) and living space. The result is an H-shaped plan, with a services block linking an 8-storey dormitory 200 metres long to a 3-storey study block. Since students kept everything they owned, from textbooks to daytime clothes, in lockers in the services block, Nikolaev reduced the bedrooms to sleeping space. Even the Soviet avant-garde found this too radical, and the sleeping cabins were enlarged to 2.7 by 2.3 metres with proper windows. A steel frame carries the residential block.

The crypt at Colonia Güell, in Santa Coloma de Cervelló, belongs to an unfinished church by Antoni Gaudí. Work began only in 1908, ten years after the commission. The plan called for two naves, one above the other, two towers and a central dome forty metres high. Gaudí started the design with his own method of gravity and rope, a funicular system that let him model the church's curves at 1:10 scale. This way of working produced a new architectural vocabulary, including hyperbolic paraboloids and hyperboloids, forms that recur across many of his designs. In 1914 the Güell family stopped construction after Count Güell died. The crypt, built from 1908 to 1915, is the only part of the church that was ever fully finished.

Dallas City Hall, the city's fifth, was completed in 1978 to designs by I. M. Pei, replacing the Dallas Municipal Building. Planning for a municipal center began in 1964, when the City Council set up a citizens' committee to choose a site for new administrative offices. Construction started on June 26, 1972, with Pei and the contractor Robert E. McKee in charge. The city accepted the parking garage in November 1974, Park Plaza followed in May 1976, and the main building in December 1977. Cost overruns on an original estimate of $42.2 million, and arguments over whether the design was too avant-garde, stirred controversy, but most problems were settled and the work was finished. The City Council first met in its chamber on February 1, 1978, and on March 12, 1978, the complete facility received its formal opening and dedication.

The Everett McKinley Dirksen United States Courthouse in Chicago rises 384 feet (117 m) over 30 floors and takes its name from U.S. Congressman Everett Dirksen. With the Kluczynski Federal Building, the Loop Station post office and Federal Plaza, it forms Mies van der Rohe's modernist Chicago Federal Center, which brought together more than thirty agencies once scattered in poor rented space. Four Chicago firms joined for the commission: Mies led the design, with A. Epstein and Sons, C. F. Murphy Associates and Schmidt, Garden and Erikson also involved. A street-level loading dock for the post office would have broken the openness of the plaza, so after further study Mies gave the post office a separate building with vehicle access below grade. The courthouse was the first of the three finished, and tenants moved in during 1964.

Robin Boyd's Domain Park Flats is a 20-storey apartment building in Melbourne, finished in 1962. Facing the Royal Botanic Gardens, it set a precedent for high-rise housing on park frontages. On completion it was Victoria's tallest residential building, overtaking the 13-storey Edgewater Towers in St Kilda (opened 4 March 1961). Each flat is placed on the floor slab so its occupants look north, and the mix of flat sizes inside shows outside in the free placing of windows and balconies, above all facing north. Southern towers, kept apart from the slab to cut noise in the living spaces, hold the lifts, fire stairs and cooling plant. Concrete is the main material, faced in Selkirk Bricks' manganese brick, with a steel roof deck and aluminium windows. With fan coil units, it became Melbourne's first high-rise housing with air conditioning.

The Fondazione Prada opened its new permanent home in Milan, on Largo Isarco, on 9 May 2015. Designed by OMA under Rem Koolhaas, it widens the range of spatial types in which art can be shown and shared with the public. The complex turns a former distillery from the 1910s into a mix of existing buildings and three new structures, called "Podium", "Cinema" and "Torre". Its signature is the "Haunted House", as it is known, a four-storey building wrapped in 24-carat gold foil that permanently displays works from the foundation's collection. The entrance building leads to two facilities made through special collaborations: a children's area designed by students of the national school of architecture at Versailles, and a bar where the director Wes Anderson recreated the feel of old Milan cafés.

Sultan Bayezid I ordered this mosque to mark his victory at Nicopolis, and the architect Ali Neccar designed and built it between 1396 and 1399. It stands at the centre of Bursa's old city, next to the historic markets, and is among the chief works of early Ottoman architecture. Inside, twelve columns carry twenty domes in four rows of five. A popular story says the sultan had vowed twenty mosques if he won the battle, and built one mosque of twenty domes instead. The dome over the şadırvan was left open to the sky as a skylight for the dark interior; glass covers it today. Of the three entrances, on the north, west and east, the northern one is the grandest. An earthquake in 1855 brought the roof down, and the mosque stayed shut for several years.

This terminal at King Abdulaziz International Airport, the main airport for both Jeddah and Mecca, is given over to the yearly Hajj pilgrimage. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, credited here together with Fazlur Rahman Khan, won the design contract in 1975. A conventional closed building, the architects judged, would not reflect the culture of Saudi Arabia, so they took traditional Bedouin tents as their model. From a local and cultural point of view, the main terminal space was meant to be open and shaded. The roof is a thin fibre sheet, made from a translucent material that Owens-Corning developed. At that time a terminal with tents as a permanent part of it was unheard of. Hochtief, an engineering firm from West Germany, acted as general contractor. Work began in 1979 and was finished three years later, in 1982.

Also known as the Jerusalem Centre for the Performing Arts, this complex was dedicated in October 1971. Its design came from Michael Nadler, Shulamit Nadler and Shmuel Bixson, who took first prize. Four halls share the building: the Sherover Theatre (950 seats), the Henry Crown Symphony Hall (750), where the Jerusalem Symphony Orchestra is based, the Rebecca Crown Auditorium (450) and the Little Theatre (110). Sculptural pieces in bare concrete are combined with traditional building in Jerusalem stone. The theatre stands in a big public square used for open-air concerts and other events. A later wing, named after Crown's parents, was planned by the same practice and continues the original design without a break. In 2012 the Jerusalem Municipality listed the complex for preservation along with two neighbours, the Van Leer Institute and the Presidential Residence.

Only architects resident in South Africa could enter the design competition, which Leonard Stokes, vice-president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, judged, reaching a decision in March 1910. The Cape Town firm Hawke and McKinlay won, yet the building contract went to Mattheus Meischke only on 17 February 1912, at a cost of £503,000. The building was finished in 1914. Its style is called Edwardian Baroque, with an Ionic portico, while the tower with its half-dome entrance is described as neo-Renaissance. The plan has two halves: municipal offices on the east, facing Rissik Street, and the Town Hall on the west, facing Harrison Street. In 1937 the tower was taken down, a floor added and the tower rebuilt. Declared a National Monument on 12 October 1979, it became home to the Gauteng Provincial Legislature on 21 October 1995.

Jo van den Broek and Jaap Bakema designed the Lijnbaan as part of Rotterdam's rebuilding after the German bombing in 1940, and it opened on 9 October 1953. It has been called Europe's first street purpose-made for people on foot. The plan split up uses that had mixed on the streets before the war: shops face a car-free promenade and are supplied from service streets behind, while homes sit in separate apartment blocks. The 66 shopkeepers doubted the idea until a 1:100 model won them round; they also disliked the name, which recalls old local ropewalks, preferring 'the Promenade'. Lewis Mumford praised it in a 1957 New Yorker piece, and it has been cited abroad as an example for pedestrian shopping, as in Stevenage's town centre. Its original section has been a national monument since 2010.

Of Moscow's 'Seven Sisters', built in the Stalinist style between 1947 and 1953, this headquarters of Moscow State University is the tallest. Boris Iofan bid for it in 1947 but placed his draft tower right on the edge of the Sparrow Hills, where a landslide was feared, so the job went to Lev Rudnev, who set the building 800 metres back from the cliff. The main tower's frame took over 40,000 tons of steel, with 130,000 cubic metres of concrete, and it opened on 1 September 1953. No building in Europe was taller until the Messeturm in Germany passed it in 1990. Lower towers flank the centre, and dormitory wings of 18 and 9 storeys frame a cour d'honneur. Its skyline inspired buildings in socialist countries, such as Warsaw's Palace of Culture and Science, and the 1980 Moscow Olympics logo.

T. R. Hamzah & Yeang, the Kuala Lumpur practice co-founded by Ken Yeang, received the design contract for Singapore's new National Library from the Ministry of National Development. The result is two 16-storey blocks in the Civic District, joined by bridges on the upper floors, with three basement levels below. It replaced the old National Library on Stamford Road, which shut on 31 March 2004; some bricks from that building were reused in the new one. The library moved in on 22 July 2005, and President S. R. Nathan opened it officially on 12 November that year. As the National Library Board's flagship, it holds both the Lee Kong Chian Reference Library and the Central Public Library. On the 16th-floor roof sits The Pod, an enclosed space shaped like a bubble that hosts functions and events.

The idea of a new courthouse at Porta Vittoria, to take the place of seven small, outdated judicial offices then in use in Milan, was first put forward in 1925. Marcello Piacentini designed the building with the architect Ernesto Rapisardi and oversaw its construction, which ended in July 1940. On a central site, one large block brings together three courts: the Court of Appeal, the Tribunale and the Pretura, or Magistrates Court. A tower 61 metres high rises at the southwest corner; it was first meant to hold the archive. The structure is mostly reinforced concrete. Outside, the building looks restrained and rather severe, but the inside is full of bas-reliefs, mosaics, frescoes and sculptures, with decoration in marble and precious stones. Among the artists were Mario Sironi, Fausto Melotti, Carlo Carrà, Romano Romanelli, Achille Funi and Arturo Dazzi.

Jean Nouvel won the competition in April 2007, and the 2,400-seat symphonic hall at the core of the Philharmonie opened in January 2015. After a delay of about twenty years, it completes the Cité de la Musique, the music institution by Christian de Portzamparc that opened in 1995. Nouvel worked with Brigitte Métra as partner, Marshall Day Acoustics on room acoustics, Nagata Acoustics on peer review and a scale model, and dUCKS Scéno on scenography. The hall is said to keep a real sense of intimacy: floating balconies bring even the most distant listener within 36 yards of the conductor. From the Belvedere on the roof, which looks towards the Eiffel Tower, a path winds down to the park. President François Hollande attended the opening concert; Nouvel stayed away, in a dispute over final costs and the completion date.

Bruce Kuwabara of KPMB Architects designed this 11,582-square-metre art museum together with Architecture49. It sits at River Landing, on the South Saskatchewan River's west bank, in the central business district of Saskatoon. Construction ran from June 2013 to 2017, and the museum opened to visitors that October. The Prairie style of Frank Lloyd Wright shaped the design, and the outside draws on the open prairie of the region and on the silos, barns and field sheds found there. Stacked volumes cantilever out towards the river, wrapped in glass and metal mesh. The mesh shades the building from the sun and casts shifting shadows as the sun moves across the sky. The prairie's sense of openness carries inside too: the main atrium rises to the fourth floor, and its glass walls look out over the river.

Thailand's parliament stands on the Chao Phraya River's east bank, in the Kiakkai area of Bangkok's Dusit District. Theerapol Niyom's team designed it after winning the competition. A Thai pagoda sits at the centre, with Surya Hall, the Hall of the Sun, for the House of Representatives and Chandra Hall, the Hall of the Moon, for the Senate. In all, 5,018 teak trees were used, standing for the "DNA of Thailand". Trai Bhum Phra Ruang, a classic Thai Buddhist tale, inspired the design, which was given a temple's look to remind officials of "Thainess" and morality; the name means "peaceful parliament". Offices, a banquet hall, a seminar room, museums and a convention centre are also inside. Critics have called it "religious architecture" drawing on Buddhist and Hindu cosmology. After long delays, it opened officially on 1 May 2021.

Philip Johnson designed the Sheldon, at 451 North 12th Street in Lincoln, as a dedicated home for the university's art collection; the museum was established when the collection moved there in 1963. The siblings Mary Frances and Adams Bromley Sheldon met the full cost, together more than $1.5 million. It is built of Italian travertine. Inside, a richly decorated great hall holds a grand staircase that hangs in space. Johnson aimed to spare visitors what he called "museum fatigue", the tiredness of body or mind common among museum visitors, and he judged it the finest building of his career. As part of the opening, Isamu Noguchi was asked to make and install a work for the great hall; he titled it "Song of the Bird". It joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.

The Athens Conservatoire is modern Greece's oldest school for the performing arts. Its building, by Ioannis Despotopoulos, the only Greek to study under Bauhaus founder Walter Gropius, is the one finished part of a large cultural complex the government commissioned for Athens in 1959; the plan won him the leading architecture prize of its day. His archive at the Benaki Museum shows the scheme had an opera house for 1,800, a round theatre stage, a National Gallery extension, a new Byzantine Museum, a Byzantine-style church, a hotel, halls for dance and experimental theatre, and underground garages. Building started in 1969 and stopped, unfinished, in 1976 when money ran out. In 1980 the state paid to finish it in return for the school's old premises on Pireos Street. It is seen as an outstanding Bauhaus work in Greece.

The Emir of Bahrain, Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa, opened the national museum on 15 December 1988. The Danish architects Krohn & Hartvig Rasmussen designed it, and many regard it as the first modern museum in the region. The way had been prepared in 1967, when UNESCO and the government of Bahrain signed a cultural agreement that helped make a national museum possible. The complex cost $30 million and covers 27,800 square metres, with two buildings sharing 20,000 square metres of floor space. It stands on a man-made peninsula that looks across to the neighbouring island of Muharraq. No other tourist attraction in the country draws more visitors.

Konstantin Melnikov designed this Moscow bus garage in 1926, working out its floor plan and architecture, while Vladimir Shukhov handled the structural engineering. Melnikov had won over the city transport board with his idea of a garage where buses could flow through freely. Completed in 1927, it showed avant-garde design methods put to work on an industrial building. Even so, it is sometimes linked with constructivism when its outside is really a plain red-brick industrial dress; round attic windows, long since destroyed, were its only avant-garde touch. Because the garage is a parallelogram on a larger rectangular plot, Melnikov filled the awkward leftover spaces with workshops and offices. After decades of neglect it came close to demolition, but it was restored in 2007 and 2008, reopening in September 2008 as a modern art gallery.

This preserved coal-fired power station stands on the Thames's south bank at Nine Elms, Wandsworth, to designs by J. Theo Halliday and Giles Gilbert Scott. It went up in two stages. Battersea A was built from 1929 to 1935, and Battersea B, to the east, from 1937 to 1941, when the worsening war halted work. Because B almost copies A, the finished building has its four chimneys. It ranks among the largest brick buildings in the world and is known for its original Art Deco interiors and fittings. The structure was listed Grade II in 1980, three years before B closed, and raised to Grade II* in 2007. Its picture is on the cover of Pink Floyd's 1977 album Animals. Since October 2022 the public has been able to go inside the main building.

Youssef Aftimus, the Lebanese architect of Beirut's city hall, designed and built this house in 1924, and Fouad Kozah gave it its present form in 1932 by adding two storeys. Its airy structure and its place on the demarcation line, commanding the Sodeco crossroads, made it strategically important. Heritage activists rescued it, above all the architect Mona Hallak, who first studied the house in 1994 on a visit with APSAD, an independent group that protects historic monuments and buildings. In 2009 the Beirut municipality hired the architect Youssef Haider to lead its restoration. Beit Beirut, "the house of Beirut", is now a museum and urban cultural centre on the city's history, focused on the Lebanese Civil War. A decree also allows a modern annex on the empty land around it, for the municipality's urban planning offices and underground parking.

The centre was first built to host the events of Portugal's 1992 Presidency of the European Council, with a longer aim of giving Lisbon lasting venues for conferences, exhibitions, opera, ballet and concerts, plus meeting rooms, shops and cafés. An international competition drew 57 entries, and six were asked to develop a preliminary project. The winning team paired Vittorio Gregotti of Italy with the Portuguese practice Atelier Risco, then headed by Manuel Salgado. Their plan had five modules, but only the conference, performing arts and exhibition centres went up at first, ready by January 1992. With over 140,000 square metres of usable space, no Portuguese building with cultural facilities is larger. It faces the Praça do Império beside the Jerónimos Monastery, among landmarks such as the Tower of Belém and the Monument to the Discoveries.

The Bullitt Foundation, a Seattle non-profit working on urban ecology, built this Miller Hull design, aiming for the greenest commercial building anywhere. It was planned to last 250 years. Power comes from 575 rooftop solar panels, and saving measures cut its energy use to about 15 percent of a typical office of its size; in 2016 the panels made almost 30 percent more energy than the building used. Twenty-six geothermal wells reach 400 feet (120 m) down, where the ground stays at 55 °F (13 °C). Collected rainwater will be filtered for every use once regulators approve, and an onsite composting toilet system is the world's only six-storey system of its kind. Suppliers kept more than 360 toxic chemicals out of the materials. In April 2015 the International Living Future Institute certified it as a "Living Building".

In April 1944 the Burrells agreed with the Corporation of Glasgow that their collection would have a separate building, within four miles of Killearn in Stirlingshire and at least sixteen miles from the Glasgow Royal Exchange. In 1971 a postal strike pushed back the competition deadline, giving Barry Gasson time to finish his winning entry, made with John Meunier and Brit Andresen; all three taught at Cambridge's School of Architecture. The L-shaped plan is fitted to the collection, with large pieces such as Romanesque doorways set into its fabric. Its orientation admits as much daylight as possible while shielding fragile objects, with views over lawns to the south and woodland to the north. Visitors enter through a 16th-century stone arch in a red sandstone gable. It opened in 1983 and reopened after a major refurbishment on 29 March 2022.

The Egyptian architect Naoum Shebib designed this tower, built between 1956 and 1961, taking ancient Egyptian architecture as his inspiration. Its lattice, partly open, is meant to call up the lotus plant of the pharaohs. At 187 metres, nothing in Egypt stood taller for 37 years, until the overhead power line crossing of the Suez Canal passed it in 1998. A round viewing deck and a revolving restaurant at the top look out across greater Cairo. The tower rises on Gezira Island in the Nile, and some rank it second only to the Pyramids of Giza among the country's landmarks. Documents made public by Major General Adel Shaheen say the money came from the US government through the CIA, as a gift to Gamal Abdel Nasser. The Arab Contractors Company restored it from 2006 to 2009 for £E15 million.

This complex began as the headquarters for the third UNCTAD conference, which Santiago hosted in 1972. It was made up of a convention centre and a 22-storey tower next to it, and it was finished in just 275 days, with the help of several thousand volunteers. Through the 1980s and 1990s it was called the Edificio Diego Portales and served as a military headquarters, kept under guard and closed to the public. In early 2006 a fire destroyed part of the building, and the government of Michelle Bachelet then reconsidered what the building was for and turned it back into a cultural centre. Named after Gabriela Mistral and credited to the architect Cristian Fernández Eyzaguirre, the new centre was inaugurated in September 2010.

He Jingtang's design was picked from 344 proposals sent in by architects from around the world. Work started on 18 December 2007 and ended in November 2009. Rising 63 metres, the pavilion was the tallest structure at Expo 2010, and its likeness to an ancient Chinese crown earned it the nickname "The Oriental Crown". Its form draws on the dougong, the bracket used in traditional Chinese roofs, and on the ding, a Chinese vessel: four huge columns stand in for the legs of a ding, and the upside-down pyramid above them for its bowl. Seen from the air, the roof shows a grid that recalls the Jiugongge pattern. When the Expo was over, the building became a museum, reopening on 1 October 2012 as the China Art Museum, the largest art museum in Asia.

Zagreb hosted the Universiade in 1987, and this tower by Marijan Hržić was built that year for the event. It is a cylinder 25 metres across that steps inward four times as it rises and finishes in a radio mast. The outside is clad in dark steel, fully reflective glass and black granite. Twenty-six reinforced concrete pylons carry the tower's rim, which lets it withstand an earthquake of magnitude 7 on the Richter scale and the impact of a small aircraft. The tower belongs to a larger complex that also takes in lower office buildings, a basketball hall seating 5,400 and an art installation. The company Agram bought the tower in 2022, and renovation has been under way since 2023.

Adolf Leonard van Gendt designed the Concertgebouw, drawing inspiration from the Gewandhaus in Leipzig, finished two years before it and destroyed in 1943. Building started in 1883 on pasture then beyond the city edge, in Nieuwer-Amstel, the municipality renamed Amstelveen in 1964. The ground needed 2,186 wooden piles, each 12 to 13 metres long. The hall opened on 11 April 1888 with a concert by 120 musicians and 500 singers, playing Wagner, Handel, Bach and Beethoven. Its acoustics rank it with the finest concert halls anywhere, alongside Carnegie Hall in New York, Symphony Hall in Boston and the Musikverein in Vienna. Around 900 concerts and other events a year draw more than 700,000 people, among the highest numbers for any concert hall. For its 125th anniversary, on 11 April 2013, Queen Beatrix gave the building the royal title "Koninklijk".

Hack Kampmann and Aage Rafn designed the Politigården in 1918 in a Neoclassical manner often called Nordic Classicism. Kampmann died in June 1920 and never saw the building finished in early 1924. It is said to be the last Neoclassical building in Northern Europe. The foundations rest on 3,816 reinforced concrete piles. For the facade, Rafn took his cue from the warehouses of the London docks. The plain exterior is deliberate: it makes the colourful, carefully shaped interior all the more appealing, with dark terrazzo floors and outsized, finely made door and window frames. At the heart of the plan is a round courtyard 45 metres wide, ringed by a colonnade of 44 Doric columns.

A garden first stood on this site under the Southern Song dynasty, in its Shaoxing period (1131–1162). In 1513 Wang Xianchen, a Ming dynasty imperial envoy and poet, laid out a new one where the run-down Dahong Temple had stood, burnt during the Ming conquest. The work went on until 1526. Its name, recorded from around 1517, comes from a verse in An Idle Life by Pan Yue, a Jin dynasty scholar official. Wen Zhengming wrote an essay on the garden and, in 1533, honoured it with a set of 31 paintings and poems. Covering 78 mu (5.2 hectares, or 13 acres), it is the biggest garden in Suzhou, and some judge it the finest in southern China. Since 1997 it has been one of Suzhou's Classical Gardens, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

This hybrid funicular runs between Innsbruck's centre and the Hungerburg district. The present line, which replaced a route in use from 1906 to 2005, opened in December 2007. Zaha Hadid, already the designer of the city's Bergisel ski jump, won an open contest for the stations, which Leitner AG built. Innsbruck's city government, STRABAG and Leitner AG financed and delivered the scheme as a public-private partnership. Unusually for a funicular, the gradient keeps shifting, along the track and at the stops: a fairly flat southern stretch, with ramps into tunnels on both sides of the river crossing, gives way to a steep northern part of a more usual kind. It crosses the Inn on a 242-metre steel bridge, S-shaped and cable-stayed from two pylons, follows the north bank through St. Nikolaus, then enters the 445-metre Weiherburg tunnel.

Eero Saarinen's plans for the company's headquarters were approved in 1958, but he died soon after building began in 1962. The complex was opened on 20 April 1964, with room left to link further buildings to the south and west. Saarinen designed the first two buildings, the main block and the display building. The seven-storey main block sits in a ravine, and fourth-floor footbridges link it to the display building on the east and to Deere West on the west; Roche-Dinkeloo were hired to design Deere West in 1975, and it opened in 1978. All three are clad in glass and Cor-Ten weathering steel. The display building holds a two-level auditorium and an exhibition space where Alexander Girard made a sculpture mural. Sasaki Associates designed the landscape, which includes two lakes. Its many awards include the Twenty-five Year Award.

Hans Poelzig designed this building, put up in 1928 and 1929, in the Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity) style. It belonged to a larger scheme whose finished blocks held 170 flats and 80 shops, and it is the only block of Poelzig's quarter that came through World War II wholly intact. Bands of windows and a broad overhanging cornice at the roof give the outside a strong horizontal emphasis. The front is ochre plaster, painted with stripes in a pale yellow. Inside, in keeping with the style, materials were used sparingly, while colour and form were used for their emotional effect. The cinema began with a single screen of 1,200 seats, since divided into three, now seating 500, 68 and 43. In 2002 its restoration won the German Award for Monument Protection.

Kerstin Thompson Architects designed these eleven Fitzroy homes, finished in 2001; the scheme won the RAIA Residential Multiple Award a year later. Each home has a generous roof terrace and can be lived in flexibly. The design responds to varied neighbours: old terraces and row houses, reused industrial buildings and post-war housing towers. It takes the long plan of the traditional terrace house, with formal rooms at the street, narrow service rooms behind, a side light court and a small back garden, and turns it on end. Garages and secondary bedrooms fill the ground floor around narrow light courts, freeing the first floor for the main living space, which opens onto generous outdoor areas. The four detached rear houses have fronts that read as sections through their rooms. Skillions on either side recall Alvar Aalto, an influence on Thompson.

On 29 October 1810, the date now taken as the library's official founding, Prince Regent John, later King John VI, decreed that a royal library be set up with money from the royal treasury. Its collection came in three stages, one in 1810 and the other two the next year. The present building, designed by Sousa Aguiar, a military engineer, mixes neoclassical and Art Nouveau features in an eclectic style, with decoration by artists including Rodolfo Amoedo, Modesto Brocos, Eliseu Visconti, and Henrique and Rodolfo Bernardelli. It stands at 219 Rio Branco Avenue, on Cinelândia Square in central Rio de Janeiro, where it forms a fine group with the Municipal Theatre and the National Museum of Fine Arts. UNESCO counts it as Latin America's largest library and the seventh largest in the world, with about 9 million items.

This palace is a water pumping station. Olaf Boye, an architect from Norway, designed it in 1877 together with two engineers, Carlos Nyströmer from Sweden and John Bateman from Britain. Work began in 1887; it opened in 1894. Inside, twelve tanks over three floors held 72,000 tons of water; the building stands on 180 columns and an iron frame made in Belgium. The French Renaissance exterior is faced with more than 300,000 glazed terracotta tiles in many colours, imported from the British maker Royal Doulton, under a tin mansard roof bearing the shields of what were then Argentina's 14 provinces. It also housed the head office of state-owned Obras Sanitarias de la Nación. In 1978 the pumps were taken out and a museum moved in. One of Argentina's leading eclectic buildings, it became a National Historic Monument in 1989.

Peter Stewart, a Dallas businessman who helped found the Thanks-Giving Foundation, chose Philip Johnson for this project after a long worldwide search. Dedicated in 1976, the privately owned park anchors downtown Dallas's Thanksgiving Commercial Center district. It brings together a garden, a chapel open to all faiths, the Bullington Truck Terminal and a large part of the city's underground walkways. Sunk fifteen feet below the street behind a four-foot wall that screens out cars, the square forms a calm green island, and fountains mask city noise. Overt religious symbols are left out on purpose. The chapel spirals 90 feet (27.5 m) over the street, meant to suggest the human spirit's endless upward reach; it draws on the Great Mosque of Samarra and the ancient spiral of life. A 125-foot bridge over a cascading waterfall leads to its door.

The aristocracy of São Paulo called for a new theatre built along the lines of some of the world's best, able to stage large opera productions. The site chosen was Morro do Chá, or Tea Hill, where the newer São José Theater had stood. The engineer Ramos de Azevedo was put in charge of construction, with help from the Italian architects Cláudio and Domiziano Rossi. Following the custom of the time, most of the building materials came from Europe, and the design took the Palais Garnier in Paris as its model. Building took about eight years. Today the theatre is seen as one of the city's landmarks, for its architecture and for its history: in 1922 it hosted the Week of Modern Art, which transformed the arts in Brazil.

This museum on Djurgården island shows the 64-gun warship Vasa, which sank on her first voyage in 1628; she is the only 17th-century ship ever raised almost entirely intact. In the competition 384 architects sent models, and the winning entry, Ask ("box"), came from Göran Månsson and Marianne Dahlbäck. Prince Bertil marked the start of work on 2 November 1987 at the old naval yard, over and around its dry dock, and the museum opened in 1990. A large copper roof dominates it, topped by stylised masts that show the ship's true height when fully rigged. Outside, wooden panels are painted tar black, dark green, ochre yellow, blue and dark red; inside are similar colours and much bare concrete, the whole ceiling included. Visitors see the ship from six levels, from keel to the top of the sterncastle.

Oberlin College runs this art museum in Oberlin, Ohio, which was founded in 1917 and now holds more than 15,000 works. Cass Gilbert gave it an Italian Renaissance-style building, with ironwork by Samuel Yellin, and it carries the name of its founder, Dr. Dudley Peter Allen, an Oberlin graduate and trustee. Its Central Rotunda holds the wings for Egyptian, Greek and Roman art. The museum works chiefly as a teaching collection for the college's students, faculty and staff, and serves the surrounding community as well. In 1977 Venturi and Rauch, the firm led by Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown, added the Venturi Wing, counted among the earliest postmodern buildings in the United States and a case of their "decorated shed" idea. A two-year retrofit that began in 2011 won the building LEED Gold certification.

Herzog & de Meuron were the main designers of this Munich stadium, begun on 21 October 2002 and opened on 30 May 2005. Its skin is made of 2,760 ETFE-foil panels filled with dry air at a pressure difference of 3.5 Pa, and it was the first stadium in the world with a fully colour-changing exterior. Each panel can glow white, red or blue on its own. Other schemes are possible in theory, but Munich Police insist on one colour after drivers distracted by shifting lights caused several crashes on the nearby A9 Autobahn. Roller blinds in the roof can be drawn across during games for shade. The main entrance is from a raised esplanade, kept apart from the parking in Europe's largest underground car park. Later venues such as MetLife Stadium in New Jersey adopted the same facade lighting.

Also known as Isozaki Tower and il Dritto, "the straight one", this Milan skyscraper rises 260 metres (850 ft) over 50 floors. The Japanese architect Arata Isozaki and the Italian architect Andrea Maffei designed it as the head office of Allianz SpA, the Italian subsidiary of Allianz. The tower is a stack of eight modules, each six floors high, and every module is wrapped in triple glazing that bows slightly outward. Repeated one over another, these rounded forms make the mass seem to quiver gently as it climbs. The short ends are fully glazed, putting six panoramic lifts on show. Its idea of an endless tower has been likened to Constantin Brâncuși, who in 1937–38 placed one of his endless columns in the park at Târgu Jiu. In 2016 Emporis nominated it as the third-best skyscraper finished in 2015.

Italy's largest aquarium, and among Europe's most significant, stands in the Porto Antico, the Old Harbour of Genoa in Liguria. The Genoese architect Renzo Piano designed it with the Renzo Piano Building Workshop within the redevelopment of the city prepared for Expo 1992, which marked 500 years since Christopher Columbus sailed to the Americas. Some people see in the building a ship about to put out to sea. A design team from Cambridge Seven Associates, led by Peter Chermayeff, shaped the interiors and the first exhibits. In 1998 the aquarium grew with the addition of a ship 100 metres (330 ft) long, linked to the original building by a walkway.

In Tehran, ASA North turned the Argo Factory, put up in the early 1920s and one of Iran's first industrial factories, into a museum of contemporary art. The Pejman Foundation bought and rebuilt the factory in 2016. The architects kept the original load-bearing brick walls, which carry its industrial character. Above them sit five concrete roof volumes, lifted 50 centimetres clear of the old brickwork, which quietly hide the climate control and mechanical plant. These roofs reinterpret Tehran's traditional halabi, or metal, roofs, and each gives the programme below it a lighting mood of its own. Sanctions made concrete necessary, and it adds to the industrial feel of the site while setting the new work apart from the old. The project greatly enlarged the building, taking its area from 480 m² to 1,890 m².

The Arizona Biltmore opened in Phoenix on 23 February 1929, one of the hotels in the Biltmore chain. Albert Chase McArthur, a brother of the owners, is its architect of record, though the design is often wrongly credited to Frank Lloyd Wright.
