McArthur had been Wright's draftsman and asked him for help with the "Textile Block" system, and Wright spent four months advising on site in 1928; the blocks became a defining part of the hotel's look. Original linen drawings kept by Arizona State University's library, along with a 1929 Architectural Record feature, confirm McArthur as the architect. The main lobby above all recalls Wright, whose unit block design had appeared on four Los Angeles-area homes six years before. A stained glass design here, "Saguaro Forms and Cactus Flowers", began as a Liberty Magazine cover Wright drew in 1926.

By 2008 the earlier building on this Tokyo site had decayed, and Kengo Kuma won the contest for its successor. He thought of the nagaya houses of Edo-period Tokyo and piled modern versions of those dwellings on one another, seeking an uneven void between floors. Architizer likened the steel-based result to separate wooden buildings stacked at different angles. The voids hold technical equipment; Kuma said he hoped to make people re-think the habit of assuming floors must be flat. Japanese cedar and glass dominate outside, recalling traditional Japanese architecture with a contemporary twist. An atrium joins the first and second floors, and on the sixth the sloping roof forms a stepped theatre. Planned at 41.3 m, the center was cut to 38.9 m when the city's assembly worried about the surrounding scenery. It won a 2012 Good Design Award.

Beneath the hilltop Albert Park in central Auckland, this gallery was founded in 1888 as New Zealand's first permanent art gallery. Its original home, built of brick and plaster in the manner of the early French Renaissance, was finished in 1887 and extended in 1916. At first the building also held the Auckland public library, and the gallery started out with collections given by Governor Sir George Grey and by James Tannock Mackelvie. In the late 2000s a proposed major extension met heavy criticism in some quarters over its cost, its design and the need to take land from Albert Park. The 2011 expansion, by the Australian firm FJMT working with Auckland-based Archimedia, raised exhibition space by half, with room for as many as 900 artworks, and added dedicated spaces for education, children and families.

H. H. Richardson designed this Harvard Law School classroom building, raised in 1882–1884 in the Romanesque Revival style. It was the first building made on purpose for an American law school, and the school's first home of its own. A heavy two-storey centre is flanked by single-storey wings, and the reading room runs back from it so the plan forms a T. The entrance, framed by a Romanesque triple arch, sits deep in the flat front, beside an off-centre stair tower that pushes forward. Longmeadow sandstone clads the walls in polychrome patterns, pale stones making checkerboards on dark, reddish surfaces. The three big first-floor classrooms suited Dean Christopher Columbus Langdell's new curriculum of large core classes taught by the Socratic method. The reading room is admired for its ornamented fireplace and its tie beams carved with dragon and boar heads.

Built in Brussels in 1893, this was the first house Victor Horta designed in the Art Nouveau style, a key step in the Belgian architect's development. On a tight budget, the family wanted a simple but comfortable home, and many of the made-to-order details of Horta's other town houses were left out. Still, every typical Art Nouveau trait appears: slender iron columns on the front, sgraffito, stained glass and mosaics, plant-inspired ornament and close attention to natural light. The decoration was new in making no reference to earlier styles, yet the plan stayed fairly traditional. Of three rooms in a row, only the first and last had windows, so the middle one, mostly used for dining, was rather gloomy. The municipality of Schaerbeek bought it in the 1990s; thoroughly renovated, it is now open to the public.

Two architects, Uglješa Bogunović and Slobodan Janjić, designed this Belgrade tower with the engineer Milan Krstić, and it was finished in 1965. It was the world's only tower whose cross section was a triangle with three equal sides, and one of very few that stood on legs instead of rising straight out of the ground. Those legs made a tripod, a symbol drawn from the Serbian three-legged chair, the tronožac. An enclosed observation deck took up the height from 102 to 135 m (335–443 ft); people entered it at 122 m (400 ft), carried up by two fast lifts. Though the work was high-risk, no worker was hurt or killed, rare for a project of that size. NATO bombing of Yugoslavia destroyed the original tower on 29 April 1999, and reconstruction began on 21 December 2006.

This complex in Hamadan honours the Persian polymath Avicenna. Beside a library and a small museum it has a spindle-shaped tower 28 metres (92 ft) tall, inspired by the Kavus Tower of the Ziyarid era. Houshang Seyhoun won the competitions for both this mausoleum and Ferdowsi's before leaving for France. A grand ceremony dedicated it in May 1954, timed for the thousandth anniversary of the philosopher's birth, and the avenue in front was renamed after Avicenna too. Since the Pahlavi government had built the monument, it was at risk of being defaced; yet because Khomeini admired Avicenna, the square kept its name after the 1979 Revolution. Listed as part of Iran's national heritage on 11 May 1997, the complex is now in the care of the Cultural Heritage, Handicrafts and Tourism Organization of Iran.

The Ayala Foundation runs this private museum in Makati, Metro Manila, which shows archaeological, ethnographic, historical, fine arts, numismatic and church collections. Fernando M. Zobel, a Philippine abstract painter, imagined it in the 1950s as a museum of the country's history and iconography. The Filipinas Foundation, the body now called the Ayala Foundation, founded it in April 1967. Its present home, a six-storey building of granite, steel and glass, came from the firm Leandro V. Locsin Partners under Leandro Y. Locsin Jr., whose father had designed the earlier museum. It stands where the original did; pulling down the old building drew some criticism from heritage conservationists. The new museum was formally dedicated on 28 September 2004, the Ayala Corporation's 170th anniversary, and after a two-year renovation it reopened on 4 December 2021.

Bahá'ís call this House of Worship, on the edge of Kampala, Uganda, the "mother Temple of Africa". When Bahá'ís in Iran faced a wave of persecution in 1955 and an earlier plan became impossible, two other Houses of Worship were announced, in Kampala and Sydney. A first design was turned down, and Charles Mason Remey drew a new one in Haifa, directed by Shoghi Effendi; it was approved in August 1956. Dedicated in 1961, it was the third Bahá'í House of Worship finished anywhere and then East Africa's tallest building. Italian mosaic tiles cover the dome and Belgian tiles the lower roof, while the wall panels have windows of German glass in green, pale blue and amber. Ugandan timber went into the doors and benches, and Ugandan stone into the walls. Against earthquakes, the foundation reaches 3 metres down.

George Chakhava and Zurab Jalaghania designed this Tbilisi building for the Georgian SSR's Ministry of Highway Construction, and it was finished in 1975. In the 1970s Chakhava was himself Georgia's Deputy Minister of Highway Construction, so he was both client and lead architect and could pick the site that best suited the design. The idea was to take up and cover less ground, giving the space beneath back to nature. A forest served as the model: the cores act as trunks and the horizontal parts as crowns. El Lissitzky's Wolkenbügel, the horizontal skyscrapers he designed in 1924, look very much alike. Its fair-faced concrete and sharp geometric volumes mean it can also be counted as Brutalist. The Bank of Georgia bought the building in 2007, and that same year it was made an Immovable Monument under the National Monuments Acts.

Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed this International Style library on Hewitt Quadrangle at Yale University, completed in 1963. A glass tower of book stacks, six storeys above ground, rises inside a windowless façade carried on four monolithic corner piers. The marble, from Danby, Vermont, was milled just 1.25 inches (32 mm) thick so that daylight seeps through in a soft golden amber glow. Bunshaft credited the idea to stone he had taken for onyx in an Istanbul palace, in fact the alabaster of the Dolmabahçe Palace hammam. A hexagonal grid of Woodbury granite veneer from Vermont frames the marble panels and is fixed to a steel structure. Height, width and length follow the Platonic ratio 1:2:3. Around the stack tower runs a raised public exhibition mezzanine, where one of the 48 surviving Gutenberg Bibles is on show.

Charles Correa designed this multi-arts complex and museum in Bhopal. The Government of Madhya Pradesh, through its Department of Culture, set it up and funds it, while an autonomous body of 12 members, the Bharat Bhavan Trust, runs it. Facing the Upper Lake, it opened in 1982, inaugurated on 13 February by Indira Gandhi, then Prime Minister. It brings together several art galleries, workshops for graphic printing and for ceramics, an open-air amphitheatre, a studio theatre and an auditorium. There is also a museum of tribal and folk art, along with libraries given over to Indian poetry, classical music and folk music.

Steven Holl won a 1999 international competition for this addition to the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City. With design partner Chris McVoy, he set five glass pavilions, called lenses, east of the original building by Wight and Wight. They crown the Bloch Building, an underground structure of 165,000 sq ft (15,300 m²). Placed at right angles to the main building, the addition was meant to engage the sculpture garden and join art, architecture and landscape in one experience. It houses galleries for contemporary, African and photographic work and special exhibitions, a cafe, the Spencer Art Reference Library and the Isamu Noguchi Sculpture Court. The plan was controversial during construction. It cost about $95 million and opened on 9 June 2007; that year Time magazine put it top of its list of ten best new and upcoming architectural marvels.

Boeri Studio, the team of Stefano Boeri with Gianandrea Barreca and Giovanni La Varra, designed this pair of residential skyscrapers in Milan's Porta Nuova district, both inaugurated in 2014. What sets them apart is planting: more than ninety species, tall shrubs and trees among them, spread across the facades. The towers share 800 trees, plus 5,000 shrubs and 1,500 perennials, hence the name, meaning "Vertical Forest"; the greenery helps cut smog and gives off oxygen. It also evens out indoor temperatures through the year by shading rooms and blocking harsh winds, and it screens the interiors from street noise and dust. Boeri has named a 1957 novel by Italo Calvino, The Baron in the Trees, as the inspiration; its hero leaves the ground to live out his life up in the trees. It won the 2014 International Highrise Award.

Sir Albert Richardson designed Bracken House, a late work of modern classicism, on a cleared bomb site southeast of St Paul's Cathedral. Its pink sandstone from Hollington, Staffordshire, nods to the pink paper of the Financial Times, set off by red brick, bronze windows and a copper roof gone green. Frank Dobson and Philip Bentham designed the astronomical clock over the Cannon Street entrance. In 1987 it became the first post-war building in England to be listed, at Grade II, rising to Grade II* in 2013. From 1988 to 1992 Michael Hopkins and Partners kept the old north and south ranges but swapped the central printing hall for glass and structural gunmetal on a Hollington sandstone base, its boxy oriels drawn from Liverpool's Oriel Chambers of 1864. The newspaper returned in spring 2019, after a refurbishment by John Robertson Architects.

Colin St John Wilson designed the new British Library with his wife, MJ Long, and no larger public building went up in the United Kingdom during the 20th century. Elizabeth II officially opened the purpose-built home beside St Pancras station on 25 June 1998. A broad piazza fronts Euston Road, with public art including large sculptures by Antony Gormley and by Eduardo Paolozzi, whose bronze takes William Blake's picture of Isaac Newton as its source. At the centre stands a six-storey glass tower, inspired by a similar one in the Beinecke Library, holding the King's Library: 65,000 printed volumes plus pamphlets, manuscripts and maps that George III collected between 1763 and 1820. Its reading rooms, eleven in all, began opening while books were still being moved in. The building was listed Grade I on 1 August 2015.

Ralph Erskine designed this long, unbroken block of 620 maisonettes in Byker, Newcastle upon Tyne. The site had held nearly 1,200 Victorian slum terraces, condemned as unfit to live in in 1953 and pulled down from 1966; the Wall and low-rise homes south of it replaced them. Design began in 1968; building ran from 1969 to 1982. The architects kept an office on site to build trust with existing residents. The tall block was meant to shelter the site from a planned motorway that was never built. Fairly cheap concrete, brick and timber were used, with bright colours and brick bands marking each floor. Its Functionalist Romantic style, with textured facades, coloured panels, care for context and modest height, broke with the Brutalist high-rise orthodoxy of the time. Fewer than one in five original residents ended up living there.

This large Edwardian city hall of 1905 stands in central Cape Town, on the Grand Parade, with the Castle to its east. It is built of honey-coloured oolitic limestone brought from Bath in England, and much of its other material, fixtures and fittings included, also came from Europe. A city hall was first suggested in 1887, around Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, as a tribute. In 1893, after the council had approved a scheme, H S Greaves, chief architect of Public Works, judged an open competition. The architects Harry Austin Reid and Frederick George Green won it, with T. Howard and F. G. Scott as builders. A turret clock in the tower strikes the hours and plays the Westminster quarters, and the carillon, with 22 added bells, was installed as a First World War memorial.

Formally the Transitional Cathedral, this building is the interim pro-cathedral of the Anglican Diocese of Christchurch, standing in for ChristChurch Cathedral after the 2011 earthquake badly damaged it. Shigeru Ban, the Japanese architect described as a "disaster architect", designed it without fee together with the local firm Warren and Mahoney, and it opened in August 2013. It takes its nickname from the more than 90 large cardboard tubes that make up its walls and roof. The A-frame rises 24 metres (79 ft) and stands on containers 6 metres (20 ft) long. It is built of cardboard, wood and glass. The site once held the church of St John the Baptist, the first that Anglicans in Christchurch built in permanent materials, demolished after the same earthquake.

San Francisco's third Saint Mary's Cathedral, finished in 1970 on Cathedral Hill, replaced the second, built in 1891 and lost to fire in 1962. The first options shown drew negative feedback, and the archdiocese then brought Pier Luigi Nervi of Italy and the American Pietro Belluschi into the team. The aim was a cathedral for very large congregations, where even big crowds could surround the altar, and a statement of God's presence, in beauty, within the earthly city. Its saddle roof is made of eight hyperbolic paraboloid segments, square at its base and forming a cross at the top. The building is 255 feet (78 m) square and 190 feet (58 m) high, under a golden cross of 55 feet (17 m). Some likened the roof to a washing-machine agitator and called it "Our Lady of Maytag".

Nicknamed the Balance Building, this brutalist exhibition centre marks the entrance to the Centro Administrativo da Bahia in Salvador, Brazil. João Filgueiras Lima designed it in 1974, chosen by Mário Kertész, then secretary for planning, science and technology. Its rectangular concrete body, 52 by 9 metres (171 by 30 ft), hangs 5 metres (16 ft) above the ground on cables from two matching towers at its sides. Each tower holds a cylindrical shaft 4 metres (13 ft) wide, one for stairs and one for a lift. At one end, an exhibition hall has a pyramid-shaped ceiling with a skylight; at the other, an amphitheatre turns that space upside down. To prove it was stable, the architect and Kertész stood beneath it as the temporary supports came away. By 2021 the building stood unused and in poor repair.

Alcoa commissioned these twin towers in Los Angeles from Minoru Yamasaki, and they were completed in 1975. With their paired arrangement, vertical black and grey lines and aluminium skins, they recall his original World Trade Center in New York. Each sits on an unusual triangular plan, and together they stand out as landmarks seen clearly across the Los Angeles Westside. Beneath them lies a parking garage counted among the largest underground garages anywhere, with room for roughly 5,000 cars. No buildings in California are taller except those in Downtown Los Angeles and San Francisco. On television, they were where two separate fictional private detectives of the 1980s kept their offices.

Set into the red rock buttes at Sedona, Arizona, this Roman Catholic chapel went up between 1954 and 1956. Marguerite Brunswig Staude, a local rancher and sculptor, commissioned it; the newly built Empire State Building had inspired her in 1932 to create such a church. August K. Strotz of Anshen & Allen designed it, with Richard Hein as project architect. Design began in 1953; seeing the site, the architects said nature had done everything and they need only understate. The main feature is a 90 ft (27.4 m) iron cross on the southwest wall, both decorative and structural. Walls and cross are reinforced coarse-aggregate concrete a foot thick, the walls sandblasted inside and out to expose the aggregate. Smoky grey glass at both ends cuts glare. The AIA gave it an Award of Honor in 1957.

New York architect Bruce Price designed the Château Frontenac in the Château style for the Canadian Pacific Railway, which built it. Opened in 1893, it was among the first grand railway hotels in Canada. It sits at 1, rue des Carrières, where Quebec City's old Upper Town ends to the east, on the raised promontory that pushes out into the Saint Lawrence River. The hotel has 18 floors and stands 79.9 metres (262 ft) tall, made higher by ground already 54 metres (177 ft) up. Terrasse Dufferin curls around it from northeast to southeast, looking over the river, and two public streets run through the building. It has been enlarged three times, the last major expansion coming in 1993. Canada made it a National Historic Site in 1981, and it is thought to be the most photographed hotel anywhere.

Les Choux de Créteil are ten round towers, each 15 storeys high, in Créteil, a suburb of Paris. Gérard Grandval designed them, and they were completed in 1974; the nickname, "the cabbages", comes from their oddly shaped balconies. The project began in 1966 on land that for a century had grown much of the vegetables eaten in Paris. The form was meant to be practical: living spaces sit nearer the windows, and the 2-metre-tall balconies give residents outdoor access and privacy at once. Those curved balconies were to hold ornamental plants and small trees so that the buildings would change with the seasons, but that part was never carried out. On 16 December 2008 the French Ministry of Culture recognised the group as "Heritage of the 20th Century", when it was seen as a symbol of 1970s French architecture.

Spread over 13.5 acres (5.5 ha) in Boston's Back Bay, where Massachusetts and Huntington avenues meet, this plaza belongs to the Christian Science church. Open space takes up 10.4 acres, along with a children's fountain, a reflecting pool measuring 690 by 100 ft (210 by 30 m) and six buildings. These include the First Church of Christ, Scientist, made up of the original Mother Church of 1894 and the Church Extension of 1906. When the site grew in the 1970s, Araldo Cossutta, working at I. M. Pei & Associates, designed three more, among them the 26-storey former Administration Building of 1972, now 177 Huntington. Church staff worked there until 2008, and it is now leased as offices. In 2011 the Boston Landmarks Commission named the plaza a Boston Landmark, noting how heavily the public uses it.

Frank Gehry designed this venue in the city of Concord together with the landscape architect Peter Walker, and it opened in 1975 under the name Concord Pavilion, with room for 12,500 people. Gehry came back to design its renovation and expansion in 1996, which brought more parking and more seats. The City of Concord owns the Pavilion, and Live Nation operates it. Its programme mixes concerts with local community events, among them a jazz festival held every year, and graduation ceremonies for the area's high schools.

CopenHill in Amager, Copenhagen, joins a waste-to-energy plant that makes both heat and power, called a new resource handling centre, to a recreational facility 85 m (279 ft) tall, in clear sight of the city centre. The plant began working on 30 March 2017. Bjarke Ingels Group designed the sports facility, whose sloping roof serves all year as an artificial ski slope, a hiking route and a climbing wall; it opened to the public on 4–6 October 2019. Made by Walltopia, the climbing wall reaches 80 metres, the tallest permanent one in the world. The chimney was first meant to release its exhaust not continuously but as rings of "smoke", really water vapour, but technical difficulties ended the idea. At the fourteenth World Architecture Festival, it was named World Building of the Year for 2021.

The Danish Maritime Museum used to be at Kronborg Castle. In October 2013 it opened in new premises by Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG), built around a former dry dock in Helsingør. Height limits set to protect views of nearby Kronborg led BIG to go underground, where the museum fills 7,600 m² (82,000 sq ft); the Dutch firm Kossmann.dejong designed the interior. The old dock, 150 m long, 25 m wide and 9 m deep (490 by 82 by 30 ft), suited the scheme well, though its walls had to be strengthened before the museum could be built around its edges. The dock itself stays empty, crossed by ramps and bridges that lead into the museum and its exhibitions. The whole is meant to feel like the deck of a ship.

Eero Saarinen designed the first two structures of this headquarters in Moline, the main building and the display building. His plans were approved in 1958, but he died soon after work began in 1962. The complex opened on 20 April 1964, with provision for linking more buildings to the south and west. Set in a ravine, the seven-storey main building is reached by footbridges at fourth-floor level, one leading east to the display building and the other west to Deere West, which Roche-Dinkeloo was hired to design in 1975 and which opened in 1978. Glass and Cor-Ten weathering steel clad all three. The display building holds a two-level auditorium and an exhibition area with Alexander Girard's sculpture mural. Sasaki Associates designed the landscape, with its two lakes. Its many awards include a Twenty-five Year Award honouring architectural excellence.

Finished in 1965, this federal tower in Downtown Albuquerque, New Mexico, holds both government offices and a courthouse. At first it carried a plain descriptive name; in 1976 it was renamed in honour of Dennis Chavez, who served for many years as a U.S. Senator. The Albuquerque firm Flatow, Moore, Bryan, and Fairburn designed it, having already done other local high-rises such as the Simms Building and the Bank of the West Tower. Its steel frame is faced in polished granite, and New Mexico marble lines the ground-floor lobby. The building rises 197 feet (60 m) over 13 floors above ground, with a basement and an underground car park below. In 2023 it was added to the National Register of Historic Places.

Ben Thompson founded Design Research (D/R) in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1953; the shop introduced the idea of the lifestyle store, selling furnishings by designers including Alvar Aalto, Marcel Breuer, Joe Colombo and Hans Wegner. In 1969 Thompson moved it to a new home of 24,000 square feet (2,200 m²) in Harvard Square, designed by his own firm on a block later known as "Architects' Corner". Its five storeys are flat concrete slabs on interior columns, wrapped in frameless tempered glass. Butting glass together without frames or mullions was unprecedented, and it let D/R be almost a building "without architecture". It was conceived as a glass showcase faceted like a diamond. Reviews were warm at once, one saying it pointed to a way of building in glass that could make a warmer city, adding colour, light and optimism to street life.

Frank Lloyd Wright supplied the design for this Usonian house on a large site at the western edge of Columbus, Wisconsin, looking over farmland. It was built in 1955–1956 for a Columbus attorney, E. Clarke Arnold, and his wife Julia, whose family was growing. Low and single-storey, it is built of Wisconsin limestone, glass and redwood board and batten. All angles are 60° or 120°, giving parallelogram modules with equal 4-foot (1.2 m) sides. As first built, two wings met at 120° in a V, one for living and one for bedrooms, joined by a central core with the kitchen, utilities and fireplace mass. Instead of the Cherokee Red typical of Usonian homes, its floors were golden ocher. A second, partly revised design, drafted by the Wright apprentice and Taliesin Fellow John H. "Jack" Howe, set the final Y-shaped plan.

Eden Court stands beside the River Ness in Inverness, Scotland, and works as a theatre, cinema and arts venue. Law Dunbar and Naismith designed a new building that took in the Gothic Bishop's Palace, a residence that also gave the venue its name; in Scottish Gaelic it is Cùirt an Easbaig, "Bishop's Court". The actor Andrew Cruickshank opened it formally on 15 April 1976. Page\Park Architects and Robertson Construction later refurbished and extended it in full, adding a second theatre, two cinema screens, two dance and performance studios, better dressing and green rooms, and more offices. On reopening in November 2007 it became Scotland's largest combined arts centre. The main hall, now the Empire Theatre, seats just under 840, and the OneTouch Theatre about 270.

Stanley Roscoe designed Hamilton's city hall in the International style, and it was officially opened on 21 November 1960. The eight-storey building, 34.0 m tall, stands in the downtown core where Main Street West meets Bay Street South, with the FirstOntario Concert Hall and the Art Gallery of Hamilton across the street. The Pigott Construction Company built it for 9.4 million dollars. In 2005 Hamilton City Council named it a heritage structure, and the Italian glass tile mosaics on the outside are among the elements the listing protects. In May 2007 the council told staff to go ahead with renovating the building, and the project's launch phase got under way in June 2008.

Philip Johnson was asked for a private house that would one day become a museum for the art of Carmen and David Lloyd Kreeger, and the family lived in it from 1967 to 1990. On Foxhall Road, a residential area, it now shows the couple's nineteenth- and twentieth-century paintings and sculpture, bought between 1952 and 1988. Johnson's idea was a modern take on the Roman villa, with sculpture terraces, reflecting pools and gardens inside and out. Groin-vaulted cubes, each 22 ft (6.7 m) on a side, are grouped asymmetrically, and they could be adapted as living space, gallery or both. Seventeen concrete domes form the roof; three crown the two-storey Great Hall, amplifying sound naturally for chamber and piano music. Facing the street are walls of hand-picked Italian travertine, while glass walls open onto the wooded grounds.

This headquarters for Marisfrolg, a fashion brand from Shenzhen, stands in the city's Longhua District in Guangdong Province, China. The New Zealand studio Architecture Van Brandenburg (AVB) drew its forms from nature: tropical plants and the spiky outer shells of insects shaped the biomimetic design. Steel and reinforced concrete make up the main frame, while the outside is covered in a mosaic of tile, broken brick and stone. Work started in 2008, and the building took fifteen years to finish. Its architecture has been read as echoing the early work of Antoni Gaudí and of Santiago Calatrava, and the project drew notice at the 14th Venice Biennale of Architecture.

In 1963 King Mahendra ordered the old Narayanhiti Palace in Kathmandu replaced. Benjamin Polk, an American architect living in India, designed the new one, drawing on Nepalese architectural styles so that it would stand as a national symbol, and building work ended in 1969. Until the 2006 revolution it was the home and main workplace of Nepal's monarch and hosted state occasions; in 2008 the complex became a museum. Its 3,794 m² of floor space divides into guest, state and private wings. A central tower rises over the front, growing out of the Hindu temple below it. In the Gorkha Baithak, built on Hindu temple lines, a 48-foot chandelier hangs from a pagoda-style ceiling 60 feet high, carried on four concrete columns that stand for the Nāga and are decorated with the guardian demigods Astha Matrikas and Ashta Bhairava.

The Japanese architect Arata Isozaki designed this multi-purpose indoor arena, which opened in 1990 within Barcelona's Olympic Ring complex in Catalonia. Its name means St. George's Palace in English. With room for up to 17,960 people, no indoor arena in Spain is larger. At the 1992 Summer Olympics it served as a principal venue, staging artistic gymnastics, handball and volleyball. Because the hall adapts so readily, it now hosts many kinds of indoor sport alongside concerts and other cultural events. When the FINA World Championships made it their main venue, a temporary pool built to regulation size was put in.

Glenn Howells Architects won a competition run by The Crown Estate for this visitor centre in Windsor Great Park, which opened in June 2006. The scheme set out to make a gateway to the listed gardens that would reflect the park's character and quality. All the visitor facilities sit together beneath one gridshell roof, which forms a chain of connected spaces. The roof is built of larch and clad in sustainably sourced green oak from the Windsor Estate, which also supplied the timber for the floor. On the entrance side the building rests on an earth structure holding the support rooms; toward the garden it is lifted on legs to make the most of the views. The Savill Building was on the shortlist for the 2007 RIBA Stirling Prize.

The 1963 earthquake in Skopje destroyed the original station buildings along with much of the city, and this building, now the main railway station and bus terminal of North Macedonia's capital, was put up afterwards. Kenzō Tange, the Japanese architect it is credited to, wrote the plan for rebuilding the city after the disaster, though that plan was never carried out in full. Finished in 1981 in the Brutalist style, the station lifts ten tracks onto a huge concrete bridge 2 km long. Pillars of concrete built to withstand earthquakes hold it up, and a tubular hall roofs the platforms. Counters and waiting rooms lie beneath, behind glass facades facing the street, with bare concrete walls and ceilings inside. The old station, its clock stopped at 5.17, now houses the Museum of the City of Skopje.

In 1976, after the central government decided to enrich the city's cultural life, the Taipei Municipal Government set out to build a high-standard museum. The result, designed by the architect Kao Er-pan, opened on 8 August 1983 on land once used by the United States Taiwan Defense Command, and it lies within the Taipei Expo Park. No museum in Taiwan had been built for showing contemporary art before it. Its architecture adapts the ideas of Japan's Metabolist Movement to a local setting. In 1996 the building held the largest Taipei Biennial ever staged, titled "The Quest for Identity", which filled every floor with the work of 110 artists.

Finished in 1933, this Art Deco house just east of Meguro Station, in Tokyo's Minato ward, was home to the family of Prince Asaka Yasuhiko until 1947. Credit for the building goes to Gondo Yukichi of the Imperial Household Ministry's Works Bureau, while many of the rooms follow plans sent by Henri Rapin, and it has decorative glass work by René Lalique. After World War II it was the Prime Minister's official residence from 1947 to 1950 and then served as a State Guest House until 1974. It first opened as a museum in 1983. The name comes from the garden and sculptures around it, since teien means Japanese garden. Following major renovation in 2013 it reopened in November 2014, with a new annex, designed in collaboration with Hiroshi Sugimoto, holding modern galleries, a café and a shop.

Designed by Viljo Revell and engineered by Hannskarl Bandel, the city hall opened in 1965 together with Nathan Phillips Square, the public square planned alongside it. Mayor Nathan Phillips, the square's namesake, pushed for the design competition to admit entries from abroad; the local architects' association had to change its rules, making it Ontario's first architectural competition open to international architects. Two curved towers of unequal height, built of poured concrete, wrap around a saucer-shaped council chamber set on a two-storey podium. The east tower rises 27 storeys (99.5 m) and the west 20 (79.4 m). Their windowless backs carry 4,000 ribbed, concave concrete panels inlaid with strips of Botticino marble, meant to "sparkle when floodlit." A shallow dome on 23 pairs of V-shaped supports covers the chamber. In 1991 the council protected it under the Ontario Heritage Act.

Augusto H. Álvarez's 166 m tower was built as the headquarters of La Latinoamericana, Seguros, S.A., an insurer dating from 1906. It opened in 1956 and stayed the tallest finished building in Mexico for almost 27 years, until the 214 m Torre Ejecutiva Pemex was completed in 1982. Frequent earthquakes and muddy ground called for a steel frame set on deep piles. Before work began, its engineers ran soil mechanics studies on the site and designed to suit, a step that was new then but is routine, even required, today. In 1985 the tower came through the magnitude 8.1 earthquake undamaged while several other downtown buildings were harmed. No public viewing deck in Mexico City is higher than the one on its 44th floor, and the tower's central position, height and history make it one of the city's key landmarks.

Spain's Ministry of Labour built this complex in Gijón between 1946 and 1955 to educate children orphaned when their parents died working in the mines. At 270,000 m² it is the largest building in Spain, bigger even than the Monastery of El Escorial, and is seen as the most important 20th-century building in Asturias. Luis Moya modelled it on the Parthenon in Athens and turned the main gate away from the city, so visitors from Gijón had to walk around it before entering. Everything is organised around an open courtyard of 150 by 50 m. The church dome weighs 2,300 tons and reaches 32 m above the floor, and the tower is the tallest building in Asturias and Spain's tallest stone building. Left empty in the 1980s, it was restored from 2001 to 2007 and now houses several cultural institutions.

The British Raj built this memorial to Queen Victoria, Empress of India from 1876 until 1901, between 1906 and 1921. William Emerson designed it in the Indo-Saracenic style, combining British and Mughal features with ideas drawn from Venetian, Egyptian and Deccani building. Built of white Makrana marble, the building covers 103 by 69 m and rises 56 m. It recalls the Taj Mahal in its dome, chattris capped by octagonal domes, tall portals, a terrace and domed corner towers. Curzon set the central chamber's diameter at 20 m on purpose, so that it would slightly outdo the Taj Mahal. A 4.9 m Angel of Victory by Esch, cast by the Cheltenham firm H.H. Martyn & Co., stands on the central dome. Today the building is a museum under India's Ministry of Culture, within 26 hectares of gardens.

Arata Isozaki designed this arts centre in Yamaguchi, built from August 2001 to April 2003 and opened that year. The two-storey building is 170 m long, 50 m wide and 20 m tall, under a wave-shaped roof that takes its cue from the ridgelines of the mountains around it. Inside, the functions are laid out side by side: a theatre, gallery, cinema and library. It houses the Yamaguchi City Central Library and a contemporary art museum that a city cultural foundation operates. YCAM keeps no art collection; instead it keeps producing new media art shows, theatre and dance, films, concerts, workshops, talks and conferences. Its multi-purpose hall, Studio A, was picked in 2008 by Japan's Sound Engineers and Artists Society as one of its "Top 100 Excellent Halls", the only venue chosen in the Chugoku and Shikoku regions.

This office building on Rustaveli Avenue in Tbilisi went up in 1931 as the headquarters of Zarya Vostoka, a newspaper published in Russian. The Armenian architect David Chisliev designed it in the constructivist style. Until 1913 the plot held a wooden circus building that belonged to the Nikitin brothers. In later years the publishing house Merani moved in. The building was protected as a monument of national importance until 2007, and the renovation now under way is, in the view of some critics, a threat to its historical fabric.

Ernő Goldfinger designed 2 Willow Road as his own family home, the largest of three terraced houses in Hampstead, London, completed in the summer of 1939 in concrete faced with red brick. A revised scheme grouped the three into a single block while keeping the concrete frame that was central to his Modernist thinking. Part of the frame sits outside, freeing the interior to stay open and uncluttered, perhaps after Adolf Loos's Raumplan ideas. The engineer Ove Arup designed the spiral stair at its core. Goldfinger designed much of the furniture, and the rooms hold 20th-century works by Max Ernst, Henry Moore, Marcel Duchamp, Bridget Riley, Eduardo Paolozzi and Prunella Clough. The National Trust has managed the house since 1995 and opens it to visitors; it was among the first Modernist buildings the Trust acquired, which caused some controversy.

78 Derngate is a Georgian house of 1815 in Northampton's Cultural Quarter, now listed Grade II*. In 1916 and 1917 Charles Rennie Mackintosh extensively remodelled its interior for the businessman Wenman Joseph Bassett-Lowke, as the first home of his married life. Mackintosh's designs here are seen as among the earliest Art Deco work in Britain. At the back, an extension carries two raised balconies that, in 1916, looked out over meadows at the edge of Northampton. The extension may not be Mackintosh's alone: recent research suggests Bassett-Lowke and Alexander Ellis Anderson, a local architect who oversaw the remodelling, may have helped design it. Restoration to Mackintosh's original scheme began in 2002, led by John McAslan + Partners with specialist contractors who restored or recreated period features. After eighteen months of work, the house opened to visitors in late 2003.

Aino Aalto and Alvar Aalto designed this Helsinki house as a shared home and workplace, finished in August 1936. It forms an L with an open, functionalist plan: the studio on the ground floor, the living quarters upstairs. The slim office wing is lightly rendered brick painted white, while the living part is wrapped in thin, dark-stained timber battens. The roof is flat; a big terrace opens south from the courtyard side. The street front is closed and severe, eased by creepers and a slate path to the door. The house points ahead to the later Villa Mairea and hints at a romantic functionalism. In 1955 the growing office moved to Studio Aalto nearby; both are now run as public museums by the Alvar Aalto Museum. In July 2026 it joined UNESCO's World Heritage list in the Aalto Works entry.

Abdullah Al-Faisal commissioned this mixed-use complex in Riyadh's Al-Olaya district, appointing Foster + Partners in 1994; building began in 1997 and finished in 2000. At 267 m, its tower was Saudi Arabia's first skyscraper and the country's tallest from 2000 to 2002. Its form takes its cue from the Umar ibn al-Khattab Mosque in Al-Jouf Province. Besides the central office tower, the complex holds a three-storey shopping mall, a five-star hotel and a hall for banquets and conferences. Thirty floors of offices rise to an observation deck 200 m up, looking out across Riyadh. In the lobby is stained glass by Brian Clarke, made with Norman Foster. Clarke's first designs, from 1994, joined leaded glass with a linked glass mosaic floor and grew into a five-storey glass art skin, seen as a landmark in the history of stained glass.

This museum and research centre in Santillana del Mar, Cantabria, exists to conserve, study and share knowledge of the cave of Altamira, which UNESCO lists as a World Heritage Site. The building, designed by the architect Juan Navarro Baldeweg, went up in 2001. Part of what it shows is the Neocave, or New Altamira Cave: a man-made copy of the original caves, created so that huge numbers of visitors would not harm the real ones. The paintings in the copy were made with the same techniques that Paleolithic painters used. The centre belongs to the National Museums of Spain and comes under the Ministry of Culture.

This memorial in Lucknow honours B. R. Ambedkar, the jurist who became India's first law and justice minister, and also Kanshi Ram, Birsa Munda, Jyotirao Phule, Shahu of Kolhapur and Narayana Guru. Uttar Pradesh's Chief Minister, Mayawati, first opened it to the public on 14 April 2008. The design is credited to Hafeez Contractor, and the whole complex is built of red sandstone brought from Rajasthan. Visitors come in through the Pratibimb Sthal, the main entrance, lined with 62 elephant statues on either side, 124 in all. Behind it, the Drashya Sthal sits on an 80-foot pyramid-like structure with water flowing down from its top, giving a viewpoint from which the shrines, structures and grounds read as one. The Ambedkar statue takes as its model the sculpture of Abraham Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.

Raja Man Singh originally built Amer Fort, and Jai Singh I enlarged it in the early 1600s. Its ramparts, gates and cobbled paths overlook Maota Lake, the palace's main source of water. It is a fine case of Rajput architecture, with Mughal influence in parts. Built of red sandstone and marble, it rises over four levels, each set around a courtyard. Its parts include the Diwan-e-Aam for public audiences, a raised platform with 27 colonnades and elephant-shaped capitals; the Diwan-e-Khas for private ones; the Sheesh Mahal, or mirror palace; and the Sukh Niwas, cooled by breezes passing over an indoor water cascade. A tunnel, meant as a wartime escape route, links it to Jaigarh Fort, and the two count as one complex. Since 2013 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site within the Hill Forts of Rajasthan.

Norman Foster designed this museum with Chris Wise of Arup, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 1 August 1997; the project cost £13.5 million in total. The brief wanted a landmark that would still sit quietly behind the aircraft collection, control the climate inside and stay cheap to run. Its size was set by the collection's B-52 Stratofortress, whose wings span 61 m and whose tail stands 16 m tall. The result is a slice of a torus: a curving roof of concrete, 90 m wide, 100 m deep and 18.5 m high. That roof is a two-layer shell assembled from 924 precast reinforced concrete pieces. The building won Foster and Partners the 1998 Stirling Prize, and the judges praised it as a big clear-span hangar, simple yet rich in imagery.

Diego Rivera designed the Anahuacalli, whose Nahuatl name means "house surrounded by water", as a temple of the arts that would keep his vast collection of pre-Hispanic pieces safe while showing the finest of them in the main building. Its forms draw on Mesoamerican structures, chiefly mixing Mayan and Toltec influences, though Rivera called the style a blend of Aztec, Mayan and "Traditional Rivera". It is built of volcanic stone from the Xitle eruption, quarried from the very land the museum stands on. Inside, twenty-three rooms are spread over three levels. On the level meant to represent the Underworld, narrow windows let in only dim daylight. Building work ended in 1963, and the museum opened on 18 September 1964.

Antwerp's main railway station is one of Belgium's key hubs and one of four in the country on the high-speed network. Louis Delacenserie's stone-clad terminal building went up between 1895 and 1905, replacing the first station. A vast dome over the waiting hall earned it the nickname spoorwegkathedraal, "railroad cathedral". The engineer Clément Van Bogaert designed the train hall, first built of iron and glass: 185 m long, 43 to 44 m high and covering 12,000 m²; the station's height was needed to clear steam locomotive smoke. A tunnel between Antwerpen-Berchem to the south and Antwerpen-Dam to the north passes beneath it, with platforms on two underground levels. It is widely seen as Belgium's finest railway building, though its many influences make its style hard to name. In 2011 it won a Grand Prix at the Europa Nostra Awards.

The Art Gallery of Alberta ran an architectural competition in 2005, which 27 architects entered, and that September picked the design of the Los Angeles architect Randall Stout. Between 2007 and 2010 the building went through a CA$88 million redevelopment, reopening on 31 January 2010. Around two-thirds of the older museum was kept, mainly as the base and lower floors of the new one. The 8,000 m² building on Churchill Square in downtown Edmonton is built with patinated zinc and stainless steel. A 190 m steel ribbon on the outside is meant to evoke the North Saskatchewan River, the aurora and the city's geography, and it twists back on itself like a Möbius strip as it passes into and through glass walls. In 2012 the Chicago Athenaeum gave Stout an American Architecture Award for it.

The Asian Art Museum's home across from San Francisco's Civic Center began life as the city's main library, a Beaux-Arts building that George Kelham designed in 1917 and one of San Francisco's most important historic structures. The museum had been in the park before, and closed during its final year there to make the move. In 1995 Chong-Moon Lee, an entrepreneur from Silicon Valley, gave $15 million to start fundraising for a new building. The Italian architect Gae Aulenti led the renovation, which included a seismic upgrade using base isolation, and the museum reopened on 20 March 2003. Its collection holds over 20,000 objects, some as old as 6,000 years. In July 2023 the Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion was added, opening with an exhibition by the Japanese art collective teamLab.

Ragıp Buluç designed this 125 m communications and observation tower in central Ankara, and it was built between 1987 and 1989. Prime Minister Turgut Özal opened it on 13 October 1989. Standing in the hilltop Çankaya district, it is visible from nearly all of the city on a clear day, and it ranks among Ankara's main landmarks. At the top are an open terrace and Sevilla, a revolving restaurant that turns a full circle once an hour. The name joins two Turkish words: kule, meaning tower, and ata, meaning ancestor (or father in Old Turkic), often used as a nickname for Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the Republic of Turkey's founder and first President.

Designed by Charles Bohringer and William T. Leighton, Auckland's Civic Theatre was put up by Fletcher Construction in eight months and opened on 20 December 1929. It was New Zealand's first purpose-built atmospheric cinema, and no larger one survives in Australasia. Lighting and decoration turn its ceiling into a night sky with twinkling stars, so the audience seems to sit outdoors. The foyer looks to India, with domed ceilings, twisted columns and seated Buddhas; the auditorium imitates a Moorish garden of spires, minarets, turrets and tiled roofs, with two life-size panthers on the proscenium arch. After lobbying by the Friends of the Civic, the council spent $41.8 million on a major renovation and two years of conservation. The theatre reopened for film and stage on its 70th birthday, 20 December 1999, and the Wintergarden followed in 2000.

Baghdad's main railway station links Iraq's northern and southern rail networks. The British built it to a design by the Scottish architect J. M. Wilson, who had worked as Lutyens's assistant in New Delhi and later set up his own practice in Baghdad. Work began in 1948 and ended in 1953, and no station in Iraq is bigger. Beyond the trains, the building had a telegraph service, a bank, a post office, a saloon, shops and a restaurant. A renovation costing $5.9 million started in 2004 and was finished in June 2006.

Jørn Utzon designed this Lutheran church outside Copenhagen in 1968; it was completed in 1976. Lying on a Hawaiian beach soon after quitting Australia over the Sydney Opera House disputes, he watched rows of cylindrical clouds and saw a model for a church ceiling. The ceiling's reinforced concrete shells are just 12 cm thick yet span 17 m. It is counted among the finest modern churches, above all for its vaulted ceiling and bright, daylit interior. High windows across the full width of the nave bring in light, and smaller rooms take it from the courtyards. The modular plan, courtyards and linking corridors are said to draw on Buddhist temples in China. Outside, white precast concrete panels and glazed tiles face the walls under an industrial-looking aluminium roof. Kenneth Frampton counts it an outstanding case of critical regionalism.

Banyuwangi's airport lies about 12 km from the town centre, and its passenger terminal, credited to Andra Matin, made it Indonesia's first green airport. Between 2015 and 2017 the terminal was enlarged to 20,000 m² at a cost of roughly 100 billion rupiah, and it can now take up to two million passengers a year. Its design draws on the traditional houses of Banyuwangi's Osing people and follows an open-air approach, so the building depends less on air conditioning. In 2022 the airport was one of six winners of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

The City of London paid £161 million for this arts centre within the Barbican Estate, built as its gift to the nation, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 3 March 1982. Chamberlin, Powell and Bon designed it in the Brutalist style, with a complicated layout over many levels and many ways in. The firm owed much to Le Corbusier, and its project architect, Leopold Rubinstein, had trained with him in Paris. The building's form, a concrete ziggurat, has always split opinion. Outside, the focus is a lake and its terrace, and the theatre's fly tower is wrapped in glass as a high-level conservatory. The London Symphony Orchestra and the BBC Symphony Orchestra are based in its Concert Hall. In September 2001 the arts minister, Tessa Blackstone, announced a Grade II listing, recognising its scale, cohesion and ambition.

The Basílica del Voto Nacional is a Roman Catholic church in the historic centre of Quito, rising to 83 metres. It began with an idea put forward in 1883 by Father Julio Matovelle: a monument that would forever recall Ecuador's consecration to the Sacred Heart. Emilio Tarlier's design, which cost 40,000 French francs, took Bourges Cathedral as its inspiration. The first stone went down on 10 July 1892. To keep the work going, donations were taken from believers, who gave stones and had their names carved into them in return. Pope John Paul II blessed the basilica on 30 January 1985, and it was consecrated and opened on 12 July 1988. Its crypt holds Ecuador's National Pantheon, where several former presidents lie buried.

Built in 1897–1899 at 65 Bleecker Street in Manhattan's NoHo, this 12-storey commercial block in the Chicago School style is Louis Sullivan's only New York building. He is sometimes named its sole architect, though Lyndon P. Smith, a New York architect, assisted him. It was among the city's first skeleton-frame skyscrapers, and the Department of Buildings objected often before approving it. City officials were reluctant to approve the Gray system Sullivan and Dankmar Adler had used at the Prudential Building. The Bleecker Street front shows Sullivan's thinking on tall buildings in three parts: a decorated base, a shaft of identical floors and an ornate crown, with six winged angels under the cornice. Projecting mullions and pilasters stress the frame; broad spandrel panels hide its horizontal beams. It became a city landmark in 1975 and a National Historic Landmark in 1976.

The Bergisel Ski Jump stands on the Bergisel in Innsbruck, Austria, with a stadium that holds 26,000 people. Ski jumping began here in the 1920s on simple timber structures. The first larger hill dates from 1930; it was rebuilt for the 1964 Winter Olympics, where it held the individual event on the large hill, and twelve years on the same contest came back for the 1976 Games. The hill as it stands today was completed in 2003 to a design by Zaha Hadid, the British-Iraqi architect. It remains one of the main venues on the FIS World Cup circuit for ski jumping, and each year it stages the third competition of the Four Hills Tournament.

Berlin's Musical Instrument Museum sits on Tiergartenstraße in the Kulturforum, at the Kemper Platz beside the Berlin Philharmonic. Its building, which the museum moved into in 1984, went up between 1979 and 1984 under Edgar Wisniewski, who worked from designs by Hans Scharoun; Scharoun had died in 1972. The two had a contract stating that if one partner died, the other would carry the work on. The collection numbers more than 3,500 instruments from the 16th century onwards, among the largest and most representative in Germany. Chamber concerts are held regularly in the museum's own hall, the Curt-Sachs-Saal, and visitors can hear something rare here: a theatre organ played live, the 1929 Mighty Wurlitzer, which has 1,228 pipes, 175 stops and 43 pistons.

The Potsdamer Straße building is the newer home of the Berlin State Library, part of the Kulturforum in what was West Berlin. Hans Scharoun designed it, with Edgar Wisniewski taking a large part. Work started in 1967 on a building for the library's evacuated holdings that, when the Second World War ended, lay in the western Allied zones. It rose near the Berlin Wall, only 1.5 km from the older library in the East. After eleven years of construction, President Walter Scheel dedicated it in 1978 and it opened to the public. It was renovated from 1999 to 2001. In February 2026 the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation said it would close for eleven years from 2030 for a thorough renovation; as a listed monument, every piece must be photographed, catalogued and numbered before being cleaned and put into storage.

Biltmore House is a Châteauesque mansion in Asheville, built between 1889 and 1895 as the home of George Washington Vanderbilt II. Richard Morris Hunt drew on French Renaissance châteaux, and he set the four-storey Indiana limestone house facing east, its 375-foot (114 m) front fitted to the mountain landscape behind. No privately owned house in the United States is larger: it has 178,926 sq ft of floor space and 250 rooms, among them 35 bedrooms, 43 bathrooms, 65 fireplaces and three kitchens, with new 19th-century comforts like an electric Otis lift and forced-air heating. Rafael Guastavino's patented self-supporting ceramic tile vaults were used widely inside and out, and he oversaw their installation himself. The largest room, the Banquet Hall, measures 42 by 72 feet beneath a barrel vault 70 feet high. The estate became a National Historic Landmark in 1963.

One of the largest university art museums in the US, the Blanton at the University of Texas in Austin has 189,340 square feet holding exhibition and collection galleries, storage, offices, teaching rooms, a room for studying prints, an auditorium, a shop and a cafe. Herzog & de Meuron were first hired for the project but stepped down in 1999 after disagreeing with the university's Board of Regents over how closely to follow the Campus Master Plan. The job then passed to Kallmann McKinnell & Wood. The Michener Gallery Building opened in 2006 with a 24-hour celebration, and the 56,000-square-foot Edgar A. Smith Building, for education and administration, followed in 2008. Additions include twelve three-storey "petals" shading the new Moody Patio, and Carmen Herrera's mural Verde, que te quiero verde, along the full length of the gallery building's loggia.

The Blauwe Theehuis, or Blue Tea House, is a Modernist pavilion from the 1930s in Amsterdam's Vondelpark. The brothers H.A.J. and Jan Baanders designed it in the Nieuwe Bouwen, or Nieuwe Zakelijkheid, style, the Dutch version of Bauhaus. Built of concrete, steel and glass, the ring-shaped building recalls a flying saucer: two round floors sit one above the other, and a round roof forms a third "saucer" on top. The eight-sided ground floor carries a twelve-sided upper floor, which was first the home of the owner. Twelve pillars hold up that upper level, and they, the balustrades and the roof edges are all painted blue. The pavilion is protected as a rijksmonument, a Dutch national monument.

Zaha Hadid's BMW Central Building in Leipzig won a competition for a central block that would physically join the plant's three units and also hold its administration and staff spaces. Every day 650 BMW 3 Series cars ride through it on a raised conveyor, moving from one production shed to the next. Offices, meeting rooms and PR spaces are arranged around these conveyors, linking employees, cars and the public. Inside, levels and floors seem to cascade beneath tilting concrete beams and a roof held up by H-shaped steel beams. The structural walls, floors and office decks are concrete cast in place, while the roof uses steel beams and a space frame. Corrugated metal, channel glass and glazed curtain walls form the facade. The building received a 2006 European Award from RIBA, among others, and reached the Stirling Prize shortlist.

In April 2016 the Council of Paris and François Pinault set out a plan to turn the Bourse de Commerce, one of the city's landmark buildings, into a museum of contemporary art. Those who worked on Tadao Ando's conversion included Pierre-Antoine Gatier, chief architect of French National Heritage, Lucy Niney and Thibault Marca from the agency NeM, and the engineers Setec Bâtiment. The facades and roof were restored, as was the round painting inside the dome. Under the central cupola sits a "building within a building": a concrete cylinder 30 feet tall and 100 feet across that forms the main gallery. There are 32,000 square feet of adaptable exhibition space and a third-floor restaurant, with furniture inside and out by Ronan and Erwan Bouroullec. The work reportedly cost over 100 million euros, and the doors opened on 22 May 2021.

Completed in 1974, the Buffalo City Court Building is a ten-storey courthouse on Niagara Square, next to Buffalo City Hall. Its official name, Frank A. Sedita City Court, honours Frank A. Sedita, a Buffalo mayor. The local firm Pfohl, Roberts and Biggie designed it with few windows, so that courtrooms and judges' chambers would be shielded from distractions outside. Large precast concrete panels pierced by slim windows dominate the facade, and the building is held up as a textbook case of brutalism. It houses the 8th Judicial District, Buffalo Housing Court and courts for landlord and tenant disputes, small claims, commercial claims and criminal cases, plus several parts of the New York State Supreme Court serving Erie County.

This war memorial honours the roughly 253,000 Turkish soldiers who served in the Battle of Gallipoli, fought from April to December 1915 in the First World War. Its design, by the architects Doğan Erginbaş and İsmail Utkular with the civil engineer Ertuğrul Barla, won the official competition. The decision to build came in 1952 and the foundation stone was laid on 19 April 1954, but money problems halted the work more than once; meanwhile the newspaper Milliyet ran a nationwide fundraising drive, and the memorial opened on 21 August 1960. Standing 41.70 m (137 ft) high, it is made of four square columns, each 7.5 m wide and 10 m apart, carrying a 25 by 25 m concrete slab. It can be seen clearly from the Dardanelles. The museum beneath it and the reliefs on the columns came later.

Christ the Light in Oakland was the first cathedral built wholly in the 21st century. It took over from Saint Francis de Sales Cathedral, which the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake had damaged beyond repair. A design by Calatrava had fallen out of favour by the time the site was settled, so the job went to the competition runner-up, Craig W. Hartman of the San Francisco office of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. The worship space is a vesica piscis, the shape made where two circles overlap. Overlapping wood and glass panels rise like fish scales to form the vault, and Hartman likened its light to light through tall redwoods. The 58-foot omega window shows Christ in three dimensions through holes pierced in aluminium panels, after a 12th-century carving at Chartres. Ground was broken in 2005 and it was consecrated in 2008.

The Cathedral of Maringá, formally the Catedral Basílica Menor Nossa Senhora da Glória, is a Roman Catholic cathedral in the centre of Maringá, in the Brazilian state of Paraná. It rises to 124 metres (407 ft); no church building in the Americas is taller, and it ranks 18th in the world. The architect, José Augusto Bellucci, took the Soviet Sputnik satellites as the inspiration for its conical modernist form. Its foundation stone, laid on 15 August 1958, was blessed by Pope Pius XII and is a fragment of marble taken from Rome's St Peter's Basilica. Building ran from July 1959 to 10 May 1972, the city's 25th anniversary.

Since 2011 the Central Government Complex on the Tamar site has been the seat of the Hong Kong government. It houses the Chief Executive's office, the Legislative Council Complex and the Central Government Offices. Rocco Yim shaped its massing around the idea of a "door always open", and the design draws on neither Chinese nor European models for government buildings, mixing postmodern architecture with plain international design instead. Tamar Park runs through the complex down to the promenade along Victoria Harbour. It was built under a design-build contract, which went to a joint venture of Gammon and Hip Hing; work was due to start in mid-February 2008 and finish in 2011. Its first open design has since been heavily fortified after a series of protests.

Central Hall at the University of York, nicknamed "The Spaceship" because it looks like a UFO, was designed by John Speight in the brutalist style and built between 1966 and 1968. It sits prominently on the West Campus, in the middle of the lake's bank. Most buildings of this phase used the CLASP system, but the hall's size meant it was built in reinforced concrete instead. Its cantilevers let it stand apart from its surroundings without being aggressive. The ground floor is mostly a large foyer with glass walls facing the lake. Holding up to 1,100 people, the hall serves mainly for exams and lectures. It is Grade II listed.

Osaka Prefecture's Chikatsu Asuka Museum, in Kanan, is given over to the history of the Chikatsu Asuka area in the Kofun and Asuka periods. Tadao Ando designed it, and it opened in 1994. The exhibition hall has three parts: foreign influence during those two periods; the kofun and the beginnings of the ancient realm; and the application of science to cultural heritage. Over two hundred burial mounds lie in the Fudoki-no-Oka Historical Park of Chikatsu Asuka; four are imperial tombs, and others belong to Ono no Imoko and Shōtoku Taishi.

The Church of Christ the Worker and Our Lady of Lourdes stands in Estación Atlántida, Uruguay, where it serves as a Catholic parish church. The engineer Eladio Dieste designed it in 1958. Its plan is a plain rectangle whose side walls rise in waving curves, carrying a roof that waves in the same way, made of a row of reinforced brick Gaussian vaults. This vault was Dieste's own innovation: a thin roof shell of single-thickness brick that gains stiffness and strength from a doubly curved catenary form, which resists buckling. A round bell tower of open exposed brick stands to the right of the front, and an underground baptistery to the left, entered through a triangular prism and lit by a central oculus. In 2021 UNESCO made the church a World Heritage Site.

Liam McCormick modelled this Roman Catholic chapel beside the N13 road in Burt, County Donegal, on the Grianán of Aileach, the ancient stone ringfort on top of Greenan Mountain in Burt, which dates to around 1700 BC. Building started in 1964, and the chapel opened in 1967. Its windows are by Helen Moloney, the stained glass artist McCormick hired for eleven of his buildings. In 1999 a readers' poll, run jointly by the Sunday Tribune and the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, chose St Aengus' Church as the Irish "Building of the 20th century".

This non-denominational chapel sits on the Harvard Business School campus in Boston. Moshe Safdie designed it in 1992 under a master plan to let the school grow along the Charles River while complementing McKim, Mead and White's 1927 campus. It is an 8.2 m concrete cylinder clad in patinated bronze, with a glass pyramid on one side: a greenhouse over a sunken koi pond with plants, a small waterfall and concrete stepping stones. Inside, half-round concrete forms scallop a two-storey stone drum. Long prisms by Charles Ross in slim windows at the top cast raking light and sometimes rainbows over the bare concrete. The tower is a clock by Karl Schlamminger: lines on it mark the time as a ball moves up and down a pole. Weidlinger Associates engineered it and Richard White Sons built it, for about $2.5 million.

County Hall in Cork is an office tower of 17 storeys that Cork County Council owns and uses as its administrative headquarters. By the 1950s the old premises were becoming inadequate, and in 1965 work started on a new building by Patrick McSweeney, who was then County Architect. It opened officially in April 1968. At 67 metres (220 ft), it was Ireland's tallest storied building when finished. The original concrete facade wore badly over time, and rather than mend it, it was decided to replace it during an expansion: louvred glass cladding now covers the tower, and a six-storey extension at the base, along with a new council chamber and concourse, was finished in June 2006. Outside stands Two Working Men, a statue by Oisín Kelly. The building is now protected.

In May 2001 the museum and Hall of Fame moved to a new building of 140,000 square feet in the middle of Nashville's downtown arts and entertainment area, to be easier to reach. The local firm Tuck-Hinton Architects designed it, with Seab Tuck as project architect. From the air, the building traces a huge bass clef. The tip of its sweeping arch hints at the tailfin of a Cadillac from 1959, and the front windows look like piano keys. The Rotunda roof's four stacked discs stand for the stages of recording: 78, LP, 45 and CD. Wood, concrete, steel and stone from the Mid-South recall the music's roots in the lives of working Americans. A $100 million expansion in 2014 doubled the museum to 350,000 square feet.

Zagreb's Croatian National Theatre, usually called HNK Zagreb, stages theatre, opera and ballet, and its bright yellow front makes it one of the city's best-known landmarks. Fundraising began in April 1880, when Marijan Derenčin, an MP, petitioned the government for a new building. The designs came from the Viennese pair Ferdinand Fellner and Hermann Helmer, who built theatres across Europe as Fellner & Helmer. Khuen-Héderváry chose the site, the city fairgrounds, despite objections that it lay on the outskirts. Over two hundred workers started building on 22 May 1894, and within four months the roof was on. The Viennese painter Alexander Demetrius Goltz painted the auditorium ceiling. The official opening was on 14 November 1895; Emperor Franz Joseph I was at the unveiling during a visit that year. By the entrance is Ivan Meštrović's 1905 wall fountain, Well of Life.

Kevin Roche designed this modernist office building in Columbus, Indiana, as the headquarters of the engine maker Cummins, and it was built in 1983. The site was an old railroad yard, and Roche wrapped the new precast concrete structure around the Cerealine Building, which had been Cummins' first factory and offices. That older building was renovated to become the staff cafeteria. Precast concrete and glass are the main materials of the 200,000 sq ft building. Jack Curtis did the landscaping, including a large green space on the east side that the public can use as a park. In the lobby, Roche included a sculpture by Rudolph de Harak called the Exploded Engine.

The Davenport Public Library traces its history to 1839, and its Main Library now occupies a building from the 1960s by Edward Durell Stone, architect of the Kennedy Center. The library was enlarged in 1963 to give children's services more room, but the expansion shifted the sand beneath the foundations and damaged the structure. The Carnegie Building had to come down in 1966, and the library moved for a time into an empty department store while a new home was built. Stone's building opened on 6 October 1968, with the Davenport firm Stewart-Robison-Laffan as associate architects. In 2019 it joined the Davenport Register of Historic Properties, and in 2020 it became a contributing building in a downtown commercial historic district on the US National Register of Historic Places.

Philip Dowson of Arup designed this Oxford building in 1967 for what was then the Department of Nuclear Physics, and it was first called the Nuclear Physics Laboratory. It stands where Banbury Road, on its west, meets Keble Road, on its south. It was designed around particle physics research: most of the accelerator equipment and the experimental target station are below ground, and attached to it is a large fan-shaped structure built to hold a Van de Graaff generator. The thick concrete walls of the lower floors are loaded with boron, not to keep radiation in, as many locals believed, but to keep natural background radiation inside as low as possible. Nikolaus Pevsner saw it as the moment "the 'New Brutalism'" reached Oxford. In 2001 it was renamed after the British nuclear physicist Sir Denys Wilkinson, who helped create it.

Jean Nouvel designed this $125-million office tower in Doha, which rises 238 metres (781 ft) over 46 floors. It has no central core, which frees more floor space for the people who work there. It was the first skyscraper to use internal reinforced concrete diagrid columns, and these form an X shape that meets the cylindrical facade. Islamic screens shade the building from the heat and from the sand that settles on glass across the region. The cylinder, 45 metres (148 ft) across at its base and topped by a dome, recalls Nouvel's Torre Glòries office building in Barcelona, which was the tower's conceptual starting point. On 18 October 2012 the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat named it Best Tall Building Worldwide.

Dokk1 is a public library, culture centre and government building in Aarhus, Denmark, designed by Schmidt Hammer Lassen Architects with Kristine Jensen. Ground was broken in June 2011, with NCC AB managing construction, and the building opened in June 2015. A seven-sided metal disc of offices seems to float over a glass prism set on wide, irregular steps. The prism holds the library; it is see-through on all sides, showing the activity inside and giving views of harbour, bay, forest and city. Light rail trains run through and under it, and it includes a station. A 2,432 m² solar panel tops the roof, seawater is used for cooling, and LED lighting is widespread. A bell here rings when parents at Aarhus University Hospital press a button after a birth. In 2016 IFLA named it Public Library of the Year.

The Avianca Building is a 161-metre office skyscraper in Bogotá, on the corner where Seventh Avenue meets 16th Street, beside Santander Park. The firm Esguerra, Sáenz, Urdaneta, Samper y Cía. designed and built it with Ricaurte Prieto Carrizosa and Doménico Parma, an engineer from Italy, following a competition among several leading Colombian firms. The design was finished in 1963, and construction ran from 1966 to 1969 where the demolished Hotel Regina had stood. Opened in late 1969 for the airline's head office, it became Bogotá's and Colombia's tallest building, and one of South America's tallest office towers. A fire once spread through floors 14 to 37 and burned for over 12 hours, killing four people and injuring 63, but the structure came through without major damage.

The Figge Art Museum stands in Davenport, Iowa, on the Mississippi's north bank. Its new building, by the British architect David Chipperfield, opened on 6 August 2005 and was one of his first commissions in the United States. It cost $47 million to build, and $13 million of that came from the V.O. and Elizabeth Kahl Figge Foundation. The museum covers 115,000 square feet and has been accredited by the American Alliance of Museums from 1973 onwards. More than 4,000 works make up its collection, from the 16th century to today. It is best known for its Midwestern, Haitian and Colonial Mexican art, above all works by Grant Wood, Marvin Cone and Thomas Hart Benton, among them the one self-portrait Wood ever made.

The Guaranty Building in Buffalo, also called the Prudential Building, began as an idea of the local businessman Hascal T. Taylor. Louis Sullivan and Dankmar Adler designed it, and it was finished in 1896, rising 13 floors and 167 feet (51 m). As in many Chicago School buildings, the floors above the base form a U in plan, so that every office gets daylight and fresh air. Sullivan based the design on his belief that "form follows function". Terracotta blocks dress the steel frame, a different kind for each of the three visible zones. Although he had urged other architects to give up ornament for some years, Sullivan gave the Guaranty rich floral terracotta ornament. Metal cages, not walls, enclosed the lifts and stairs, letting light into the corridors. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1975.

Gyumri's station is the main one in the city and the oldest railway station in Armenia, at a junction that dates from 1897 and is both the oldest and the largest in the country. The present station building went up in 1979 to a design by Rafik Yeghoyan, a local architect. Some of its features, above all the way the entrance hall is composed in space, recall medieval Armenian architecture, a leaning sometimes found in Armenian modernism of the Soviet era. As of 2018, regular trains ran from here to Yerevan, Tbilisi and Batumi.

The Astrodome in Houston was the world's first domed stadium built for many sports. With Houston's hot summers and subtropical climate, a major league team was thought to need a covered stadium. Hermon Lloyd & W. B. Morgan and Wilson, Morris, Crain and Anderson were the architects; the Houston firm Walter P Moore did the structural engineering. The dome spans 710 feet (220 m), with the ceiling 208 feet above a field sunk 25 feet below street level. Nearly round, it served football and baseball alike, with movable lower seats. After its natural grass died, it became in 1966 the first major venue to lay artificial turf, later called AstroTurf. It led the way for fully domed stadiums such as New Orleans' Superdome, and listing on the National Register in 2014 saved it from full demolition.

Kaédi Regional Hospital, in the Gorgol Region of southern Mauritania, is Kaédi's biggest health facility and is known for its inventive architecture. It was designed by Fabrizio Carola, an Italian architect with ADAUA (the Association for the Development of Traditional African Urbanism and Architecture). It is built of local brick, fired by hand, and its design rests on a series of domes, some simple and some complex. The aim was a building that stays cool on its own while still letting in plenty of daylight. ADAUA used the project to develop and spread a new "urban vernacular" for the region and to teach builders new construction methods that were cheap and suited to local conditions; the workers learned them on site. In 1995 the hospital received an Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

Le Corbusier's Sanskar Kendra in Ahmedabad was meant to be one part of a larger cultural centre, but the museum alone was realised, starting with a foundation stone on 9 April 1954. The block is raised on his trademark pilotis, here 3.4 metres tall, and its outside is plain brick with exposed raw concrete (béton brut) structure on a 7-metre grid. The design guards against the hot climate, and the roof holds several large basins first meant as planters. Visitors enter from below, into an open court with a big pool, and climb a ramp to the galleries. Like his museums in Tokyo and Chandigarh and his "Museum of unlimited extension" project, the plan follows a spiral so that it could grow. The museum shut in March 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic and has stayed closed for renovation.

Founded in 1861, the National Gallery of Victoria is Australia's oldest art museum and its most visited. Sir Roy Grounds, who kept the commission after leaving his partners Romberg and Boyd in 1962, designed its St Kilda Road home, now NGV International. The bluestone-clad building was finished in December 1967, and Premier Henry Bolte opened it in August 1968. A moat and fountains surround it, and people enter through a water wall that has also carried art by Keith Haring. Inside, Leonard French's stained-glass ceiling, among the largest pieces of suspended stained glass in the world, throws coloured light onto the floor. Mario Bellini later rebuilt the galleries, keeping only the shell, central courtyard and Great Hall; it reopened in 2003. After public protests, a new water wall replaced the old one, set slightly forward.

The Torres de Satélite, or Satellite Towers, are dated 1957–58 by Luis Barragán working with the sculptor Mathias Goeritz, drawing on ideas from the painter Jesus Reyes Ferreyra. They are described as an urban sculpture and as a significant piece of modern sculpture and architecture. The group stands in the middle of the Periférico, the main freeway of Mexico City. Because nobody was sure who owned the land beneath them, no government took care of the towers and they fell into poor repair. Late in the 1990s they were given fresh coats in their first colours, which Barragán himself had chosen.
