Radio City Music Hall is a theatre inside Rockefeller Center in Midtown Manhattan. Its plot had first been meant for a Metropolitan Opera house, a plan dropped in 1929, and the hall opened instead on 27 December 1932 as part of the Rockefeller Center project. Edward Durell Stone and Donald Deskey gave it Art Deco decoration whose sharp lines broke with the ornate rococo then usual in movie palaces. Stone faced it in Indiana limestone, like the rest of Rockefeller Center, while adding features of its own. Roxy asked for red seats, believing they would bring success, and an oval hall, since ovals were then thought to sound better. When it opened, the four-tier auditorium was the largest in the world. Made a city landmark in 1978, it was restored and kept open, then renovated in 1999.

The Pulitzer Arts Foundation stands in St. Louis's Grand Center Arts District. After nearly ten years of planning and four of construction, it was finished in October 2001 as the first public building in the United States by Tadao Ando, winner of the 1995 Pritzker Prize. The design shows Ando's long interest in natural light and water and his signature concrete. Its concrete forms were poured on site over almost four years, using methods rare in America at the time. Working with Ando's office, the foundation later enlarged the public space from 6,800 to about 10,400 square feet, reopening in May 2015 with three solo shows. In the main gallery, beneath a skylight, is Ellsworth Kelly's Blue Black, a 28-foot vertical wall sculpture. Art here is shown without wall labels, so that visitors meet each work directly.

The home of Canada's top court sits just west of Parliament Hill, on a bluff high over the Ottawa River. Once the design was settled, work started in 1938, and Queen Elizabeth, consort of George VI, laid the cornerstone in May 1939. Finished in 1941, it was first used by government staff for the war effort, and the court only moved in during January 1946. Ernest Cormier's design is noted for Art Deco details, such as two fluted metal lamp standards shaped like candelabra beside the entrance and a lobby lined and paved in marble, set against a châteauesque roof. In 2000 the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada listed it among the 500 best Canadian buildings of the past thousand years. A neighbouring archives building of 1967 was given a Canadian granite exterior to harmonise with it.

The Singapore Flyer, an observation wheel in Singapore's Downtown Core, is credited to Kisho Kurokawa Architects & Associates with DP Architects; Takenaka and Mitsubishi were the main contractors, with Arup as structural engineer. At 165 metres overall, it was the tallest Ferris wheel in the world when finished. The spindle was fitted in December 2006 and the outer rim finished in April 2007, with the official opening on 15 April 2008. Its 28 air-conditioned capsules each take 28 people and hang outside the rim, so the view is never blocked. One full turn lasts about 32 minutes. The project includes a three-storey terminal building, on a 33,700 m2 site along the Marina Promenade. In August 2008, after feng shui masters gave their advice, the wheel was made to turn the other way.

8 House, also called Big House, is a mixed-use block on the southern edge of Ørestad, a new suburb of Copenhagen, laid out as a figure 8. Bjarke Ingels of BIG designed it to hold 61,000 square metres of homes in three types, plus 10,000 square metres of shops and offices. The parts of a neighbourhood are stacked, with commercial space below and flats above, joined by a walkway and cycle track rising to the 10th floor. A perimeter block is pinched in the middle into a bowtie with two courtyards, and a 10-metre passage at its centre joins the park to the west with the channel area to the east. One corner is raised and the opposite one lowered, letting light and air into the southern courtyard. The looping ramp is meant to bring neighbours together.

The Alhambra in Granada is one of the best-known works of Islamic architecture and the only medieval Islamic palace still well preserved. Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, first Nasrid emir, began it in 1238 on Sabika hill. The palaces gained most of their character in 14th-century campaigns under Yusuf I and Muhammad V. In Nasrid times it was a self-contained city apart from Granada below, with a Friday mosque, baths, houses, workshops and an advanced water supply. Rooms gather around courtyards, usually with a pool or fountain at the centre. Decoration is focused inside: tile mosaic low on the walls, carved stucco above, and muqarnas shaped like stalactites in the vaults. The red in its name refers to the reddish colour of its rammed-earth walls. In 1526 Charles V ordered a Renaissance-style palace there, in direct contrast with the Nasrid ones.

The Bibliotheca Alexandrina is a library and cultural centre on the Mediterranean shore in Alexandria, Egypt, built in memory of the ancient Library of Alexandria. The idea dates to 1974, when Alexandria University chose a site near where the old library had stood. In 1988 UNESCO held a design competition, which the Norwegian office Snøhetta won against 524 other entries. Work began in 1995 and the complex opened on 16 October 2002. The main reading room spreads over eleven stepped levels and 20,000 square metres, the biggest of its kind when built. Its glass-panelled roof, some 160 m across and 32 m high, tilts toward the sea like a sundial. The grey granite walls carry letters from 120 scripts, drawn by the Norwegian artist Jorunn Sannes of the Snøhetta team.

The Bank of China Tower stands at 1 Garden Road in Central, Hong Kong, and holds the headquarters of Bank of China (Hong Kong). The design came from I. M. Pei and L. C. Pei, with Leslie E. Robertson as structural engineer. The 72-storey tower is 315 metres tall, and its two masts reach 367.4 metres. It held the height record for both Hong Kong and Asia from 1990 to 1992, and was the first skyscraper outside the United States to pass 305 metres. Triangular frames clad in glass curtain walls give the tower its shape, and they carry the load down to four steel columns at its corners. Some feng shui practitioners criticised its sharp edges and the many X shapes in the first design, and Pei changed it somewhat before building began.

The Virgilio Barco Public Library is in the western part of Bogotá and belongs to BibloRed, the district's network of public libraries. Rogelio Salmona designed it, and it forms part of the Simón Bolívar Metropolitan Park. It was inaugurated in December 2001, carrying the name of the former president Virgilio Barco Vargas. The design is noted for its handling of water, with pools set outside the building. Salmona shaped the library in close relation to the public space around it, bringing together values of geography, landscape, history and lived experience. The library and its park are one of seven sites in a serial nomination on Salmona's architectural legacy, which Colombia's delegation to UNESCO put on the country's World Heritage Tentative List in 2022.

Calgary Central Library, flagship of the city's public libraries, opened on 1 November 2018 in the Downtown East Village, replacing a 1960s central branch. Snøhetta and the Canadian firm DIALOG won the 2013 design competition with a joint bid, and the four-floor building cost CA$245 million. The first step, from May 2014 to September 2015, was to enclose a 135-metre stretch of the Red Line light rail where it comes out of a tunnel under the site. The oval building is lifted one floor above the street over that rail line and an open plaza, meant to link East Village with downtown. Wood-clad arches at the entrance recall the cloud arches formed by Chinook winds. Fritted glass screens study areas, while clear glass opens public spaces to view. Inside, 22,000 square metres wrap a four-storey atrium under a skylight.

Dipoli sits on the Otaniemi campus of Aalto University in Espoo. A 1961 competition sought a new Student Union building, but the rocky site and the need for flexibility meant no entry fully satisfied the jury, so no first prize was given. The second prize was shared by Reima and Raili Pietilä and Osmo Lappo, and in the end the Pietiläs' scheme became the basis of the building, which opened in 1966. It draws heavily on Finnish natural materials such as pine, copper and natural stone, and of its 500 windows only four are the same. It is seen as a key work of organic architecture. Its name is a pun, reading as "dipole" in Finnish but also as "the second Poly" for polytechnic students. A renovation from 2015 to 2017 made it the university's new main building.

The METI Handmade School is a primary school for 168 pupils in Rudrapur, in the Dinajpur district of Bangladesh. Anna Heringer and Eike Roswag based the design on regional methods and materials, adding new ideas for efficiency and strength. It was built with the help of local craftsmen, mostly from mud and bamboo, over four months, from September to December 2005. Better bamboo framing and lashing made a second floor possible. Brick foundations shield the earth walls from damp, and the team also added a damp-proof course and mixed straw into the loam. Downstairs, the classrooms are closed in by mud walls; upstairs, walls of bamboo slats let in soft light and fresh air. In 2007 it received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for its simple, humane approach, its beauty and the teamwork of architects, craftsmen, clients and users.

Santiago Calatrava's Auditorio de Tenerife stands beside the Atlantic in the southern part of the port of Santa Cruz de Tenerife. Building ran from 1997 to 2003, and Felipe, Prince of Asturias, attended the opening on 26 September 2003. Much of the outside is covered in white trencadís, broken-tile mosaic, with coloured pieces brightening the walls of the plaza it rests on. The arched roof, 15 to 20 cm thick, is held at only two points while its tip seems to hang in the air; it is described as the only large arch of this kind. Under a dome, the main symphony hall seats 1,616 people in an amphitheatre; the 422-seat chamber hall is a smaller copy. The building is home to the Tenerife Symphony Orchestra. Its tiles now show visible damage, and the interior suffers from damp.

The Danish Jewish Museum in Copenhagen occupies the old Galley House of the Royal Library and shows art and objects from Danish Jewish history. No official museum in Denmark had been given to a minority or immigrant group before it. Daniel Libeskind's design remembers the Danish Jews whose fellow citizens saved them from Nazi persecution in October 1943. Building started in March 2003, and the doors opened in June 2004. The building is organised as a set of planes, each tied to a theme of religious thought and with names such as Exodus, Wilderness and The Promised Land. Together they carve out fractured corridors with slanted floors, which hold the exhibitions. As they wind, the corridors trace the letters of the Hebrew word Mitzvah, which means "good deed". The project received an American Architect Award in 2005.

Ristinkirkko (Church of the Cross), the main church of Lahti, was one of Alvar Aalto's last designs. Aalto won a competition for it in 1950, but plans to pull down the old church caused a dispute that lasted nearly twenty years, and only in 1969 could the parish order full drawings. He died in May 1976; his wife, the architect Elissa Aalto, saw the work through, and it was consecrated in Advent 1978. Outside it is mostly red brick, with a cast-concrete bell tower 40 metres high. Inside, white walls and big windows keep it bright. The plan is an equilateral triangle with two corners cut off. From the door, the nave narrows and the fan-shaped ceiling drops toward the chancel, like a concert hall. On the south front, facing the market square, 52 small windows form a large cross.

21_21 Design Sight is a design museum in Roppongi, in Tokyo's Minato ward, which opened in 2007. It was created by the architect Tadao Ando together with the fashion designer Issey Miyake. Ando has said the aim was a place not only for showing exhibits but for researching how design can enrich daily life, and for stirring public interest by offering new ways of seeing the world and the objects around us. His building sits at the edge of a park and holds 1,700 square metres of floor space, including two galleries and a cafe run by the chef Takamasa Uetake. The concrete structure is split into levels. Its hand-sanded steel roof has a design inspired by Miyake's A-POC, or "A Piece of Cloth", idea, and the building uses glass panels 14 metres long.

Jože Plečnik, an architect from Slovenia, designed this Roman Catholic church on Jiřího z Poděbrad Square in Vinohrady, and it went up between 1929 and 1932 as his last work in Prague. It was one of three new Prague buildings of 1929 inspired by the thousand years since St Wenceslas died. Plečnik drew on old Christian and ancient models. The broad tower wall rises 42 metres and holds a glazed clock 7.6 metres across, the biggest in the country. Below the church lies a roomy chapel with a coffered timber ceiling. The church is regarded as one of the most important Czech religious buildings of the 20th century, and since 2010 it has been listed as a national cultural monument.

Al-Azhar Park, a public park in Historic Cairo, was created through the Aga Khan Trust for Culture and its Historic Cities Support Programme. Historically the land served as a dump for rubble from rebuilding, a habit that grew in the 16th century under the Mamluks, until the fill reached 40 metres deep in places. More than a million cubic metres of it were taken away. Halfway through, the government required three cisterns for Cairo's drinking water to be set into the ground, so work stopped and the design was changed to fit them. Digging also exposed a forgotten Ayyubid wall with towers, 1.5 kilometres long and 15 metres deep. The park opened in 2005 and recalls historic Islamic gardens, with formal terraces, fountains, Mamluk coloured stonework, sunken gardens and crossing water channels set in a modern plan.

The Atatürk Cultural Center, or AKM, is a concert hall, theatre and arts centre along the east side of Taksim Square in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district. The original building, once called the Istanbul Culture Palace, took 13 years to build and opened on 12 April 1969, twenty-three years after it was proposed. It closed for renovation in 2008 and was finally torn down in 2018. The new AKM, by Murat Tabanlıoğlu, son of the original architect Hayati Tabanlıoğlu, broke ground on 10 February 2019 and opened on 29 October 2021, thirteen years after the closure. Its five parts cover 95,000 m2 and hold a theatre, cinema, concert halls, exhibition and convention spaces, a library, a museum, a gallery, cafés and restaurants. Werner Sobek AG engineered the facade, keeping it transparent so the building opens toward the square.

Renzo Piano's Parco della Musica is a group of music venues in Rome, built from 1994 to 2002 in the district that hosted the 1960 Summer Olympics. It has three halls; the biggest seats 2,800 and was the largest symphonic concert hall in Europe when finished. Piano said the interior plan was inspired by the vineyard-style seating that surrounds the orchestra at the Berlin Philharmonic. The three brick halls sit under steel shells that the New York Times critic Sam Lubell compared to a weathered armadillo, adding that they look forbidding in photos but lovely in person, and that the interiors are rich in wood and fabric. The complex belongs to a period when each of Piano's projects differed from the last, and the common thread was careful craft and close attention to detail.

No building in Kuwait is taller than Al Hamra Tower in Kuwait City. Work began in 2005 and ended in 2011. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it together with Ramshir and Callison, and at 414 m it holds the world record among curved concrete skyscrapers. Glass wraps the east, north and west faces, both for its look and to limit reflective surface on the south side, which also carries brushed Jura limestone. Flared walls run up the full height of the tower from two corners of its core, southwest and southeast, and there is a 24-metre-high lobby with no columns. Time magazine named the tower among 2011's best inventions, and in the same year it received an Emporis Skyscraper Award.

4 World Trade Center stands on Greenwich Street, at the World Trade Center site's southeast corner. Designed by Fumihiko Maki, the 978-foot tower broke ground in January 2008 and opened in November 2013. Engineering News-Record reported that Maki and Associates aimed for a minimalist tower whose presence is abstract and sculptural. Floors 7 to 46 are parallelograms of 44,000 square feet, echoing the shape of the site, while floors 48 to 63 are trapezoids of 36,000 square feet. Reflective glass covers most of the outside, switching to clear glass at the lobby. The two-storey lobby, with a 46-foot ceiling, fills the ground floor's west side, facing the National September 11 Memorial. That face has no louvers; according to the New York Daily News, the architects wanted the design to defer to the memorial. New York magazine called it "pretty exquisite."

The Federal Palace in Bern houses Switzerland's parliament, the Federal Assembly, and its government, the Federal Council. The listed, symmetrical complex, a little over 300 metres long, ranks among the country's key historic buildings. To ease a shortage of space, Hans Wilhelm Auer built the east wing between 1884 and 1892, then oversaw the central parliament building from 1894 to 1902. Plain wings suit their office role, while the parliament building is more monumental, in a neo-Renaissance style with a portico and dome. Inside, a domed hall laid out as a Swiss cross divides the National Council chamber to the south from the Council of States to the north. At least 30 kinds of stone from 13 cantons and half-cantons went into it. Despite its size, its Bernese sandstone fronts let it blend into the city.

Founded in 1989, the Yokohama Museum of Art stands in the Minato Mirai 21 district of Yokohama, beside the Yokohama Landmark Tower. Its building was designed by Kenzō Tange, the Japanese architect who received the Pritzker Prize in 1987. Its main hall is 18 metres high, with the second and third floors looking into it. Daylight comes in through a glass ceiling, with louvers to adjust how much enters. The building has been described as spacious, airy and well lit. After its renovation, the museum was to host the Triennale for the first time in 2023, its eighth edition.

From 2004 to 2008 the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto went through a CA$276 million redevelopment led by Frank Gehry with Adamson Associates Architects. Asked to extend and renew the gallery, not replace it, he had to unite parts left as "a bit of a hodgepodge" by six earlier extensions going back to the 1920s. Along Dundas Street he added the Galleria Italia, a 200-metre canopy of glass, steel and wood that doubles as a second-floor viewing hall, made with about 1,800 glulam pieces. To the south rose a five-storey gallery block in glass and custom titanium panels, with a spiral stair jutting out between its top two floors. Reopened in November 2008, the gallery gained 20 percent more floor area and 47 percent more space for art, and the result was widely praised for its restraint.

A church has stood on the Munich site of the Herz-Jesu-Kirche since 1890; the present one, the third, was built from 1997 to 2000. Allmann Sattler Wappner won the archdiocese's competition, which drew 158 entries. The church is a glass box 16 metres high, 21 metres wide and 48 metres long, held up by a steel frame. On special days the entire front swings open as two double-winged doors, said to be the biggest church doors anywhere. Inside it stands a second, wooden box for worship. The outer glass shifts from clear at the entrance to opaque near the altar. The inner walls are maple and oak slats set at angles that open up toward the altar, letting in daylight that changes with the sun. A separate metal bell tower, 37 metres tall, rises on the square's street side.

Now named after David N. Dinkins, the Municipal Building rises 40 storeys and 580 feet in Manhattan's Civic Center. Built from 1909 to 1914 for $12 million, it met the need for government space after the five boroughs merged in 1898. William M. Kendall of McKim, Mead & White designed it, among the last New York works of the City Beautiful movement. It was the first building in the city with a subway station, Chambers Street, beneath it. On an irregular six-sided lot, the plan forms a ten-sided C, so every window gets direct sun and no inner light court is needed. Its walls are granite ashlar, with terracotta above the 23rd floor, and a three-storey Corinthian colonnade lines its base. On top stands Civic Fame, a 25-foot gilded copper statue. The building became a city landmark in 1966.

The Chicago Board of Trade Building stands at the foot of the LaSalle Street "canyon" in Chicago's Loop. Holabird & Root designed it to replace the Boyington building, unsound and demolished in 1929, and the 44-storey, 604-foot Art Deco tower opened on 9 June 1930. It was Chicago's tallest building until the Richard J. Daley Center passed it in 1965. Grey Indiana limestone covers the outside, and the tower steps back as it rises to let light into the street below, ending in a copper pyramid roof. On top stands John H. Storrs's 31-foot aluminium Ceres, Roman goddess of grain, with wheat and corn for the commodities trade. The exchange has traded on the fourth floor since opening, then the biggest trading floor in the world. Inside are polished surfaces, black and white marble and an open three-storey lobby.

Alvar Aalto designed Lappia Hall, a performing arts and conference centre in Rovaniemi, near the Arctic Circle. Its wavy roofline recalls the fells of Lapland. The second phase, finished in 1971, holds the Rovaniemi Theatre, and the conference centre followed in 1975; it was the last of his buildings Aalto saw completed before he died in 1976. Inside, light timber and plain white surfaces with touches of blue are typical of his later work, and lamps and furniture in the public rooms come largely from Artek, his own design firm. A 2013–2015 renovation added performance and service spaces underground; today there are three auditoriums with about 600 seats in total. The hall belongs to the Aalto Centre, with his library of 1965 and city hall of 1988, protected as a built environment of national importance.

After a design competition announced in 1964, Mario Ciampi, with his associates Ronald Wagner and Richard Jurasch, designed the Berkeley Art Museum, which opened in 1970. The concrete building is counted among the most inventive Brutalist works, leading visitors in a fan-shaped route down a spiral of partly open galleries. In 1996 it earned Ciampi the AIACC's 25-Year Award. A year later it was judged unsafe in earthquakes, and iron bracing was fitted in 2001. Berkeley made it a city landmark in 2012, and the empty building was added to the National Register in 2014. After seismic strengthening and a redesign, at the end of 2021 it opened again as the Bakar BioEnginuity Hub, a space for young biotech companies, under the name Woo Hon Fai Hall, after the father of the donor David Woo.

The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace is a Catholic minor basilica in Yamoussoukro, Ivory Coast's administrative capital. Guinness World Records names it the world's biggest church, passing St Peter's in Rome when it was finished. Its 30,000 square metres include a rectory and a villa besides the church, and it rises 158 metres. It holds 18,000 worshippers, against 60,000 at St Peter's. The Lebanese architect Pierre Fakhoury based his dome and ringed plaza on St Peter's without copying it: the dome is a little lower than St Peter's but crowned with a bigger cross, and at 90 metres across it is more than twice as wide. It is built of Italian marble, with 8,400 square metres of French stained glass. Built from 1985 to 1989, it was consecrated by Pope John Paul II on 10 September 1990.

The Biblioteca Gabriel García Márquez, a public library, opened on 28 May 2022 in the Barcelona neighbourhood of Sant Martí de Provençals. It specialises in Latin American literature and takes its name from Gabriel García Márquez, the Colombian writer who lived in the city from 1967 to 1975 and whose novel The Autumn of the Patriarch was written there. Suma Arquitectura, the studio of Elena Orte and Guillermo Sevillano, designed the building. Its six floors hold about 4,000 square metres, making it the third biggest library in Barcelona. From outside, it looks like a pile of open books. Wood is used throughout, giving the rooms a warm feel and helping to cut the building's environmental impact. In August 2023 the international library federation IFLA named it the world's best new public library.

CINiBA, the Scientific Information Centre and Academic Library, is a research library shared by two Katowice universities, the University of Silesia and the University of Economics. It stands at the heart of their campus, in the middle of the Silesian urban region. Its design came from a two-stage competition held by SARP, the Polish architects' association, which ended on 24 March 2003 with a win for architects from Koszalin and Radom. The library opened to readers on 27 September 2012. The building has seven floors and 4,004 windows, and up to 1,000 people can be inside at once. Run jointly by the two, it keeps most of its collection in open areas where readers can help themselves.

The Petroperú Building in Lima's San Isidro district is the head office of Petroperú, the state company that refines, transports, distributes and sells oil in Peru. Its design, by the architects Daniel Arana Ríos and Walter Weberhofer, won a contest that Juan Velasco Alvarado's military government held early in the 1970s, and the building was inaugurated in 1973. It rises twenty-two floors above three basement levels, has a helipad on its roof, and belongs to the Brutalist style. Besides the oil company, it houses other public offices, among them the housing and construction ministry and the agency that promotes private investment, as well as several art galleries. It sits in a strategic spot in central San Isidro.

The City of Justice, or Ciutat de la Justícia, spans Barcelona's Sants-Montjuïc district and the neighbouring suburb of L'Hospitalet de Llobregat. It gathers most of the metropolitan area's legal departments, which had been spread across 17 separate buildings in the two cities, and it was planned as part of L'Hospitalet's urban renewal through the 2000s and 2010s. Courtrooms take the ground floors, with offices above, and four of the buildings are linked by a four-storey hall. Every facade is the same: concrete cast in place, each given a light tint of its own. The complex also includes shops and a block of homes for people on low incomes. David Chipperfield wrote that he wanted to undo the idea of justice as stiff and monolithic, but The Guardian's critic Rowan Moore found it "uncomfortably prison-like."

The Aviva Stadium in Dublin, by Populous with Scott Tallon Walker Architects, replaced Lansdowne Road Stadium, torn down in 2007, on the same ground beside Lansdowne Road railway station. It opened officially on 14 May 2010 and is now home to Ireland's national rugby union side and the Republic of Ireland football team. Every one of its 51,711 places is a seat. The designers shaped it as a sweeping, crystal-like bowl under a clear roof that lets daylight into the spaces inside. Rainwater is collected to water the pitch, and waste heat is used again for hot water. It was the first stadium in Ireland to reach UEFA Category 4, and it hosted the Europa League finals of 2011 and 2024. It also won a British Construction Industry Award in 2011.

Dunelm House in Durham, England, is a Brutalist building of 1966 owned by Durham University and home to its students' union. The angular concrete block was designed by Michael Powers and Richard Raines at the Architects' Co-Partnership and finished under the engineer Sir Ove Arup, whose nearby Kingsgate Bridge had opened two years earlier. Set into the steep bank of the River Wear, its levels step down the slope, echoing the city's vernacular buildings and breaking up its bulk. Inside, the main stair runs dead straight through all five floors, meant to feel like a street. It won a Civic Trust award in 1968, and the historian Nikolaus Pevsner judged it Brutalist, yet gentle on the landscape. After a second appeal, it was listed at Grade II in 2021, described as England's foremost post-war students' union building.

Paul Rudolph led the design of this Brutalist state government complex in Boston's West End. Two large buildings, structurally separate but joined, wind around a plaza, following the street except at three squared-off corners that form small plazas. Desmond & Lord worked with Rudolph on the Lindemann Building, and the Hurley Building was the work of Shepley Bulfinch Richardson and Abbott. Planned as a contrast to City Hall nearby, the scheme drew on the idea of an amphitheater where citizens could watch civic dramas unfold. Ribbed, bush-hammered "corduroy" concrete, a finish Rudolph had developed at Yale's Art and Architecture Building, covers it inside and out. Tall, evenly spaced columns hold elevators, stairs and bathrooms, and stepped terraces with concrete sunshades face the plaza. Work ran from 1966 to 1971; cuts in 1970 cancelled a tower and its swirling terraces.

This national monument to Chiang Kai-shek, the Republic of China's former president, was put up during Taiwan's martial law period. Yang Cho-cheng's competition-winning design draws on many traditional Chinese elements to mirror Nanjing's Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum. The blue octagonal roof plays on the number eight, which Chinese culture links with abundance and good fortune. Two white stairways of 89 steps each, matching Chiang's age when he died, climb to the entrance. The hall stands at the eastern end of Memorial Hall Square, with the National Theater and the National Concert Hall to either side. It opened on 5 April 1980, five years after his death. The square became Taipei's favoured place for mass gatherings, and in the 1980s and early 1990s the hall and square were the focus of events that brought Taiwan into modern democracy.

Hong Kong Design Institute is a public school of design at Tiu Keng Leng in Tseung Kwan O. The Vocational Training Council founded it in 2007, and in 2010 it moved into a campus built for it. In April 2006 the VTC launched an international architecture competition for a campus that could hold 4,000 students. A jury of architects that included Richard Meier and Rocco Yim chose the scheme by the French firm Coldefy & Associés, ahead of 162 other entries. The building is a huge rectangular block lifted seven storeys over the street, carried on four towers held up by an exoskeleton of steel lattice. The podium contains four auditoriums and lecture theatres, a cafe, and room for galleries and exhibitions.

Madrid's Casa Sindical, the "Syndical House", stands opposite the Prado Museum and now holds the headquarters of Spain's Ministry of Health. The commission went jointly, ex aequo, to Francisco de Asís Cabrero and Rafael de Aburto. At its centre rises a prism-shaped brick tower of 16 floors, reaching 60 metres. The building was finished in 1951, though some parts only opened in July 1955, during the III National Congress of Workers, and Francisco Franco formally inaugurated it on 27 October 1955. In symbolic terms, it marked the Francoist regime's acceptance of a modern architectural language and a move away from the traditionalist look it had favoured before. The building is often linked with the work of the Italian Fascist architect Giuseppe Terragni.

Kolonádový most, the Colonnade Bridge, spans the Váh river and links the town of Piešťany with the Spa Island. Emil Belluš designed it between 1930 and 1933 in Streamline Moderne, an international strand of Art Deco from the 1930s; he worked in a functionalist manner but was willing to temper it with classical elements, as this bridge shows. At mid-span are glass engravings by Martin Benka, "Detva Songs" and "At Sheepcote". The western entrance carries a Latin inscription, "Saluberrimae Pistinienses Thermae" (The healing Piešťany Spa), and the eastern one the motto of the spa, "Surge et ambula" (Get up and walk). The "Crutch Breaker", a 1934 statue by Robert Kuhmayer that serves as the spa's symbol, stands at the west end. Retreating German troops destroyed the bridge in 1945; rebuilt, it reopened on 30 December 1956.

Giulio Ulisse Arata designed this multi-purpose stadium in Bologna, opened in 1927 as the Stadio Littoriale and now mainly a football ground, home to Bologna FC. It was among the first stadiums to make the stands part of the architecture, an idea that later served as a model for stadiums around the world. Its large arch once held an equestrian statue of Benito Mussolini, destroyed when the city was liberated in 1943. The ground hosted games at the 1934 and 1990 FIFA World Cups, and the second required enlargement and modernisation. For that, an exposed steel frame of 120 columns was lined up with the old pilasters, carrying the extended terrace and giving access by stairwells around the perimeter. It seats around 36,000, and up to 55,000 for concerts.

Cambridge University Library serves as the University of Cambridge's chief research library, and UK law makes it one of six legal deposit libraries. Its current home, by Giles Gilbert Scott, went up between 1931 and 1934, when it opened, and is now Grade II listed. The largest share of the funding came from John D. Rockefeller, the American philanthropist, who thought the library deserved a grander entrance and persuaded Scott to add the tall tower on its front. That tower reaches 157 feet (48 m): 6 feet lower than the top of the chapel at St John's College, and 10 feet higher than the peak of King's College Chapel. The building recalls Scott's industrial work, including Bankside Power Station, today Tate Modern. Annexes at ground level and extensions underground have enlarged it several times to store new legal deposit material.

Galway Cathedral, formally the Cathedral of Our Lady Assumed into Heaven and St Nicholas, is a Roman Catholic cathedral built where the old Galway Gaol once stood. John J. Robinson was hired as its architect in 1949. Many people at the time felt a cathedral in a 1950s style was the right choice, but the client wanted a traditional building. Work began in 1958 and ended in 1965, which is why it has been called Europe's last great stone cathedral. It is made almost entirely of local limestone and is considered Ireland's last stone public building. The dome and pillars follow a Renaissance style, while the rose windows and mosaics draw on the wider tradition of Christian art. Rising 44.2 metres (145 ft), the dome stands out on the city skyline.

Ellis & Clarke designed this Fleet Street building in 1932 for the Daily Express, and it ranks among London's most prominent Art Deco and Streamline Moderne buildings. The black front, with rounded corners, is made of vitrolite and clear glass, with chromium strips. Its structure is a massive stacked portal frame of reinforced concrete by Sir Owen Williams, which the Grade II* listing protects along with the architecture. Robert Atkinson designed the flamboyant lobby, with Eric Aumonier's plaster reliefs, silver and gilt ornament, a silvered pendant lamp and an oval stair. As part of a redevelopment in 2000, John Robertson Architects refurbished the whole building, recreating the foyer largely from photographs, upgrading the façade and keeping the concrete frame. Of the three Express Buildings, Williams designed only Manchester's.

Sir Francis Willoughby had this Elizabethan country house built from 1580 to 1588 on a modest, prominent rise in Wollaton Park, Nottingham. Its design is believed to be by Robert Smythson, who had already completed Longleat and later designed Hardwick Hall. A classic prodigy house, described as "the architectural sensation of its age", it stretched the means Willoughby gained mainly from coal mining. A three-storey hall dominates the central block; at every corner stands a square three-storey pavilion with ornament rising above the roof. The plan is said to come from Serlio's drawing of the Villa Poggio Reale near Naples and the elevations from Hans Vredeman de Vries. The house, of Ancaster stone, was reportedly paid for in coal from Willoughby's pits, as were the labourers. The exterior and hall carry extensive carved decoration, strapwork among it.

Manchester's Bridgewater Hall houses the Hallé Orchestra, its choir and youth orchestra, and is the BBC Philharmonic's main concert venue. RHWL (Renton Howard Wood Levin) won the design competition. Built for around £42 million, it staged its first concert on 11 September 1996; the formal opening, by Queen Elizabeth II and the Duke of Edinburgh, followed on 4 December. A road and the Metrolink line run alongside, so the 26,500 tonne superstructure stands on 280 GERB isolation bearings, steel springs in rows between concrete piers; no concert hall had been built this way before. Rob Harris of Arup Acoustics designed the acoustics, consulting closely with the intended resident musicians. Most of the structure, even the ceiling, is solid reinforced concrete. The lower part is deep red Corsehill Quarry sandstone from Annan, Scotland; aluminium and glass clad the upper ones.

Bradfield Hall stands on Cornell University's central campus in Ithaca, New York, along Tower Road at the eastern edge of the Agricultural Quadrangle. Ulrich Franzen designed it in the Brutalist style, and it was finished in 1969. Franzen, a German-born American architect, was known for Brutalist buildings described as "fortresslike". Because most of its laboratories are climate-controlled, no room on the lowest ten floors has windows; only the corridors get them, one at each end. Three Cornell departments work here: Plant Breeding and Genetics, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, and Crop and Soil Science. The eleventh floor houses the Northeast Regional Climate Center, one of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's six regional climate centers.

Richard Meier designed this courthouse, which serves the United States District Court for New York's Eastern District from 100 Federal Plaza, Central Islip, on Long Island. Opened in 2000, it is the country's third largest federal courthouse, behind the Thomas F. Eagleton and Daniel Patrick Moynihan buildings; on Long Island outside New York City, only two buildings are taller and only one is bigger. Twelve storeys contain 870,000 sq ft (81,000 m2), with 23 courtrooms, 24 judges' chambers and a law library. Visitors enter through a conical drum, the building's signature. Courtrooms rise two storeys, and upper-floor corridors look out over the Great South Bay, Fire Island and the Atlantic. The site was once part of the 788-acre Central Islip Psychiatric Center, closed in 1996 after its last patients were moved.

H. H. Richardson won the competition for this courthouse in Downtown Pittsburgh, which forms a complex with the old jail; building began in 1884. The courthouse, finished in 1888, and the jail are considered among the finest Romanesque Revival works, the style Richardson is known for; he later called the courthouse his "great achievement". Its plan was new in wrapping around an inner courtyard, so daylight and fresh air reach most of it. Large rusticated granite blocks, with wide arches over doors and windows, give it a heavy, dignified look. A "Bridge of Sighs", modelled on the one in Venice, links prison and courthouse. When Pittsburgh lowered its streets in the 1900s, finished masonry Richardson had buried in anticipation came into view, leaving the ceremonial entrance a storey above the street. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1976.

Henry Hobson Richardson designed this University of Vermont library in Burlington, built in 1883 and modelled on Woburn's Winn Library in Massachusetts. Frederick H. Billings of Woodstock gave it to the university. Since opening in 1885 it has been central to campus life, and despite a century of university growth the building still looks much as it first did. Short of space, the university built a new library in 1961, the Guy W. Bailey Library, today called the Howe Library, and in 1963 Billings became a student center. An $11.4 million renovation, finished in summer 2018, brought academic departments back into what is the university's most important building architecturally, among them Special Collections, the Humanities Center, the Center for Research on Vermont and the Miller Center for Holocaust Studies.

Local architect George Pearl designed this downtown public library, the main branch of the Albuquerque Bernalillo County libraries. It opened in 1975, and in 2019 it was listed on the US National Register of Historic Places; Pearl ranked it among his "three or four most important" works. Concrete-framed, it belongs to Brutalism yet draws on the Southwest's traditional adobe buildings. Brown brick clads the walls, and upper-floor cantilevers shade large ground-floor windows that engage people on the street; the floor above has little glass. Restrooms, stairs and heating and cooling equipment are pushed into wings around the edge, so each floor's main rectangle is open but for concrete columns at 36-foot (11 m) centres. Floors are planned on a 9-foot (2.7 m) grid, every square having its own lighting, ventilation and services, so sliding partitions can divide them freely.

The Centre Block is the main building of Canada's Parliament on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, holding the House of Commons and Senate chambers. Today's Gothic Revival building is the second on the site: fire destroyed the first in 1916, sparing only the Library of Parliament behind it. Rebuilding began at once under a team led by John A. Pearson and Jean-Omer Marchand, whose design kept close to the original but was larger and plainer, in step with the Beaux-Arts thinking of the day. The symmetrical block is 144 m long, 75 m deep and six storeys high. Its walls use over 50,000 blocks of more than 24 kinds of stone, mostly rustic Nepean sandstone, under a copper-covered concrete roof with dormers. Just inside the entrance, the octagonal Confederation Hall is ringed by clustered limestone columns and dark green syenite pillars.

The Peace Palace in The Hague, an international courthouse, houses the UN's principal court, the International Court of Justice, as well as the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), which the Hague Convention of 1899 created to end war and for which the palace was first built. Andrew Dickson White obtained US$1.5 million from Andrew Carnegie, the steel magnate, to pay for the building and a library of international law. A competition run by a new Foundation drew 216 entries and picked the Neo-Renaissance design by French architect Louis M. Cordonnier. Cordonnier and his Dutch associate, J.A.G. van der Steur, adjusted the design to stay within budget. Two large front towers and two small rear ones were planned; one of each was built. The palace opened on 28 August 1913 and received the European Heritage Label on 8 April 2014.

Built for six Dutch shipping companies as one large cooperative office, the Shipping House stands where the Waalseiland ends in the west. It is usually called the Amsterdam School's first real example. The van Gendt brothers took charge of the engineering and the concrete frame; the architecture was given to Johan van der Mey, little known at the time, with input from Michel de Klerk and Piet Kramer. One part went up in 1913–1916, during World War I, and another in 1926–1928, with all the bricks fired at once so the colour would match. Meant as a practical office that also recalls Dutch seafaring, it carries many maritime symbols, and its outer carvings and reliefs reflect the Dutch colonial empire. Nearly all the stained glass was designed and made by glazier William Bogtman. It has been a Rijksmonument since 1972.

Manila City Hall, in the historic centre of Ermita, is the city's seat of government, home to the Mayor's office and the City Council. It was first planned as part of a national government centre conceived by Daniel H. Burnham in the 1900s. Juan M. Arellano drew an Art Deco design for it, but he quit, and his replacement, Antonio Manalac Toledo, designed the Neoclassical building that stands today. Finished in 1941, just before World War II, it was heavily damaged by shelling in the Battle and Liberation of Manila in February 1945. Rebuilding departed from the original plans, adding a fifth-floor attic and windows where shells had struck. Three arches on Corinthian columns frame the south balcony, and an octagonal clock tower with a dome rises at the north. In 2019 it was named an Important Cultural Property.

Opened in 1952 as State Fair Arena, this 7,610-seat arena stands on the North Carolina State Fair grounds in Raleigh. Maciej Nowicki of NC State's architecture department designed it but died in a plane crash before building started; local architect William Henley Deitrick saw it through. It was the world's first structure with a cable-supported roof: a saddle of steel cables in tension, held up by parabolic concrete arches in compression. The arches cross some 26 feet up and continue underground, where further cables tie their ends, and the outer walls carry next to no weight. In 1953 it was one of just two new US buildings to win the American Institute of Architects' National Honor Award, and it inspired many architects and civil engineers in the US and abroad.

The larger of Istanbul's two international airports lies well outside the city, in Arnavutköy on its European side. Atatürk Airport could not expand, boxed in by urban areas on three sides, with the Sea of Marmara closing the fourth, and Sabiha Gökçen had reached capacity, so a site with ample room was chosen. Grimshaw Architects, Nordic Office of Architecture and Haptic Architects produced the concept design; Scott Brownrigg was lead delivery architect and, with IGA Design, shaped the interior concept. It opened on its planned date, 29 October 2018. The first stage's main terminal covers 1,440,000 m2 and can handle 90 million passengers a year, ranking third in the world among terminal buildings. The control tower takes the form of a tulip, Turkey's national flower. It is the country's largest airport and among Europe's busiest.

The biggest post office building in Turkey stands in Sirkeci, in the Eminönü quarter of Istanbul's Fatih district. Vedat Tek designed it, and it was built from 1905 to 1909 among the first works of the First Turkish National architectural style. Stairs lead up to a raised main entrance, two turrets frame the building, and the front is faced in cut stone and marble. Ottoman ornament in the classical 16th-century manner dominates: two-colour stonework, tile panels carrying geometric Islamic designs and Kufic calligraphy, tiled sills, and muqarnas on pillar heads and corbels. Inside, the entrance gives onto a large central atrium, a rectangular hall three storeys high, lined with offices on every floor and roofed with glass, mostly orange and blue. On 6 May 2000, four floors of the building became the Istanbul Postal Museum.

Polish architect Józef Płoszko designed this Neo-Gothic house in central Baku for the oil baron Murtuza Mukhtarov, who had it built for his wife, Liza-Khanum Tuganova. On a trip to France the couple saw a French Gothic building, and Liza remarked how happy its tenants must be. Mukhtarov said nothing, but on returning he sent people to France to buy its blueprints, and an exact copy rose in Baku within nine months. When it was finished in 1912, he drove his wife there in a carriage and told her it was her new home. Above the entrance stands a statue of the medieval Polish knight Zawisza Czarny (Zawisza the Black). In Soviet Azerbaijan it was the Palace of Marriage Registrations. Protected since 2001 as a cultural monument of Azerbaijan, it reopened after major restoration on 5 July 2012.

Edificio Lapido, or Palacio Lapido, is a modernist building in central Montevideo, on 18 de Julio Avenue. Juan Aubriot designed it, and it was completed in 1933. It is seen as typical of the renewal Uruguayan architecture went through in the early 20th century under international influence. The building rises fourteen storeys. Until the 1960s the newspaper La Tribuna Popular had its headquarters here, and under the civic–military dictatorship of 1973–1985, opposition publications were secretly produced inside. In 1989 it was named a National Heritage Site. Today it holds homes and offices.

Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh built the Hawa Mahal, the "Palace of Winds", in Jaipur in 1799, to a design by Lal Chand Ustad. Made of red and pink sandstone, it sits at the edge of the City Palace and reaches into the zenana, the women's quarters. The palace is a five-storey pyramid about 50 feet (15 m) high, and its exterior resembles a honeycomb, with 953 small jharokha windows decorated with fine latticework. The screens let royal women watch street life and festivals below without being seen, and they also let cool air through by the Venturi effect, easing summer heat. Domed canopies, fluted pillars and lotus and floral patterns come from Rajput building, the stone inlay filigree and arches from Mughal work. The face seen from the street, often taken for the front, is in fact the back.

Named after C. N. Annadurai, a former chief minister of Tamil Nadu, this state library of the Tamil Nadu government stands in Kotturpuram, Chennai. C. N. Raghavendran designed it. The nine-floor building sits on 8 acres, has 333,140 sq ft of floor area and holds up to 1.2 million books. It is planned so that daylight reaches the reading areas well; service spaces line the western end to keep out solar radiation, and a seven-storey atrium brings in plenty of natural light. In July 2010 it received a LEED NC Gold rating from the IGBC, the first library building in Asia to earn one. Facilities include a 50,000 sq ft auditorium seating 1,280, a terrace amphitheatre for more than 800 people, and two conference halls for 151 and 30.

This arch monument, also known as Kolkata Gate and credited to Vector Designs, stands over the third roundabout on Biswa Bangla Sarani in Action Area 1 of New Town, Kolkata, close to Rabindra Tirtha. Construction began on 6 March 2017. It rises 55 metres (180 feet). Two parabolic arches, rising from four corners of the junction, carry a ring whose circular viewing gallery, 60 metres across, sits about 25 metres above the ground. The four legs rest on concrete foundations, and 70 tonnes of steel went into the structure. Two staircases and a lift lead up to the gallery, which takes up to 100 visitors at a time. Paintings of notable figures line the inner wall of the ring, while its outer side is a glass façade looking over the township. The gate also contains India's first hanging restaurant.

Dhaka's Novotheatre, a planetarium, stands in Tejgaon on Bijoy Sarani Avenue. The Bangladesh government's Ministry of Science and Communication Technology commissioned the space centre, and architect Ali Imam designed it. It opened to the public on 25 September 2004. Its curved ceiling stands for the sky: moving pictures of stars and planets are projected onto a large dome screen set at a 120-degree angle. It was formerly known as Bhasani Novotheatre and as Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Novotheatre; on 20 March 2025 an ordinance of Bangladesh's interim government changed the name from the latter to Novotheatre.

Also known as Independence Square, Black Star Square is a public space in Accra whose neighbours are the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park and the Accra Sports Stadium. Kwame Nkrumah commissioned it to mark Ghana's independence, and the Ghanaian architect Theo Lawson designed it. It was finished in 1961, in time for Queen Elizabeth II's state visit. Its stands seat 30,000 people. Every civic and military parade and other national gathering takes place here, and the yearly independence celebrations are often held here. Three monuments recall the struggle for independence and liberation: the Black Star Gate (or Black Star Monument), the Independence Arch and the Liberation Day Monument. Facing the Independence Arch, a statue of a soldier stands for the Ghanaians who died fighting for independence.

The Al-Rifa'i Mosque stands in Citadel Square, beside the Citadel in Islamic Cairo, and doubles as a royal mausoleum for the family of Muhammad Ali. It faces the Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Hassan and was conceived to complement it, part of a wide effort by Egypt's 19th-century rulers to tie themselves to the supposed glory of Egypt's earlier Islamic eras while modernising the city. Commissioned for Hoshiyar Qadin, mother of Khedive Isma'il Pasha, it was built in two phases between 1869 and 1912. The first architect, Hussein Fahmi Pasha, died during the first phase, and work stopped when Isma'il abdicated in 1880. It resumed only in 1905, under Abbas II, with the Hungarian architect Max Herz supervising. The design is Neo-Mamluk, then in fashion in Cairo, and its two minarets rise from circular bases like those of the Sultan Hassan Mosque.

The Bank of China Building occupies No. 23, the Bund, in Shanghai, where the old German Club (c. 1907) once stood. Once the bank's headquarters, it now holds its Shanghai Branch. In April 1934 the board chose to put up an 18-floor building there for the Head Office and Shanghai Branch. The original design had 34 floors and would have been the tallest in the Far East, but Victor Sassoon insisted that no building next to his could rise above the spire of Sassoon House, so the tower was cut almost in half, ending 1 foot below its neighbour. Palmer & Turner drew up the design together with Lu Qianshou (Luke Him Sau), the bank's chief architect. The structure was topped out in 1937, just as the Second Sino-Japanese War began, which delayed its completion.

Broadway Mansions rises near where Suzhou Creek meets the Huangpu River, at the northern end of the Bund in Shanghai. Built between 1930 and October 1934 for $10 million (Mexican), it began as an exclusive residential hotel; the Ye Guang Estate Property Company built it for Shanghai Land Investment Company, which Sir Victor Sassoon controlled. B. Flazer of Palmer & Turner designed it, and John William Barrow of the same firm supervised construction as structural engineer. Its steel frame is clad in red brick and stands 78 metres (256 ft) high with 24,596 m2 of floor space, and its plan follows the Chinese character for eight, a sign of luck and prosperity. It was Shanghai's tallest apartment building for decades and marked the start of Asia's high-rise era. It now operates as a five-star hotel of nineteen floors.

Dallas Hall was the first building at Southern Methodist University (SMU), whose campus lies in University Park, Texas. Robert Stewart Hyer, SMU's first president, chose Georgian architecture after Thomas Jefferson's buildings for the University of Virginia, and the hall, by the firm Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge, also shows the influence of the Roman Pantheon. Work started in 1912, with the cornerstone laid on 28 November, and the hall was dedicated in 1915. The three-storey brick building occupies one of Dallas County's highest points. It once stood alone on flat prairie, and that, with its monumental size, gave SMU its nickname, "The Hilltop". Its crest was aligned exactly with the Praetorian Building, then Dallas's tallest. A highly symmetrical campus has since grown around it. It joined the US National Register of Historic Places on 17 November 1978.

The Dr. Phillips Center, a performing arts center in Downtown Orlando, Florida, takes up two city blocks and held its grand opening on 6 November 2014. Barton Myers was design architect, and two firms, Theatre Project Consultants and Artec Acoustic Consultants, co-designed the theatres; HKS Architects served as executive architect, together with Baker Barrios Architects. The largest room is the Walt Disney Theater, an amplified hall of 2,700 seats for Broadway musicals and concerts of many kinds, and the 300-seat Alexis & Pugh Theater takes smaller shows and events. A third venue, Steinmetz Hall, was begun on 6 March 2017 and opened on 14 January 2022. This 1,700-seat multiform theatre can be set up as a symphony concert hall, a proscenium theatre or a banquet hall.

Council House stands on St Georges Terrace in central Perth, next to Stirling Gardens and Government House; it has 13 storeys and rises 49.8 metres (163 ft). Howlett and Bailey Architects won it in competition, the jury, Harry Seidler among them, praising their scheme as "a remarkably simple solution to a complex problem". Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1963. No earlier Perth building had used complete window walling; to cut the heat entering through the full-height glass, it has internal blinds and external sunbreakers, white and T-shaped, finished in fine mosaic tiles and set in an alternating pattern. In the 1990s the State Government refused heritage listing and urged demolition, but the City of Perth renovated the tower and kept it as its headquarters. It was Jeffrey Howlett's favourite, and has been called Perth's most important modernist building.

The Bauhaus Museum Weimar shows the State Bauhaus's Weimar collections; the school itself was founded in Weimar in 1919. The museum, a project of the Klassik Stiftung Weimar, first opened in 1995 and moved into a new building near the Weimarhallenpark in April 2019. Because the new museum would shape future planning decisions in the city, every possible site in central Weimar was studied carefully before the review board chose the Weimarhallenpark in April 2010. The open international competition drew registrations from 2,189 architects in 60 countries. It awarded two third prizes, one to Bube/Daniela Bergmann of Rotterdam and one to Heike Hanada and Benedict Tonon of Berlin, and the Berlin pair were eventually appointed principal architects. The budget set aside for construction was 14.5 million euros.

Brooklyn officials held a design competition for this museum and chose McKim, Mead & White, who designed it in the Beaux-Arts manner. With 560,000 sq ft (52,000 m2) and around 500,000 objects, it ranks second in size among New York City's museums. It opened on 2 October 1897, one of the last major buildings put up in Brooklyn before the City of Greater New York was formed in 1898. Its steel frame is clad in masonry. The original plan was four times larger than what was built between 1893 and 1927. The 510-foot (160 m) north front on Eastern Parkway has west and east wings either side of a projecting pavilion, whose portico of six Ionic columns carries a pediment with sculptures by Daniel Chester French. Polshek's 2004 renovation added today's entrance: a glazed pavilion and four metal pylons.

This art museum in the city of Akita grew out of the Akita Prefectural Museum of Art, which first opened on 5 May 1967; the new museum opened on 28 September 2013. Tadao Ando designed its triangular building. Just inside the entrance, a staircase that stands free and a three-sided skylight greet visitors. Upstairs, the shop and cafe sit behind glass panels along one side, with views over Senshu Park, where Akita Castle once stood. Its main exhibit is the work of Tsuguharu Foujita, from the Masakichi Hirano Art Foundation's collection.

Frank Gehry designed this outpatient neurological centre in downtown Las Vegas, run by the Cleveland Clinic for research, clinical treatment and education on brain disorders. Ground was broken ceremonially on 9 February 2007, and it opened on 21 May 2010. It stands in the city's 61-acre (25 ha) Symphony Park, on land the City of Las Vegas deeded to the centre's fundraising arm, Keep Memory Alive. Its roughly 65,000 square feet (6,000 m2) hold 13 examination rooms, offices for clinicians and researchers, a community auditorium and a "Museum of the Mind". Opinions split. One account called the design "riotously sculptural", its opposed sections alluding to the old divide between left brain and right brain; others found it modern architecture adrift from aesthetics, even "hideously awful".

Curve is a theatre in the cultural quarter of Leicester's city centre, beside Leicester Athena, a conference and banqueting centre. Rafael Viñoly designed it, working with Kahle Acoustics and with ducks scéno and Charcoalblue as scenographers; Adams Kara Taylor engineered the structure, and Arup did the mechanical and electrical design. There are two auditoria: the 970-seat Theatre and the 350-seat Studio, which has its own power flying system. Together with their stages they can open into one space for 1,300. Two 18-tonne steel walls divide stage from foyer; raise them and the stage is visible from the street. The glass façade wraps an open-plan foyer with views of the café, bars, backstage and stage. Costs on the project, built by Lendlease, more than doubled the first estimates. It opened on 11 November 2008 with the show Lift Off.

Foster + Partners designed this New York office building for L&L Holding and GreenOak Real Estate, redeveloping a 388-foot (118 m) building originally by Kahn & Jacobs. L&L sought bids from 11 firms and shortlisted four: OMA, Zaha Hadid Architects, Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners and Foster + Partners. According to the news site YIMBY, Foster's three concrete fins, each roughly 200 ft (61 m), promised "the most pronounced skyline effect" of the four. Rules let a redeveloped pre-1961 building keep its original floor area if a quarter or more of the old structure stayed. Twelve new jumbo columns were raised, six at the front and six at the centre, with a new core at the back. Work began in 2016; Lord Norman Foster attended the topping out on 4 December 2018, and it was completed in October 2022.

Frank Lloyd Wright's design for this Wauwatosa, Wisconsin, church dates from 1956. It was completed in 1961, after his death, and is one of his last works. Its plan is a Greek cross. Wright drew on traditional Byzantine forms, the Hagia Sophia above all, but reworked them for a modern setting rather than offering a purely historicist tribute. Wide arches carry the upper level, or balcony, and the roof dome rests on an inverted dome, or bowl. The shallow scalloped dome resembles that of California's Marin County Civic Center, another Wright design. Much of the building uses gold-anodized aluminium, at the time a new material established by Alcoa. The church is on the US National Register of Historic Places.

Stanford University's Bing Concert Hall, a venue for the performing arts, opened in January 2013. Richard Olcott of Ennead Architects designed it, while Yasuhisa Toyota of Nagata Acoustics handled the acoustics; Toyota's other work includes Los Angeles's Walt Disney Concert Hall and Miami Beach's New World Symphony. At the centre sits an oval hall of 842 seats, set in terraces around the stage in the vineyard manner. No seat is more than 75 feet from the conductor, and the middle section starts level with the stage itself. To the north lies the smaller Bing Studio, which can be rearranged for cabaret, club, theatre and other kinds of performance. In the end the building cost $111.9 million to construct.

Alvar Aalto designed this church in Imatra, finished in 1958, and it is said to be the most original of his church designs. Its name comes from the three crosses at the altar. Inside, three halls follow one after another and can be divided by sliding walls, so that during the week parts of the building can serve parish activities. Outside, white walls meet a roof covered in copper. In 1998 a committee named by the Finnish Heritage Agency to mark a hundred years since Aalto's birth chose it as one of the five most important buildings he designed. The agency also lists it as built heritage of national significance, and Docomomo counts it as a significant work of modern architecture in Finland. In July 2026 UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site together with 12 other Aalto works.

The main venue of the 1972 Summer Olympics stands in the middle of Munich's Olympiapark. The German architect Günther Behnisch and engineer Frei Otto designed it with help from John Argyris, and its light tent structure was thought revolutionary at the time. Canopies of acrylic glass held by steel cables were used here on a large scale for the first time. The roof was meant to echo the Alpine skyline and to answer the 1936 Berlin Olympics, held under the Nazis; its sweeping, transparent canopy was to stand for a new, democratic and optimistic West Germany. Otto tested parts of the roof by trial and error on larger models; Andrä and Leonhardt used a CAD program. Postwar bomb rubble was heaped into the Olympic Mountain, deliberately made oval to serve as a base for a stadium's stands.

CaixaForum Madrid occupies a former power station on the Paseo del Prado. The old plant, known as Central del Mediodía, dates from the 1900s. Herzog & de Meuron, the Swiss practice, designed the cultural centre, and the firm Ferrovial built it between 2001 and 2007. It opened to the public in 2008 and shows temporary exhibitions of art alongside cultural events. The centre belongs to "la Caixa", a banking foundation run on a not-for-profit basis. Out on the square, Patrick Blanc's Vertical Garden is also well known.

Mérida's National Museum of Roman Art is a museum of archaeology given over to Roman art. It shows a great deal of material from the city's own remains: Mérida was the Roman colony of Augusta Emerita, and its ensemble of ruins is one of Spain's largest, most extensive archaeological sites, on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1993. The museum took its present name in 1975, when it was refounded to mark two thousand years since the city was founded. Its current building is by the Spanish architect Rafael Moneo. Work on site started in 1981, and the new premises were unveiled on 19 September 1986.

Known informally as the Cheesegrater, this skyscraper in central London rises 225 metres. Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners designed it, and it opened in July 2014. Most tall buildings rely on a concrete core for stability; here a steel "Megaframe" engineered by Arup steadies the whole structure, the tallest of its kind in the world. One side is a tapering glass face through which the steel bracing shows, with a ladder frame stressing the height. The flat side, also glazed, holds the lift shafts and other services, put on show as at the nearby Lloyd's Building, with bright orange counterweights and lift motors. At the base, a public atrium 30 metres high extends the plaza next door. The slanting wedge was meant to lessen the impact on the protected view of St Paul's Cathedral from Fleet Street and the west.

The Dutch government gave the commission for a Van Gogh museum to Gerrit Rietveld, a Dutch architect who also designed furniture, in 1963. He died a year after that, and the building was not finished until 1973, the year the museum opened. It now holds more of Van Gogh's drawings and paintings than any other collection in the world. Rietveld's building is the principal one, home to the permanent collection, and rises four storeys over a rectangular plan. During 1998 and 1999 Martien van Goor, also a Dutch architect, renovated it, and a new exhibition wing by Kisho Kurokawa of Japan was added. A tunnel leads from the Rietveld building to the entrance of the Kurokawa wing.

Art Tower Mito opened in 1990 as part of the celebrations for the hundredth anniversary of the municipality of Mito. Arata Isozaki was the architect, and Nagata Acoustics was responsible for the acoustic design. The complex brings together a concert hall with 680 seats, a theatre for up to 636 people, a gallery of contemporary art and a landmark tower that rises 100 metres. The design draws on the Boerdijk–Coxeter helix. One account of Isozaki's career dates the project to 1986–90 and names it among the buildings of a later, more modernist style that he developed.

Known as the Arctic Cathedral, this church in Tromsø is in fact a parish church rather than a cathedral. Jan Inge Hovig designed it in 1960, and it was built in 1965 to his plans, in concrete and metal and in a long church style; it is regarded as his most notable work. The church is built of cast-in-place concrete panels coated with aluminium. Its shape is thought to refer to Håja, a nearby island with two peaks. The church seats about 600 people. In 1972 a glass mosaic by Victor Sparre, titled "The Return of Christ", was added on the eastern side.

This Catholic church stands in the centre of Rouen, in northern France, in the middle of the old market square, the Place du Vieux-Marché. It was here, in 1431, that Joan of Arc was condemned for heresy and put to death by burning. Louis Arretche received the commission in 1969 and designed both the church and the market halls beside it; the church was finished in 1979. Its sweeping curves are meant to recall the flames that killed Joan and an upturned longship. The tiled roof carries the same theme and shelters a walkway across the square. The stained glass came from the 16th-century Church of Saint Vincent, whose ruins lie a few metres away. That church was almost wholly destroyed in 1944, in the Second World War, but its windows had been removed and stored safely.

Barra da Tijuca, a district in Rio de Janeiro's Southwest Zone, is home to this cultural complex. It was first planned as the Cidade da Música, or City of Music, with an opening set for 2004, but it was formally opened only in January 2013, with a "Rock in Rio" musical. Christian de Portzamparc, a French architect, designed it, and the city paid for construction. The cost caused much controversy: budgeted at R$86 million, the project reached R$515 million, roughly US$250 million. With 1,780 seats, it is South America's largest modern concert hall and the new home of the Brazilian Symphony Orchestra. Spread over about 90,000 square metres, the complex also holds a hall for chamber music, three theatres and a dozen rehearsal rooms, and its terrace gives wide views over the surrounding district.

Carlos Raúl Villanueva designed this stadium for the Ciudad Universitaria de Caracas, the city's university campus. The first designs were reworked in 1949; the stadiums went up the following year and were inaugurated in 1951. Building them opened a new stage in the growth of the campus's Conjunto Central, or Central Complex. UNESCO picks out the university's Olympic Stadium as one of the campus's design elements. Football is its main use: it is the home ground of Caracas F.C. and has seats for close to 24,000 spectators. Besides the pitch, it holds a full-size running track and areas for field events, among them jumping tracks and sandpits.

On the Grand Canal in Venice's Dorsoduro district, close to the basilica of Santa Maria della Salute, stands a palace that was never finished. Lorenzo Boschetti, who also designed the facade of the church of San Barnaba, drew it up in 1749 for the Venier family. His scheme set out to blend the manner of Palladio with that of Longhena, both architects whose legacy in Venice is large. Money troubles in the Venier family halted the work, and only part of the first floor was built. What stands today is a single storey with a rusticated front of Istrian stone, while a wooden model in the Correr Museum shows how the full palazzo would have looked. Peggy Guggenheim bought it in 1948, making it her Venetian home and the setting for her small but valuable collection of modern art.

Run by the federal government, the Australian National Maritime Museum stands at Darling Harbour in Sydney. The federal government and that of New South Wales both saw it as a key part of the area's redevelopment, expecting it to draw crowds and help the precinct do well commercially. Philip Cox, Richardson Taylor & Partners designed the building. Its corrugated metal roof is shaped to suggest billowing sails, standing more than 25 metres high on the west side and dropping sharply to the east. Construction ended on 17 November 1989, by which time the cost had grown to $70 million. The federal government would pay the first $30 million, but it and the state argued over who should find the other $40 million. That dispute, together with delays and overruns, pushed the planned 1988 opening back to 1991.

The Dentsu Building, the company's headquarters, is a high-rise in Tokyo's Shiodome district, part of Minato. The French architect Jean Nouvel designed it, and it was completed in 2002. Its 48 floors reach 213.34 metres, ranking it twelfth in height among Tokyo's buildings and second within Shiodome. It stands where Tokyo's first train station once was, beside the Hamarikyu Gardens, where a shōgun once had a holiday home. Collectors on the roof gather rainwater for the plumbing, and ceramic dots on the glass work with computer-controlled shades to keep down the cost of climate control. Apart from sludge, every kind of waste produced while it was being built was recycled.

Aurora Place in Sydney is made up of two towers: an 18-storey residential building beside a 41-storey office building. Their facades differ, but both carry similar sunscreens of metal and glass on their roofs. The office tower has a quietly unusual form, its east face bulging slightly outward from the base and reaching its greatest width on the top floors. That curved, twisted east face echoes the Sydney Opera House on the harbour. The glass curtain wall runs past the main frame, so the wall seems to stand apart from the building. Renzo Piano designed an outer skin of glass and ceramics to temper the strength of the sunlight, and earth-coloured ceramic tiles add a touch of colour to the facade. Inside the office building, every floor has its own winter garden.

This museum in Rome shelters the Ara Pacis of Augustus, which was first inaugurated on 30 January 9 BC. The American architect Richard Meier designed it using steel, glass, travertine and plaster, and it is the first large piece of architecture and urban design placed in Rome's historic centre since the Fascist era. It replaced Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo's building of 1938, part of Mussolini's remaking of Piazza Augusto Imperatore. After seven years of work the new museum opened on 21 April 2006, the anniversary of Rome's traditional founding date. Broad glazing and skylights bring light into the central pavilion. White is a hallmark of Meier's work; travertine panels on part of the building replaced the aluminium first planned, after criticism of its effect on the cityscape. Opinion on it is split; The New York Times called it a flop.

Louis Naidorf, working at Welton Becket Associates, designed this 13-storey tower in Hollywood, Los Angeles. It is considered the world's first circular office building, and its design grew from Naidorf's graduate school drawings; he was 24 when he designed it. Capitol Records' president Glen Wallichs at first wanted a rectangular building, so Naidorf gave him both. Wallichs's lender preferred the round one, thinking it would draw notice and lease more easily. The wide curved awnings over each floor and the tall spike on top resemble records stacked on a turntable, though only by chance, since Becket had kept the client's name a secret. The height keeps to the 150-foot zoning limit of the time, and the light on top blinks "Hollywood" in Morse code. Now a city landmark, it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Built between 1932 and 1936 in Barcelona's Sant Andreu district, Casa Bloc is a large housing block of more than 200 apartments. Josep Lluís Sert, Joan Baptista Subirana and Josep Torres Clavé designed it for local workers, many of whom still lived in shacks in very poor conditions. The GATCPAC group wanted it to carry its key ideas: decent homes at low cost, new forms of shared living and collective identity, and a new urbanism grounded in a fresh concept of the city. The Spanish Civil War kept the building from being completed, and the war's end also ended the thinking behind it. Catalonia's government listed it as a protected Monument in 1992.

Rising 42 storeys and 535 feet (163 m), the Cathedral of Learning is the centrepiece of the University of Pittsburgh's main campus in Oakland. No educational building in the Western Hemisphere is taller, and among university buildings only Moscow State University's main building exceeds it. Philadelphian Charles Klauder, a leading Gothic architect of his day, spent two years on a design that tried to join the modern skyscraper with Gothic tradition. A steel frame is clad in Indiana limestone. Commissioned in 1921, it broke ground in 1926, held its first class in 1931 and was formally dedicated in June 1937. On the ground floor, the Commons Room, an English Perpendicular Gothic hall, covers half an acre and rises four storeys; Guastavino acoustic tiles between the vault ribs keep it quiet. Classrooms around it include the 31 Nationality Rooms.

The Cuvilliés Theatre, or Old Residence Theatre, was formerly the court theatre of Munich's Residenz. François de Cuvilliés built it in the rococo style between 1751 and 1753, and Johann Baptist Straub supervised the carving. The room is decorated in red and gold, and four tiers of 14 boxes each curve around the ground floor in a horseshoe. Opposite the stage, the Electoral box spans the second and third tiers, held up by two Atlas figures framing its entrance. The Bavarian court opera gave the premiere of Mozart's Idomeneo here in 1781, and Weber's Abu Hassan followed in 1811. Wartime bombing hit the building, yet the carved, gilded boxes survived, having been taken down and stored beforehand. Rebuilt with care in the 1950s, it reopened in 1958 with The Marriage of Figaro, then was modernised again in 2004–08.

Emergency, an international NGO that offers free treatment to people affected by war, poverty and landmines, owns and runs this hospital in Entebbe. Here it operates on children from Uganda and the rest of Africa without charge. Renzo Piano designed the building, which was put up in association with TAM Associates. The site, 30 acres (12 ha), was a gift from the UPDF Special Forces Command. The hospital opened on 19 April 2021 with 72 beds. The Ugandan online outlet the Kampala Post put its construction cost in 2021 at USh117 billion, close to €29 million.

Minoru Yamasaki designed this meeting and event building on the Wayne State University campus in Midtown Detroit, finished in 1958. It marks a change in his style, from the International Style of his earlier work toward the New Formalism of the years that followed. The symmetrical two-storey pavilion is clad in travertine marble and rests on a Mankato stone podium; a reflecting pool and sunken garden wrap two of its sides. A triangular motif runs through both the outside and the inside. Within, a skylit entrance hall splits the interior in two, with two levels of conference rooms on either side.
