Architecture magazines praised it at once as "delightful" and "refreshing", and Yamasaki received a First Honor Award for it from the American Institute of Architects. Its architectural quality earned it designation as a National Historic Landmark in 2015.

Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) designed the architecture of this terminal at Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, and also produced the schematic design for its structure and MEP (mechanical, electrical and plumbing) systems, and the roof's detailed structural design. The X-shaped terminal serves both domestic and international travellers, with 450,000 square metres of floor space over four floors. Boarding gates line two piers reaching south from a central processing building, whose roof stands 42 metres high, uses more than 20,000 tonnes of fabricated steel and covers 30 acres. The old International Terminal 2A was pulled down in January 2009 to clear the way. The new terminal was inaugurated in January 2014, five years later, and passenger flights began a month after. The whole project had an estimated cost of ₹98 billion (US$1.0 billion), with more than 12,000 workers expected.

Baitul Mukarram stands in the centre of Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, and was completed in 1968 to a design by the architect Abdulhusein M. Thariani. Its large cubic form was modelled on the Kaaba in Mecca, which sets it apart from every other mosque in Bangladesh. The building adds modern features while keeping to the traditional principles of Mughal architecture, long dominant across the Indian subcontinent. Raised on a very high platform, the eight-storey building rises 99 feet from the ground. The main block has no dome; two domed entrance porticoes, one to the south and one to the north, make up for it. Two roofless courtyards bring light and air into the prayer hall, and the mosque can hold more than 42,000 worshippers.

Completed in 2010, this tower in Ho Chi Minh City was Vietnam's tallest building until January 2011, when Keangnam Hanoi Landmark Tower overtook it. It rises 262.5 metres over 68 floors, with three basement levels; as of May 2022 it ranked second in the city and fourth in the country. Carlos Zapata, who founded Carlos Zapata Studio, designed it, with AREP as architect of record, and took the lotus, Vietnam's national flower, as the inspiration for its shape. Because every floor differs, each of the 6,000 glass panels on its skin was cut to its own specification. On the 52nd floor, Vietnam's first helipad not placed on a roof projects 22 metres from the main structure and can bear a 3-ton helicopter. In 2013 CNN named it one of 25 Great Skyscraper Icons of Construction.

Chulalongkorn University Centenary Park covers 28 rai (4.5 ha, or 11 acres) of campus land in Bangkok. Finished in 2017 for the university's centenary, it was designed by the landscape architects Landprocess as a place to detain rainwater, drawing in part on the "monkey cheeks" project of the late King Bhumibol Adulyadej. After three decades of rapid development, this was the first time a central plot of that size, with a 1.3-kilometre length of road and an estimated value of US$700 million, had become public green space rather than commercial land. Laid on a three-degree slope, the park holds constructed wetlands and cisterns below ground with room for one million gallons (3.8 million litres). Its ecological parts show a way of adapting to water and managing the city's bond with it, instead of fearing it.

Standing in the historic Ulus quarter, Ankara's railway station is one of the city's landmarks. In 1935 President Mustafa Kemal Atatürk asked that a Turkish architect be chosen for the new station building, and Şekip Akalın, then 25, got the job. He went to Europe to prepare the design and, taking his cue from the Art Deco movement then sweeping the continent, drew the building in that style. Akalın was 27 when the building was finished in 1937. The station appears on a list by Turkey's Chamber of Civil Engineers of fifty notable civil engineering works realised during the chamber's first half-century.

Raised as a horizontal block, the Aérohabitat in Algiers went up between 1952 and 1955. Louis Miquel is credited with it, working with Pierre Bourlier and José Ferrer-Laloë; all three belonged to CIAM-Algiers (the International Congresses of Modern Architecture). The complex has 300 apartments in four buildings. Its aim was to give shape to a new kind of city, a "vertical village" known as the Unité d'habitation, and it follows the "immeuble-villas" concept begun by the architect Le Corbusier. Halfway up the main building, Miquel set an interior street resembling a shopping gallery. Le Corbusier had kept circulation inside; Miquel instead served the apartments from circulation on the outside.

Bruce Goff designed the Bavinger House in Norman, Oklahoma, completed in 1955. Nancy and Eugene Bavinger, the artists who lived there, spent five years building it, helped by a few of Eugene's students, volunteers and local firms. Its wall formed a logarithmic spiral 96 feet long. Eugene dynamited its 200 tons of local "ironrock" sandstone from farmland a few miles off near Robin Hill School and hauled it back on his 1948 Chevy flatbed. A recycled oil field drill stem became a mast over 55 feet tall that anchored the structure. In place of interior walls were platforms at various heights, some curtained for privacy. Regarded as a significant work of organic architecture, the house received the AIA's Twenty-five Year Award in 1987. Listed on the National Register in 2001, it was demolished in 2016 and delisted the next year.

Tadao Ando designed this private house in Tarumi-ku, Kobe, on the shore of Japan's Inland Sea. Built in 2003, it stands on a lot of about 65 square metres that belonged to Yoshinari Nakata. The house is a four-storey tower just 4 metres by 4 metres in plan. Bedrooms fill the middle floors, while the kitchen and living room sit at the top. That uppermost floor is a 4-metre cube shifted exactly 1 metre off the building's vertical axis toward the water, so that looking out at the horizon feels like being at sea. To resist sideways forces, the house is cased in concrete and set deep in the ground. A copy was also made: where the original is concrete with a staircase, the copy is built of wood, laminated Oregon pine and Paulownia, and has a lift.

Known by its acronym MALBA, the Buenos Aires museum of Latin American art stands on Avenida Figueroa Alcorta in the Palermo district. It was created by the Argentine businessman Eduardo Costantini and is run by a not-for-profit body, the Fundación MALBA – Costantini. Its design came from an open competition that drew 450 entries from 45 countries. An international jury of architects awarded first prize to three young Argentine architects, Alfredo Tapia, Martin Fourcade and Gaston Atelman, and the Argentine firm AFT Architects carried out the building. Construction on a big site along the avenue began under Costantini in 1998, and the museum opened on 21 September 2001. Its aim is to gather, conserve, research and promote art from Latin America, from the early 1900s up to today.

Chorsu Bazaar, also spelled Charsu, is the traditional market at the heart of the old quarter of Tashkent, the Uzbek capital. Its name comes from Persian and means "crossroads" or "four streams". Everyday goods of every kind are sold beneath its blue dome and in the areas around it. The modern building and its distinctive blue dome were designed in 1980 by Vladimir Azimov, Sabir Adylov and others, a late work in the Soviet Modernist style. On the bazaar's edge stands the Kukeldash Madrasah, built around 1570. In July 2026 UNESCO named the bazaar a World Heritage Site, together with nine more of the city's modernist sites.

The Arvo Pärt Centre, an archive for the composer, lies in Laulasmaa, a village on the coast of Lääne-Harju Parish, about 35 kilometres west of Tallinn. Its design competition drew 71 entries from 24 countries, and on 20 June 2014 Estonia's President, Toomas Hendrik Ilves, named the winner: Nieto Sobejano Arquitectos, the Spanish practice of Enrique Sobejano and Fuensanta Nieto. In its pine forest, the building stays below the treetops, apart from a helical tower with a view of the Baltic Sea. Mostly pentagonal geometries and sinuous curved walls make the spaces run on without a clear start or finish, and large glass walls join the oak-panelled interior to the forest outside. A 150-seat hall suits chamber music. The Estonian government funded the 6.7-million-euro construction, and the building was shortlisted for the 2019 Mies van der Rohe Award.

Felipe, Prince of Asturias, opened MUSAC, the Museum of Contemporary Art of Castilla y León, in April 2005. Agustín Pérez Rubio, its curator, called it a "Museum of the Present", and it collects only work by the newest generation of artists. The studio of Emilio Tuñón and Luis M. Mansilla designed the building, whose multicoloured exterior panels recall the stained glass of a cathedral. The architects took their cue from The Falconer, the main rose window of León's 13th-century Gothic cathedral, Santa María de León. Among other prizes, the building won the EU's Prize for Contemporary Architecture (the Mies van der Rohe Award) in 2007. It has become a landmark for León, and in 2006 MoMA in New York featured it in the exhibition On-Site: New Architecture in Spain.

Building 21 once held the offices of Bata Shoes, the shoe company then based in Zlín; the Zlín Region now has its headquarters there. Vladimír Karfík designed it in a Constructivist manner, and work ran from 1936 to 1938 at the direction of Jan Antonín Baťa, then head of the company, who had succeeded Tomáš Baťa, his half-brother, after Tomáš's death. Rising 77.5 metres over sixteen floors, it was among Europe's first high-rises and the third-tallest pre-war skyscraper, after the Telefónica Building in Madrid and the Boerentoren in Antwerp. A reinforced concrete frame with spirally reinforced round columns carries it. Heating and air conditioning could be set separately on every floor, and the director's office, 6 by 6 metres, was an air-conditioned lift, a technical rarity. It was listed as a cultural monument in 1958.

Known officially as Estadio Banorte for sponsorship, Estadio Azteca is a football stadium in Coyoacán, Mexico City. Designed by Rafael Mijares Alcérreca and Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, it broke ground in 1961, and Club América met Torino F.C. in its first match on 29 May 1966, with room for 107,494 spectators. A later upgrade raised seating from 83,000 to about 87,500, and it is now the largest stadium in Latin America. It was the first stadium to stage two World Cup finals, Brazil's 4–1 victory over Italy (1970) and Argentina's 3–2 victory over West Germany (1986). It was also the main football venue of the 1968 Summer Olympics and of the Women's World Cup of 1971. With games at the 2026 World Cup, including the Mexico–South Africa opener, it became the only venue to have hosted matches at three World Cups.

Most SNP, named for the Slovak National Uprising and widely called the UFO Bridge, went by Nový most, or New Bridge, between 1993 and 2012, and carries a road over the Danube in Bratislava. Built from 1967 to 1972 under a project managed by Tesár, Lacko and Slameň, it opened on 26 August 1972. The asymmetrical cable-stayed bridge spans 303 metres in its main section and 430.8 metres overall, and no bridge in the world with a single pylon and a single plane of cables is longer. Four traffic lanes run on the upper deck, with cycle and foot lanes below. A flying saucer-shaped structure crowns the 84.6-metre pylon, holding a viewing deck and restaurant, named UFO since 2005. Building its approach road meant demolishing a significant section of the Old Town below, including almost all of its Jewish quarter.

Onagawa Station is the terminus of the Ishinomaki Line, 44.9 kilometres from Kogota Station at the line's other end. The tsunami of 11 March 2011 destroyed the station building and nearby tracks, and services stopped. A little over four years later, on 21 March 2015, the rebuilt station reopened, marking the return of service along the whole Ishinomaki Line. The new building has a community centre and a public bath on its upper floors. It was designed by Shigeru Ban, winner of the Pritzker Architecture Prize, who also helped design temporary housing in the town after the 2011 tsunami.

Seinäjoki City Hall started with a competition. In 1958, while a church was going up nearby, the town asked for designs for a new town hall on the site beside it. The winners, in 1959, were Elissa and Alvar Aalto, in a competition that also included plans for a library, theatre and state office building. The town hall was built in 1961–1962, and the library followed in 1964–1965. Both belong to the Aalto Center, Seinäjoki's administrative and cultural heart: six Aalto buildings, most finished between 1960 and 1968. Aalto also shaped the courtyard that joins them, down to its fountain and outdoor lights. The ensemble ranks among his most important works, its wooden plan is held by New York's Museum of Modern Art, and in July 2026 UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site together with 12 other Aalto works.

In 1958 the Communist Party's Central Committee began planning ten large projects, the "Ten Great Buildings", to mark a decade of the People's Republic, and this station was among them. Work took a little over seven months and was finished on 10 September 1959. On opening that year it was the biggest train station in China and the country's first large modern railway terminal. The south-facing station house mixes Chinese traditional style with Soviet Stalinist architecture, visible in its gilded eaves and tall clock towers. While the design brief was being settled, Zhou Enlai suggested a turret on each wing of the main block, and his idea was adopted. Inside, twelve waiting rooms share 14,000 square metres of floor and could hold 14,000 waiting passengers.

Coliseu do Porto is a theatre and concert hall in northern Portugal, with room for 4,000 standing. Cassiano Branco became principal architect, helped by Júlio de Brito. He also invited Charles Ciclis, who had designed several Paris theatres, though it seems only Ciclis's candelabras and doors reached the final interiors, and he was never paid. The building opened on 19 December 1941 and is an example of Porto's Streamline Moderne and Art Deco. When the venue faced a sale, a group called the Associação "Amigos do Coliseu do Porto" formed and helped stop it; on 28 September 1996 the municipal council bought the building by public deed. The auditorium was entirely rebuilt for better acoustics and sightlines, with a warehouse added beneath it, and the building is classified as a Property of Public Interest.

AAMI Park, formally Melbourne Rectangular Stadium, stands in the Melbourne Sports and Entertainment Precinct. It is mainly a soccer and rugby league ground, home to Melbourne Victory FC, Melbourne City FC and the Melbourne Storm. Built in 2010, it replaced Olympic Park, a ground meant for track and field, as the city's main rectangular stadium, and is described as the first large stadium purpose-built for rectangular sports. Its 30,050 seats make it Melbourne's third largest stadium. COX Architecture gave it a "Bioframe" design: a geodesic dome roof shelters much of the seating yet lets light reach the pitch. Thousands of programmable LED lights on the outside can show patterns and images. The foundations allow for 50,000 seats, but the roof was not planned for that, so expanding would need major work. Early in construction it was nicknamed the Bubble Dome.

Christchurch Art Gallery, Te Puna o Waiwhetū in Māori, is the city's public gallery of art. A design competition opened in 1998, and the Buchan Group designed the building, which opened on 10 May 2003. It replaced the Robert McDougall Art Gallery, the city's earlier public gallery, which had been open since 1932. The design plans for earthquakes: the building rests on a concrete raft slab laid on the ground's surface, which spreads seismic forces evenly. After the 2011 Christchurch earthquake the gallery became the Civil Defence headquarters, a role it kept for seven months. Extensive refurbishment and improvement work followed, and it only reopened on 19 December 2015.

La Grande Borne is a housing estate on the southern edge of Paris, in the Essonne département, spread across the communes of Grigny and Viry-Châtillon. Émile Aillaud designed it, and it was built between 1964 and 1971. Like his earlier estates at Pantin and Forbach, it answers the sameness that came with heavily industrialised building in post-war France, chiefly heavy prefabricated reinforced-concrete panels. His answer lay in urban planning that gives each place more individuality. Blocks are pared down to smooth abstract forms and laid out in curving, serpentine lines; works of art are built into the scheme; and the public spaces are handled with care, some unusually shaped and colourfully treated. The intention was to help residents identify with their surroundings.

Once the Grande Halle aux Boeufs, a cattle hall in the abattoir district, this Paris building is now a cultural centre. During Haussmann's rebuilding of Paris, he proposed gathering the city's abattoirs and meat markets at La Villette, on the outskirts. Jules de Mérindol and Louis-Adolphe Janvier were its designers, and it went up between 1865 and 1867. Of three market halls opened there in the 1860s, only this one survives. Built of cast iron and glass, it measures 250 by 85 metres; three sides are open, and a glazed fourth side is the entrance. In 1982, the year Mitterrand's Grands Projets took in the Parc de la Villette, Bernard Reichen and Philippe Robert got the job of restoring it, and Mitterrand reopened it in January 1985. Today it hosts exhibitions, trade fairs, open-air cinema and music festivals.

Home to the Dukes of Marlborough, this Oxfordshire country house is also where Sir Winston Churchill was born. It takes its name from the 1704 Battle of Blenheim and was meant to reward the 1st Duke for beating French and Bavarian forces in the War of the Spanish Succession. One of England's largest houses, it rose in 1705–1722. John Vanbrugh was a popular playwright with no architectural training, and he usually teamed up with the trained, practical Nicholas Hawksmoor; the pair had just completed early stages of Castle Howard. Vanbrugh designed Blenheim to be viewed from afar, which a site of some seven acres also requires. His Baroque is severe: heavy masses of stone suggest strength and throw shadows that act as ornament, while three blocks make up the Great Court, meant to overwhelm arrivals. UNESCO listed it in 1987.

Once the Viceregal Lodge, Áras an Uachtaráin is where the president of Ireland lives and works, in Dublin's Phoenix Park. Its design is credited to Nathaniel Clements, an amateur, though Richard Cassels, John Wood of Bath and Edward Lovett Pearce probably guided it. Clements, whom George II made Chief Ranger of the park, built it in 1751 as the Ranger's lodge, and it was completed around 1751 to 1757. The Crown bought it in the 1780s as the Lord Lieutenant's summer home, and it was greatly enlarged in 1911 for a visit by George V and Queen Mary. Plans to demolish it were shelved when the Second World War began, and by 1945 it was too bound up with the presidency to lose, though its poor state meant the kitchens, chapel and servants' quarters had to be demolished and rebuilt.

Chichester Festival Theatre stands in Oaklands Park in Chichester, West Sussex, and is listed at Grade II*. Its founder, Leslie Evershed-Martin, compared Chichester with Stratford, Ontario, and decided the city could support a theatre like the Stratford Festival there. Philip Powell and Hidalgo Moya designed it, and Evershed-Martin opened it in 1962. Sir Laurence Olivier was its first artistic director, and the National Theatre's first company came together here. In 1989 the smaller, more intimate Minerva Theatre was added nearby. Powell and Moya's other work includes the Skylon, landmark of the Festival of Britain in 1951, the Museum of London and Wolfson College, Oxford.

First named the Grand Canal Theatre, this performing arts venue in Dublin's Docklands is Ireland's largest fixed-seat theatre, with 2,111 seats. Daniel Libeskind designed it for the DDDA, and Joe O'Reilly of Chartered Land built it, with John Sisk & Sons as main contractor and Arup as main engineers. Work ran from January 2007 to late 2009, and Harry Crosbie opened it on 18 March 2010. The site once held Dublin Gasworks Company structures, demolished in 1985 and later cleaned by the DDDA for over €50M. Libeskind's studio also designed the office blocks on either side so the scheme would read as one, and Martha Schwartz's "red carpet" piazza ties into the theatre. Its stage is the only one in Ireland able to take major London West End shows.

Henry Hobson Richardson designed this public library at 53 Main Street in Easton, Massachusetts, right beside his Oakes Ames Memorial Hall. Oliver Ames Jr. left $50,000 in his will to build it, asking that it be a private institution held in trust for the public, not owned by the town. Built in 1877–1879, it did not open until 10 March 1883. Its facade is light-brown Milford granite set as random ashlar, trimmed in reddish-brown Longmeadow brownstone, under a red-orange tile roof. The gable front has a heavily arched entrance with five arched windows above, paired short columns between them. Inside, the main rooms line up along one axis. Stanford White did most of the reading-room fireplace, and Augustus Saint-Gaudens designed medallions of Ames. It belongs to a group of small, patron-funded New England libraries that together define Richardson's style.

The Campbell Sports Center, by Steven Holl with senior partner Chris McVoy, belongs to Columbia's Baker Field athletics complex, the base of the university's outdoor sports. Standing where Broadway meets West 218th Street, it aims to give the complex a welcoming new front door. Its concept, "points on the ground, lines in space", takes its cue from the play diagrams drawn for football, soccer and baseball, and starts from point foundations set into the slope. Stairs and terraces along the facade link it to the fields, and upper floors look across the complex towards Manhattan. Opened in fall 2012, the five-storey, 48,000 sq ft building contains strength and conditioning rooms, varsity offices, an auditorium, a hospitality suite and study space for student athletes. The New York Times critic Michael Kimmelman judged it "not a beauty" yet "tough, sophisticated and imaginative".

Crawford Manor is a fifteen-storey public housing block in New Haven, started in 1964 to ease a well-documented shortage of homes for needy older people and finished in 1966. Its architect, Paul Rudolph, was then running Yale's architecture school and was a known champion of what came to be called Brutalism; the building counts as a significant work of his maturity. On an irregular C-shaped plan, it combines a steel frame with concrete block walls given a rusticated concrete finish. Windowless piers rise the full height, keeping windows and porches apart. Inside, ribbed rough concrete and poured concrete floors and ceilings echo the exterior. The city owns it and uses it for public housing, now 109 studio or one-bedroom units. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.

MIT's Building E15, the Wiesner Building, is home to the List Visual Arts Center as well as the MIT Media Lab. I.M. Pei & Partners designed it, and it was dedicated in 1985, named for Jerome Wiesner, a former president of MIT, and his wife Laya. Its form is boxy, and the box theme repeats inside and out, so the spaces read like boxes packed within one another. A flat grid of white modular metal panels sets it apart from its neighbours. The project is known for close teamwork between architect and artists. Kenneth Noland designed the exterior, whose grid recalls graph paper and number matrices as a metaphor for technology while echoing the corridor-like layout of the wider campus. Scott Burton, Alan Shields and Richard Fleischner helped shape the inner atria and outside landscaping.

Completed in 1992 to a design by Dub Architects, Edmonton City Hall houses the city government of Edmonton, Alberta. It stands at the eastern edge of the downtown financial district as the centrepiece of Sir Winston Churchill Square, whose fountain becomes a skating rink in winter. An earlier version had cones meant to recall the tipis in which First Nations people once lived here, but the public disliked them, likening them to dunce caps and nuclear reactors. The architects swapped them for pyramids that evoke the Rocky Mountains and Muttart Conservatory. Two steel and glass pyramids now sit on a three-storey concrete base, one of them 43 metres from ground to peak; one lights the main atrium, the other the council chamber. A 60-metre clock tower, Friendship Tower, carries a set of 23 carillon bells.

Rogers Centre, first called SkyDome, is a stadium with a retractable roof in downtown Toronto, at the foot of the CN Tower near Lake Ontario, and home of the Toronto Blue Jays. Architect Rod Robbie and structural engineer Michael Allen designed it; their entry beat the other finalists by offering the biggest roof opening and the soundest engineering. Built on the former Railway Lands from October 1986 to May 1989, it was the first stadium with a fully retractable motorised roof. That roof, 31 storeys high, has four panels of steel trusses clad in corrugated steel and PVC. The north panel stays fixed; the two middle ones slide over it and the south one swings round to nest inside, a 20-minute move driven by electric 'train' engines on rails. An attached 348-room hotel has 70 rooms facing the field.

Tuschinski is a cinema near Rembrandtplein in Amsterdam, now owned by the French group Pathé. Work began on 18 June 1919, and it was built for around ƒ4 million in a blend of Art Deco, Jugendstil and Amsterdam School styles, with Asian influences too. Its electro-technical systems were seen as revolutionary then, and its heating and ventilation kept the whole building at an even temperature. Two towers frame the western facade, which carries ceramic sculptures and several leaded windows. The lobby was meant to make arriving filmgoers feel they were entering an illusion. Made a national monument in 1967 for its architecture, it was restored to its original style between 1998 and 2002, when a corridor to Tuschinski 3 brought the complex to six auditoriums. At its centenary, Time Out named it the world's most beautiful cinema.

Known as the Palace of Arts between 2005 and 2015, Müpa Budapest stands in the Ferencváros district by Rákóczi Bridge and had its official opening in March 2005. It was designed by the office of Zoboki, Demeter and Partners. On a 10,000 m² footprint it packs 70,000 m² of floors and three institutions, the Ludwig Museum, the Festival Theatre and a concert hall, all raised together over 28 months. The concert hall, named after Bartók, is 52 metres long and 25 metres both wide and high, with 1,656 places, among them 126 on the podium and 60 for standing in the side galleries. Its sound can be tuned with 58 movable resonance chambers and a suspended 42-tonne canopy. Like the National Theatre, it belongs to Budapest's new Millennium City Center.

The Black House Museum, Baan Dam, is a private art museum in Chiang Rai designed by Thawan Duchanee, mixing traditional northern Thai buildings and unconventional contemporary architecture. Over 40 structures are scattered across about 160,000 square metres. Among them is the Cathedral, or Art Museum Building, which Duchanee designed and Baan Dam's engineers built in 1999–2009. It is a large single-storey rectangle aligned east to west, raised about 2.8 metres on brick. Its frame is wood, and each of its 44 wooden pillars has Thai Bua-pattern decoration at the base. A steep four-tier Lanna roof of unglazed clay tiles carries Thai and Lanna ornaments such as swan tails. Stairs lead up to three large doors at its east and west ends. The east pavilion has glass in place of a wall and a Lanna mansard roof of local terracotta.

British architect Frank W Brewer designed the Cathay Building for 16 storeys, but it was finished with 11. It was Singapore's first skyscraper and, at the time, the tallest building in Southeast Asia. Its first part, opened on 3 October 1939, held a 1,300-seat cinema, a dance hall and a restaurant, with a roof garden over the cinema. Its cinema was the first on the island, and the first public building there, to be air-conditioned; its armchairs were a rare comfort then. The 11-storey flats, with a penthouse, opened on 1 July 1940. Here Subhas Chandra Bose, on 21 October 1943, announced the formation of Azad Hind's Provisional Government. Most of it has since been pulled down, leaving only a small part of the main facade, and in 2003 it became the first demolished building gazetted as a national monument.

Atarim Square, also called Namir Square, is a public square and group of buildings in Tel Aviv designed by Yaakov Rechter, and an example of Brutalism in Israel. It was planned as a tourist hub linking the hotels, the beaches and Sderot Ben-Gurion, with a main road along the shore. Work began in 1971, and the structure was stacked on several levels to use the drop from the cliff to the beach. At the bottom are a car park and petrol station; above them runs a covered road, Eliezer Peri Street; indoor shops sit higher up; and the roof forms the square, with restaurants, an amphitheatre and a glass-clad rotunda once called the Colosseum Club. It opened in June 1975. Unlike the smooth white stucco used by his father and fellow architects, Rechter's early work exposed raw concrete.

Also known as the Bridge of Strings or the Jerusalem Light Rail Bridge, this side-spar cable-stayed bridge is the work of Santiago Calatrava, the Spanish architect-engineer. It was his 40th bridge but his first made for both trains and people on foot: the Light Rail's Red Line has crossed it since 19 August 2011, and a glass-sided walkway links Kiryat Moshe with the Central Bus Station. As at his Puente del Alamillo in Seville, an angled cantilever tower takes some of the load and reduces the stays needed. The 118-metre mast holds the deck with 66 steel cables in a parabola curving in three dimensions, and on completion was Jerusalem's tallest structure. Opened on 25 June 2008 for about $70 million, it has been likened to a harp or a desert tent, and criticised as an extravagant, costly fix.

The Royal Tank Museum is a military museum beside King Abdullah II Park in Amman, opened on 29 January 2018 after almost a decade of work. Zaid Daoud, a Jordanian architect, designed it. Across some 20,000 square metres it shows around 110 tanks and armoured vehicles from Jordan, Arab nations and beyond, in date order. The two-level building resembles a square fort on four main pillars, inspired by the desert palaces of the Jordanian Badia and meant to express the strength of tanks and echo a tank's outline. A Cobra helicopter hangs in a glass dome at the centre, standing for Jordan's move from ancient heritage to the future. Materials include a metal frame, glass and fibreglass-reinforced concrete. A reservoir beneath collects water for reuse, solar panels make electricity and LED lights save energy; it is considered a green building.

Sérgio Bernardes designed the Brasília Planetarium in a Brutalist style, and it opened on 15 March 1974. Its setting is the Cultural Diffusion Sector on the Monumental Axis, between the TV Tower and the convention centre named for Ulysses Guimarães, with the Mané Garrincha stadium and the Choro Club close by. Built in bare concrete, its geometric form looks like a flying saucer. At the centre are two half-spherical domes, one set inside the other. Around them stand sixteen identical volumes, kept apart by radial strips a metre thick, so the plan becomes a sixteen-sided figure with concave sides. Each of the sixteen faces stands for one of the sixteen points of the compass rose. Structural problems closed the building for refurbishment in 2006, and it stayed shut until 11 December 2013.

Carrasco International Airport, also named after General Cesáreo L. Berisso, is Uruguay's main international airport and its biggest, in the Carrasco neighbourhood of Montevideo. Work on a new terminal, laid out parallel to Runway 06/24, began on 3 February 2007. Designed by the Uruguayan architect Rafael Viñoly, it can handle 3 million passengers a year and came with a much bigger car park for more than 1,200 vehicles. Arrivals and departures are on separate floors, there are four jetways, and the top floor has a large viewing area. Space is left for two more jetways, and the building could serve up to 6 million passengers a year before it needed real enlargement. It was inaugurated on 5 October 2009 and began official operations on 29 December 2009. It has been cited among Latin America's most efficient and traveller-friendly airports.

The Comega Building rises at 222 Avenida Corrientes in Buenos Aires, where it meets Alem Avenue. It was Argentina's first reinforced-concrete skyscraper and the first building in the city with an outside fully faced in travertine. Engineer Alberto Stein drew up the project with Enrique Douillet and Alfredo Joselevich as architects, and it went up in a rationalist manner from 1921 to 1934. Outside, the edges are straight and there is no ornament. Two wings and a taller central tower, 88 metres high with 21 floors, wrap around an open courtyard. Its five lifts were the first high-speed lifts in Buenos Aires, rising 180 metres a minute, and the granite cladding and stainless steel counters inside were seen as very new and costly then. Listed as city heritage, it was recently renovated, with many original features restored.

La Plata Cathedral stands at the geographical centre of the city, across from City Hall on the main square, Plaza Moreno. Ernesto Meyer drew its plans under the direction of the city planner Pedro Benoit, inspired by the cathedrals of Amiens and Cologne. The cornerstone went down in 1884; the church was consecrated in 1902 as the parish of Our Lady of Sorrows while work went on, and it became a cathedral in 1932. In the 1930s builders stopped, afraid the foundations could not carry the planned size and weight, leaving the spires incomplete and the outer brick undressed. That bare brick is somewhat unusual and makes the Neogothic building resemble brick churches of northern Europe, such as Uppsala Cathedral. A refurbishment opened to the public in 2000, and its 112-metre towers rank it among the Americas' six tallest churches.

The Catedral de San Agustín de Talca stands on the city's Plaza de Armas and serves as the bishop's church for its Chilean diocese. It takes the place of the Mother Church, which the 1928 Talca earthquake destroyed on the same site. Work began in 1938 under Ramón Venegas as architect, and the building was finally consecrated on 30 September 1954. Its walls are masonry and its arches reinforced concrete. Both were damaged when an earthquake struck on 11 March 2010, leaving the church in danger of collapse. Restoration finished in 2012: the walls were strengthened with reinforced concrete and the wooden roof structure was replaced.

Also called the Horagolla Stables, this country house belongs to Sunethra Bandaranaike, and Geoffrey Bawa renovated it during the 1980s. The building was once the original walauwa of Horagolla, where her great-grandfather, a Gate Mudaliyar, lived. Work ran from 1 April 1983 to 25 November 1987. The house has two parts, the old stables and a new wing, which meet in an L shape. New doors and windows were opened up, and an inside mezzanine divides the space into a lower floor and an upper gallery. Above the former stalls, boards naming the horses once kept there are still in place. The building materials were recycled, taken either from the original building or from old houses that had been demolished.

Singha Durbar, whose name means 'Lion's Palace', is a palace complex at the heart of Kathmandu, with Babar Mahal and Thapathali Durbar to its south and Bhadrakali Temple to its west. Chandra Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana had it built in June 1908, to a design by Kumar Narsingh Rana and Kishor Narsingh Rana. Its architecture blends several building traditions, combining Palladian, Corinthian and Neoclassical mansions with Baroque. Before the fire of 1973 it had 8 courtyards and 1,700 rooms, with marble floors, painted ceilings, silver furniture and wide spreads of crystal lighting. The complex is used by Nepal's government for its administrative offices, among them the Federal Parliament and several ministries. During the Gen Z protests of 2025 its main building was destroyed, as was the prime minister's office.

The Alte Feste, or Old Fortress, is a fort and museum on Robert Mugabe Avenue in central Windhoek, beside the Independence Memorial Museum. Captain Curt von François designed it as headquarters for the Schutztruppe, the imperial German colonial force, while Germany ruled South West Africa. A Schutztruppe private, Gustav Tünschel, laid the foundation on 18 October 1890, and the design changed several times in the early years before its final layout was finished in 1915. It has an inner courtyard with high walls, troop quarters inside and four towers. No older building survives in Windhoek, and the city grew up around it. Already badly run down, it was made a National Monument in 1957 and heavily renovated in 1963. It holds the National Museum of Namibia's historic collection, but as of 2023 it was closed and urgently needed repair.

Aichi International Arena opened in Nagoya in July 2025, taking over from the Aichi Prefectural Gymnasium of 1964. In July 2017, close to a year after the prefecture and the city won unanimous selection to stage the 2026 Asian Games, Governor Hideaki Ōmura announced the plans. The site chosen was part of Meijō Park, north of the old gymnasium. Designed by the Japanese architect Kengo Kuma, it seats up to 17,000 people. It is also the venue for the grand sumo tournament held in Nagoya every July.

Baldwin Hills Village, also known as Village Green, is a Los Angeles condominium complex, listed as a National Historic Landmark and as one of the city's Historic-Cultural Monuments. Planned in the late 1930s and complete by 1942, it ranks among the country's oldest planned communities of this type, and the American Institute of Architects counts it among the 100 most important architectural achievements in American history. Reginald D. Johnson designed it with Wilson, Merrill & Alexander, Clarence S. Stein consulting and Fred Barlow Jr. on landscape. The Modernist garden-city scheme held 627 units, with all roads and garages pushed to the edges of its eighty acres. At its centre lies a long oval lawn crossed by paths, with smaller garden courts between the buildings. Plastered one- and two-storey frame homes put the living room and main bedroom facing a garden.

Seat of Lima's archdiocese and Peru's oldest and biggest church, the cathedral stands on the east side of the Plaza Mayor, next to the Archbishop's Palace and the Iglesia del Sagrario. Francisco Pizarro started it in 1535 where an Inca shrine, Puma Inti, and the prince Sinchi Puma's palace had stood; its present form dates from 1602 to 1797. Francisco Becerra drew a new plan, drawing partly on Seville and Jaén cathedrals, for a broad Renaissance church of three big naves plus two side chapels. How to guard against earthquakes was debated: chief architect Juan Martínez de Arrona wanted brick vaults, while several council members preferred wood. Juan Rher made full use of wood and quincha in the ribbed vaults and rebuilt the stone doorway. The bell towers, long unfinished, were rebuilt in 1794–1797 and completed by Matías Maestro.

The Television Cultural Center is a 34-storey tower on East Third Ring Road in Beijing's Central Business District, holding a hotel, a theatre and several television studios. On 20 December 2002 OMA was awarded the contract for the CCTV Headquarters and for this building beside it. Rem Koolhaas and his firm designed the wedge-shaped tower, and Arup, East Asia, engineered it after a long internal study of the World Trade Center collapse in 2001. Like the headquarters, it uses far less steel than ordinary skyscrapers and is built to withstand major earthquakes. One continuous ground-floor lobby leads to a 1,500-seat theatre, a ballroom, digital cinemas, recording studios and exhibition space. Hotel rooms line both sides of the tower, framing an atrium above. A major fire during construction pushed its planned 2009 opening back to 16 May 2012.

The main stadium of the Hangzhou Olympic Sports Expo Center was finished in 2018 and is used mostly for football. It stands on a 60,000 m² site on the Qiantang riverfront, across from the Qianjiang New City business district, and was built by NBBJ in partnership with CCDI. Its 80,800 seats sit on three tiers, and the stands break on the north side to let heat escape and give spectators views of the river. The outside draws on the texture of silk and the moving water of the Qiantang. It is a steel structure of 28 large and 27 small petals. Construction covers 229,000 m², of which 61,000 m² lies underground.

Built for the 2008 Summer Olympics, the Beijing National Indoor Stadium holds 20,000 people. Its design recalls a traditional Chinese folding fan, which earned it the nickname the Fan. Glöckner³ designed it with the Beijing Institute of Architectural Design after winning an international competition in October 2003; before construction started in May 2005, Cox Architecture served as design consultants. The building opened on 26 November 2007 with the artistic gymnastics test event. It returned to Olympic use in 2022, hosting ice hockey at the Winter Olympics and Paralympics.

This temple in Independence, Missouri, serves both worship and teaching and is devoted to "the pursuit of peace". It rises over the city's skyline and has become the centrepiece of the Community of Christ's headquarters. Ground was broken on 6 April 1990, and the finished building was dedicated on 17 April 1994. Gyo Obata's design recalls the spiral shell of a nautilus, crowned by a stainless steel spire 300 feet (91 m) high. A gently rising path of textured stone winds around the edge. The main sanctuary seats about 1,600 and has a Casavant organ with 5,685 pipes. A large stained-glass wall of rice and wheat in the exit foyer won an American Institute of Architects award for religious art. Wide steps open onto a plaza inlaid with a brick world map.

The Knight Building, the Akron Art Museum's 63,000-square-foot addition, came from Coop Himmelb(l)au of Vienna, chosen through an international competition partly for its record of adapting historic buildings. It was the firm's first public building in either of the Americas. Ground was broken on 22 May 2004. The design joins new galleries, an auditorium and a café to the museum's 1899 building through three contrasting parts. The Crystal, a three-storey glass lobby, is the public entrance and the visual hub linking the museum's programmes. The Gallery Box holds the collection and temporary shows. The Roof Cloud, a cantilevered steel and aluminium frame 327 feet long, reaches over old and new alike; one critic likened it to a mechanical alligator eating a Beaux Arts post office. Founder Wolf D. Prix said the design "embraces the past" instead of replacing it.

Balthasar Neumann designed this late Baroque, or Rococo, basilica, built from 1743 to 1772. It honours the Fourteen Holy Helpers, saints venerated together by Catholics, above all in Germany during the Black Death. It sits on a slope above the river Main in Franconia, looking across to Schloss Banz, once a Baroque abbey, on the facing hillside. After the foundation stone was laid, Langheim Abbey altered the plans to cut costs, and by the time Neumann found out, the three apse walls already stood. His answer was to divide the interior into three ovals and bring the altar back to the middle, at the centre of the largest oval. The interior, nicknamed "God's Ballroom", has a pulpit held up by floating white putti, with gilded reliefs of the Evangelists set in shellwork.

This nine-storey building fills a small block on the southern edge of Columbus Circle in Midtown Manhattan, bounded by 58th Street, Broadway and Eighth Avenue. Edward Durell Stone designed it for the A&P heir Huntington Hartford, and its museum, the Gallery of Modern Art, opened on 21 March 1964 and struggled financially for years. Its reinforced-concrete outer walls carry the floors. The first facade was mostly white Vermont marble, with loggias at top and bottom and small windows only at the corners; Stone kept the windows as small as he could, and the press likened them to portholes. The loggia of concrete columns at the base recalled the one at the Doge's Palace. Brad Cloepfil later reworked it for the Museum of Arts and Design (there since 2008) with a new skin of 4-inch terracotta panels cut by deep grooves.

The Güell Pavilions are a group of buildings in Pedralbes, Barcelona, by the Catalan Modernist Antoni Gaudí, built from 1884 to 1887. Gaudí was asked to remodel an existing house and enclose the estate with a wall and gates, and he proposed an Orientalist design with echoes of Mudéjar art. Its rectangular stable is covered by a high Catalan vault on a catenary curve; a square lunging ring carries a hyperboloid dome capped by an ornamental lantern; and of the three small gatehouses, the middle one is polygonal and the others cube-shaped. All are of brick shading from red to yellow, clad in coloured glass, with cement blocks in places. Gaudí planned the main gate as a wrought-iron dragon with glass eyes, standing for Ladon, guardian of the Hesperides' garden. It became a national monument in 1969.

Trinity Church, on Copley Square in Boston's Back Bay, is an Episcopal parish in the Diocese of Massachusetts. When its old home on Summer Street burned in Boston's Great Fire of 1872, the present complex was built under Rector Phillips Brooks, a famous preacher. Henry Hobson Richardson designed church and parish house, built from 1872 to their consecration in 1877. The building made Richardson's name and is the birthplace and model of Richardsonian Romanesque, a style of rough stone, polychromy, clay roofs, a massive tower and heavy arches soon used for public buildings nationwide. Its stone is Dedham Granite. Stanford White, of Richardson's office, designed the main tower in 1872 after the Old Cathedral of Salamanca. This was Richardson's first project with Augustus Saint Gaudens, and the interior is a leading American example of arts and crafts.

Santiago Calatrava designed L'Umbracle, finished in 2001, to do two jobs at Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences: mark an entrance along the complex's southwestern edge and roof over its car park. The structure runs 320 metres by 60 metres on the southern side of the site. Its parabolic arches, 55 fixed and 54 floating, rise to 18 metres. Underneath lies a landscaped walk and sculpture garden planted with species native to Valencia, among them rosemary, rockrose, honeysuckle and bougainvillea. The planting was chosen so its colours shift through the seasons, and it counts 99 palms, 78 smaller palms and 62 bitter orange trees. An open-air gallery inside, the Walk of the Sculptures, shows work by contemporary artists including Yoko Ono. Across the wider complex, ceramic mosaic tiles called trencadís cover many of the concrete surfaces.

Adolf Loos designed and built Steiner House in Vienna in 1910, while his career was still young. It met with a far warmer response than his previous work and soon became an example of rationalist architecture known around the world; it is now counted among his major works. On the street side, a quarter-round roof flattens the top of the house and keeps the two extra floors facing the garden out of sight. A recess between the two wings, carried straight up to the roof, divides the façade into a classical three-part composition. The stucco walls give a smooth, white surface with no ornament. Inside, the living area sits a little above ground level, apart from private rooms such as the bedrooms and the first-floor painting studio, while service spaces go to the basement and attic.

Dragiša Brašovan's Banovina was built from 1936 to 1940 as the administrative seat of the Danube Banovina; today it houses the Government of Vojvodina. His competition entry had fared rather poorly, yet a series of circumstances led to him getting the commission. The style is modernist, with touches of art deco and stripped classicism. The base forms a long, closed horseshoe, rounded at the west end, with a square-based tower at the east. The block is 180 by 44 metres and about 20 metres high; the tower reaches 42. In place of the clinker brick first planned, white Brač marble from the Pučišća quarry clads the outside, and Carrara marble the inside. Offices line the outer walls, off wide corridors facing four inner courtyards. Its resemblance to a big ship with a sail mast earned it the name White Cruiser.

Martin Nyrop won an architectural competition for the sixth Copenhagen City Hall, and the building went up between 1892 and 1905. The City Council has its headquarters here, and the Lord Mayor works from it too. Nyrop's style is National Romantic, yet he drew heavily on the Palazzo Pubblico in Siena, and the square in front was likewise shaped after the shell form of Siena's Piazza del Campo. The plan has two long wings, one along Vester Voldgade and one along H.C. Andersens Boulevard, tied together by three cross buildings. In the gaps between those cross buildings lie the roofed Main Hall and, open to the sky, the City Hall Garden.

Dia Beacon opened in 2003 in Beacon, New York, close to the Hudson, as the home of Dia's collection of art made since the 1960s. It fills a former box-printing plant that Nabisco put up in 1929. Dia carried out the conversion with the artist Robert Irwin and four architects then working as OpenOffice: Linda Taalman, Galia Solomonoff, Lyn Rice and Alan Koch. Its 240,000 square feet (22,000 m²) rank it among the biggest spaces in the United States for modern and contemporary art. Each gallery was planned around the works it holds. Over 34,000 square feet of skylights let in reflected north light, felt most in the rooms for Robert Ryman, Agnes Martin, On Kawara and Blinky Palermo. Irwin also laid out the grounds: an entrance court, a car park planted with flowering fruit trees, and a formal garden.

Steven Holl designed the three-storey Bellevue Arts Museum, which opened in 2001 opposite Bellevue Square. Many local residents credit it with a part in changing downtown Bellevue from a run of suburban strip malls into a city with a range of cultural attractions. Unlike most art museums, it held no permanent collection, offering changing exhibitions instead. The institution behind it, a nonprofit founded in 1975, raised $3 million and remodelled the interior extensively before reopening on 18 June 2005 with a mission centred on art, craft and design and a focus on Northwest artists. Financial trouble led to the museum space closing on 4 September 2024. In October 2025 the museum said it would sell the building and its land to KidsQuest Children's Museum, a local children's museum focused on STEM education.

Carew Tower is a 49-storey Art Deco skyscraper, 574 feet (175 m) tall, in downtown Cincinnati. The city's tallest from 1930 until Great American Tower overtook it in 2011, it is now second. The industrialist John J. Emery wanted one complex to hold offices and shops, a hotel and a parking garage, a "city within a city". Walter W. Ahlschlager was principal architect and Delano & Aldrich associate architect; the final design was prepared by Delano & Aldrich. The project was announced just before the Great Depression began in 1929, but work carried on. Raising 15,000 tons of steel in 61 days set a world record for speed, and the tower topped out in July 1930. Offices took most floors, with a shopping arcade below and an observation deck on top. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1994.

On Ham Common, in Richmond upon Thames, James Stirling and James Gowan designed Langham House Close in 1955; it was built in 1957–58 for the Manousso Group. Their first major project together, influenced by Le Corbusier, secured their standing as leaders of Brutalism. Of the three flat-roofed blocks, Stirling's has three storeys and 18 flats, while Gowan's two each have two storeys and six flats. Second-hand stock brick recalls the old Langham House, and in-situ shuttered concrete is left bare inside and out. In every flat a central fireplace with a back boiler and a linen cupboard sits in exposed brick, with shelves and lintels of concrete. In 1966 the critic Ian Nairn described it as the first example of a new tough style. It has been Grade II* listed since 2006, after pressure from the Twentieth Century Society.

Dům Radost, whose name means House of Joy, is a functionalist building beside Winston Churchill Square in Prague's Žižkov district, built from 1932 to 1934 to designs by Karel Honzík and Josef Havlíček. It stands 52 metres (171 ft) high over 13 floors, and its cross-shaped plan takes its cue from Le Corbusier. At one time it was the tallest office building in the country. It has gone by other names: the House of Trade Unions, the General Pension Administration Palace, and, because of its tiled façade, kachlíkárna, roughly the Tile House. Protected as a Czech cultural monument since 1964, the complex has held offices, flats, a theatre, a cinema, a café and an observatory since 2019.

J. R. Davidson designed Case Study House No. 1 in Los Angeles for the Case Study Houses program, which ran until 1966 and set out to develop low-cost, efficient model homes as postwar America needed housing. His imagined clients, "Mr. and Mrs. X", both worked, had a daughter in her teens, and sometimes hosted a mother-in-law. Finished in 1948, it has one storey: a timber frame on a concrete base, with glass, concrete block and plywood throughout. Tall walls face the street, while glass doors and windows, floor to ceiling, open to the garden and pool behind. It is known for its room layout, built-in storage and furniture, and guest quarters set apart from the rest. Despite its number, it came after Davidson's House No. 11 of 1946. It joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.

Late in the 1960s, John Dinkeloo and Kevin Roche were given the job of designing first-class spaces for art, music and theatre for the children of Massachusetts working families. Their answer for the Amherst campus of the University of Massachusetts, renamed the Randolph W. Bromery Center for the Arts but still commonly called the Fine Arts Center, was built from 1972 to 1974 just north of downtown Amherst and opened on 10 October 1975. The Brutalist concrete structure is 646 feet long and 66 feet high, mirrored in a nearby pond. Part of it is a bridge of art studios held 30 feet above the ground, forming a grand gateway to the campus. Inside are a concert hall and a contemporary art gallery; its 2,000-seat performance hall was the campus's main venue until the Mullins Center opened in 1993.

Le Corbusier designed the Palace of Assembly in Chandigarh, home to both the Punjab and the Haryana Legislative Assemblies. It belongs to the city's Capitol Complex, alongside the Secretariat and the High Court. Work began in 1951 and ended in 1962, eleven years later, and the building was inaugurated on 15 April 1964. The assembly chamber is circular and set off-centre in the plan, a move that questions the ordered layouts of neoclassical architecture. There is also a forum for conversation and business. Ramps take the place of stairs, so movement between levels flows without steps, while tall ceilings and slim columns make the interior feel open. The main door, close to 2.3 square metres with enamelled panels, was flown in from Paris. Since 2016 the building has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Oscar Niemeyer designed the National Congress, like most of Brasília's government buildings, in a Modernist style. It stands midway along the Monumental Axis, the city's main street, behind a large lawn used for demonstrations. Costa's justification report made the Praça dos Três Poderes a triangle, one corner per branch of government, with the legislature at the apex. Niemeyer sketched the curved forms and sent them to the engineer Joaquim Cardozo, who worked out how the concrete could carry such smooth shapes. Two distinct domes were the aim. The Chamber of Deputies dome was harder: it had to seem simply to rest on the slab, and though as high as the Senate dome, at 10 metres, it spans 62. Two 28-storey office towers complete the group. Congress opened with the city on 21 April 1960, and has been UNESCO-listed since 1987.

Casa Milà was the last private residence Antoni Gaudí designed, built in Barcelona between 1906 and 1912. Gaudí treated the whole house as one continuous curve, outside and in, using ruled geometry and forms drawn from nature. It is made of two buildings arranged around two courtyards, which bring daylight to its nine levels: basement, ground floor, mezzanine, main floor, four further storeys above, and an attic. Among its structural advances are a stone façade that carries itself, floors with a free plan, an underground garage and a terrace on the roof. The façade is built of big limestone blocks, quarried in the Garraf Massif for the first floor and at Villefranche for the levels above. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1984.

In January 2004 the LMDC's design competition picked Reflecting Absence, by Michael Arad, an architect at Handel Architects, and the landscape architect Peter Walker, from 5,201 entries sent from 63 countries. The New York memorial sets two pools of about one acre (4,000 m²) each where the Twin Towers stood, standing for the lives lost and the void left behind. Their waterfalls, the largest built by people in the United States, are meant to soften the city's noise and make the site contemplative. Around the pools, 152 bronze parapets carry 2,983 names: 2,977 people killed on September 11 and six in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. Over 400 swamp white oaks stand in rows across the plaza above the Memorial Museum, forming loose clusters, clearings and groves. It was dedicated on 11 September 2011 and opened a day later.

Casa Batlló is one of four very different buildings by Modernista architects on a stretch of Barcelona's Passeig de Gràcia known as the Block of Discord, or Illa de la Discòrdia. It began as an existing house: Antoni Gaudí redesigned it in 1904, before building work had started, and it has been refitted more than once since. Gaudí widened the central well to bring light to every part and added new floors. Straight lines are rare, and a colourful mosaic of broken ceramic tiles, called trencadís, covers much of the front. Its bony, body-like character earns it the local name Casa dels ossos, House of Bones. People have likened the arched roof to a dragon's or dinosaur's back, and inside, sixty catenary arches form a space that recalls an animal's ribcage. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.

Built by London County Council for the Festival of Britain, the Royal Festival Hall opened on 3 May 1951. The council's chief architect, Robert Matthew, led with a young team. Leslie Martin later headed it alongside Peter Moro and Edwin Williams, and the designers Robin and Lucienne Day, in furniture and textiles, took part. A 1948 sketch by Martin shows the concert hall as an egg in a box. Reinforced concrete is paired with fine woods and fossil-bearing Derbyshire limestone, and the bright white exterior was meant to contrast with the blackened city. Its broad foyers, with bars and restaurants, were for everyone, with no bars split by class. It was among the world's first concert halls built by applying science, in theory and by experiment. It seats 2,700, and in 1981 became the first post-war building listed Grade I.

The Austrian sculptor Fritz Wotruba designed this church in Vienna, and Fritz Gerhard Mayr was its planning architect. Margarethe Ottillinger started the project; she picked the site of a former Nazi barracks and wanted a bold religious and artistic statement at a time when society was growing more secular. Work ran from August 1974 to October 1976. Wotruba died before it was finished, so Mayr saw the rest through. The design drew on Chartres Cathedral, yet the result is Brutalist: 152 blocks of concrete with no visible symmetry, with clear glass windows letting in the light.

The Chapel of St. Ignatius, a Jesuit chapel at Seattle University, was completed in 1997. Steven Holl likened his design to seven bottles of light held inside a box of stone. By day, sunlight takes on colour as it bounces off coloured baffles and passes through coloured glass lenses; after dark it works in reverse, as the chapel's own lighting is tinted by the same devices on its way out. Each volume stands for one part of Jesuit worship and has its own glass colour, so areas of the building are marked by their light. Set on a former street, the long plan forms new quadrangles to the north, west and south, with another planned to the east. The design earned Steven Holl Architects the AIA's Twenty-five Year Award, and MoMA in New York keeps a scale model.

Borobudur, in Magelang, Indonesia, is the world's largest Buddhist temple, and ranks with Myanmar's Bagan and Cambodia's Angkor Wat among Southeast Asia's great archaeological sites. Built under the Sailendra dynasty, it follows Javanese Buddhist architecture, which joins local ancestor worship with the Buddhist goal of nirvana. The temple is one huge stupa; from above it forms a giant tantric mandala, picturing both the Buddhist cosmos and the nature of the mind. From a square base about 118 metres a side rise nine platforms of grey, andesite-like stone, six square and three round, under a central dome ringed by 72 Buddhas, each in a pierced stupa. Stairs and corridors lead pilgrims past 1,460 carved story panels. In restoration, over a million stones were taken down to be catalogued, cleaned and treated; the largest project, by Indonesia and UNESCO, ended in 1983.

Butaro District Hospital lies in Burera District, in the Northern Province of Rwanda, roughly 96 kilometres by road north of the capital, Kigali. MASS Design Group designed it together with Rwanda's Ministry of Health and Partners in Health. The design sets out to fit its surroundings and to cut the risk of infections caught in hospital. Local materials were used wherever possible, among them volcanic stone from the Virunga Mountains. Building the 150-bed hospital began in December 2008, employed more than 3,500 people from the local community, and finished a year ahead of plan; it opened on 24 January 2011. It now has 256 in-patient beds.

Often called the Jenga Building, 56 Leonard Street is a 57-storey tower in Tribeca, Manhattan, rising 821 feet (250 m), more than any other structure in the neighbourhood. Herzog & de Meuron, the Swiss firm that designed it, describe it as "houses stacked in the sky". Construction started again in October 2012 after a pause of almost four years, and the tower was finished in 2017. The architects also designed the interiors, down to custom kitchens, bathrooms, fittings and fireplaces, while Goldstein, Hill & West Architects acted as architect of record. At the top are eight apartments that each fill a whole floor, from 5,200 to 6,400 square feet (480 to 590 m²), with ceilings 14 to 19 feet high. In 2019 Curbed New York listed it among the city's ten most important buildings of the previous decade.

Named after the nearby Esplanade Park, Singapore's Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay is made of two rounded forms: one holds a concert hall of about 1,600 seats, the other the Lyric Theatre, for some 2,000, which adapts the horseshoe plan of a traditional European opera house. DP Architects of Singapore designed it jointly with London's Michael Wilford & Partners, though the London firm left the project in May 1995. Each form is a curved space frame fitted with triangular glass panels and sunshades, balancing views out against shade. Critics warned the glass would make a greenhouse in the tropics; DPA director Vikas Gore said shading had always been intended, and over 7,000 aluminium sunshades were added, giving the shells a spiky look. Finished in February 2001, it was officially opened by President S. R. Nathan on 12 October 2002.

The Casa das Histórias Paula Rego, or House of Stories, is a museum in Cascais on the Portuguese Riviera built to show works by the artist Paula Rego. She picked the architect herself: Eduardo Souto de Moura, whose building dates from 2009. It occupies the old tennis courts of what was once the Sporting Club of Cascais, and gives the region's historic buildings, the Palace of Sintra above all, a contemporary reading. Rego asked for something "fun, lively and also a bit mischievous", and the design followed her wishes. Two pyramid-shaped towers and red-tinted concrete set it apart, and the park's mature trees were kept within the scheme. Four wings of varying heights and sizes hold linked rooms around a central space for temporary shows. There are 750 m² of galleries, a 200-seat auditorium, a shop and a café.

The Steilneset Memorial in Vardø remembers 91 people tried and executed for witchcraft in 1621. Designed by architect Peter Zumthor and artist Louise Bourgeois, it opened in 2011 and was Bourgeois' last major work. It was a joint commission from the town, the Varanger Museum, Finnmark County and the Norwegian Public Roads Administration. Of its two separate buildings, Zumthor's is a 120-metre timber structure of sixty bays in a row, its off-site frames holding a coated fibreglass membrane on cables that narrows at each end. Its timber walkway is 100 metres long and only 1.5 metres wide, and 91 randomly placed small windows stand for those executed, each with a text drawn from original sources. Bourgeois' work sits in a square room of weathering steel and 17 panes of tinted glass, its walls stopping short of floor and ceiling.

The Bridge of Peace is a curved footbridge of steel and glass spanning 150 metres over the Kura River in Tbilisi, joining Rike Park to the Old Town. Tbilisi City Hall ordered it as a modern link between old city and new district; it opened on 6 May 2010. Italian architect Michele De Lucchi designed it; French designer Philippe Martinaud did the lighting. Made in Italy, the structure reached Tbilisi in 200 trucks; the lights went in during assembly. At night thousands of white LEDs play across the wavy canopy; the design recalls a sea creature. On the deck, 240 motion sensors switch on LED strips in the glass railings as people pass, so the lights seem to switch on for each walker. Critics, architects and planners among them, said it overpowered the historic Old Town and hid its landmarks.

On London's South Bank, the London Eye, first named the Millennium Wheel, is the tallest observation wheel of its cantilevered kind anywhere. It draws over three million visitors a year, more than any other paid attraction in the United Kingdom. It was conceived by David Marks and Julia Barfield, married architects who met in 1972 as students at the Architectural Association. A wheel, they saw, could lift people high with ease and avoid comparison with the Eiffel Tower. Unlike taller wheels, it is held by an A-frame on one side only, and tensioned steel cables carry its rim like a giant spoked bicycle wheel. Sections were floated upriver and assembled flat on piled platforms in the Thames. A turn takes about 30 minutes. Planned as temporary, on a five-year lease, it was made permanent in July 2002.

The Basilica of the Annunciation in Nazareth stands on the spot Catholic tradition gives for the Virgin Mary's house. The Italian architect Giovanni Muzio designed it, and the Israeli firm Solel Boneh built it between 1960 and 1969. Its style is sometimes called Italian Brutalism. The two-storey church sits on a site once used by earlier churches, including Byzantine and Crusader ones. On the lower level is the Grotto of the Annunciation, which many Christians believe is what remains of Mary's childhood home. Upstairs are many images of Mary, mostly mosaics, each from a different country with a large Catholic population. The Latin parish worships here, and the Franciscans still run it. Of all the churches in the Middle East overseen by the Congregation for the Oriental Churches, it is the largest.

Seat of Hungary's National Assembly in Budapest, the Országház, or House of the Country, was designed by Imre Steindl in a neo-Gothic manner. His entry won partly because it closely resembled the Palace of Westminster in London. Building began in 1885; the parliament was inaugurated in 1896, the supposed thousandth year of the nation, and opened in 1902. The Gothic Revival façade is symmetrical, and the central dome is Renaissance Revival. Inside, two identical chambers mirror each other on opposite sides. At 268 by 123 metres it has been the country's largest building since completion. Its 96-metre height recalls 896, when the Principality of Hungary was founded. It holds 10 courtyards, 27 gates, 29 staircases and 691 rooms, over 200 of them offices. The Holy Crown of Hungary has been on show in the central hall since 2000.

The Australian War Memorial in Canberra is a national memorial, museum and archive for all Australians killed by war, peacekeeping included. Emil Sodersten and John Crust shared the design, asked to combine Sodersten's Art Deco manner with Crust's thrift. The Great Depression delayed building; the Memorial Building went ahead in the mid-1930s and opened in 1941. Its interlocking masses and front pylons carry Byzantine and Egyptian motifs in an Art Deco frame. It was set on an axis on purpose, to mark its national standing and give a clear line of sight to and from Parliament House. A courtyard with a reflecting pool leads up steps at its north end to the Hall of Memory, where Waller's mosaics, the largest murals in Australia, went in during 1955, and the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier in 1993.

The Napier Museum in Thiruvananthapuram holds art and natural history collections. Its building, by Robert Chisholm, was finished in 1880, the year the museum opened its doors, and it is named after the governor of the day, Francis Napier, 10th Lord Napier. The Indo-Saracenic design mixes influences from Indian, Chinese, Kerala and Mughal architecture, and is known for its ornament. Among its features are a Gothic roof and minarets. There is no air conditioning, and good natural ventilation has meant none was needed; by contrast, an annex added in 2016 with few windows or openings has suffered from mould, insects and corrosion. The museum also has a bandstand with hidden speakers and special acoustics.

In 1977 Frank and Berta Gehry bought a pink bungalow in Santa Monica, built in 1920 in a Dutch colonial style. The following year Gehry wrapped the house in a new outer skin, leaving the old exterior in view behind it. He left the rear and south façades almost untouched and added tilted glass cubes to the other sides. The house uses unconventional materials: chain-link fencing and corrugated steel. It is sometimes counted among the earliest deconstructivist buildings, a label Gehry himself rejected. Many neighbours disliked the unusual architecture that had arrived on their street. It was once the architect's own home.

Antoni Gaudí designed Casa Calvet for a textile manufacturer, as a residence with business premises in the basement and on the ground floor. Built from 1898 to 1900, it stands at Carrer de Casp 48 in Barcelona's Eixample. Gaudí scholars agree it is his most conventional work, partly because it was squeezed between older buildings, partly because of its elegant setting. Its symmetry, balance and regular rhythm are rare for him. Modernista touches remain: curves and a double gable on top, a projecting, almost baroque oriel at the entrance, and witty details. Bulging balconies alternate with smaller, shallower ones, and the entrance columns are shaped like stacked bobbins, a nod to the family's textile trade. Lluís Permanyer praises the ground-floor gallery, a bold mix of wrought iron and stone. It won the Arts Building Annual Award.

Dresden Hauptbahnhof is the biggest passenger station in Dresden. Opened on 16 April 1898 after over five years of work, it replaced the Bohemian station of the old Saxon-Bohemian State Railway and was laid out as the city's main station. The competition gave two first prizes, one to Giese and Weidner of Dresden and one to Arwed Roßbach of Leipzig; the station built mixes both schemes, and Giese and Weidner led construction. The platform halls use 17,000 tonnes of steel from August Klönne; the stonework is Elbe Sandstone. No other station pairs an island building between the tracks with a terminal on two levels. In a full restoration early this century, the train sheds got translucent roofs of Teflon-coated glass fibre, credited to Foster + Partners, bringing more daylight to the concourses. The 34-metre dome was restored as first designed.

The General Services Administration put up this ten-storey office block in Washington, D.C. as the headquarters of HUD, the federal housing department. Marcel Breuer's brutalist design was completed in 1968; with the Humphrey Building, it is one of his two federal buildings in the city. In plan it forms two letter Ys set back to back, four curved wings springing from a long core. Like his earlier UNESCO Headquarters and IBM La Gaude, it has a curving precast concrete façade, made of panels with deeply set rectangular windows, while the ground floor sits back behind concrete pilotis. Breuer also designed a six-acre plaza that roofs an underground car park. Its design won praise when new, but its brutalism and lack of originality have since drawn criticism, notably from several HUD secretaries. It is on the National Register of Historic Places.

An arts centre in Barcelona's Raval district, the CCCB (Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona) takes the city and its urban culture as its core theme. It occupies part of the former Casa de Caritat, an almshouse built in 1802 that kept that role until 1957. Helio Piñón and Albert Viaplana remodelled the premises, and in 1993 their project won both the FAD and the Ciutat de Barcelona Architecture Prizes. The new project took the place of the north wing, closing the original U-shaped plan with a prismatic block 30 metres tall. Its glass front leans out over the courtyard near the top, reflecting the neighbouring rooftops, offering a lookout over Barcelona and holding the halls, lifts and stairs. Of the centre's 15,000 m2 of floor area, 4,000 m2 is given to exhibitions.

Messe Torhaus is a high-rise in Frankfurt's Bockenheim district, designed by Oswald Mathias Ungers. The contractor Hochtief put up the 60,000-ton building with 400 workers between 1983 and 1984, taking a record 13 months. It rises 117 m over 30 floors and holds the administration of Messe Frankfurt along with a kindergarten and the press centre. Its unusual form and choice of materials have been likened to a guillotine. Because a Mainova heat and power plant sits right beside it on the fairgrounds, the tower also goes by the nickname "Frankfurt's most beautiful fireplace".

Bodegas Güell, called Celler Güell in Catalan, is a winery complex in Garraf, within the municipality of Sitges. The design is credited to Antoni Gaudí, who took on the commission in 1882 for his patron Eusebi Güell, after Güell had seen his work at the 1878 Paris Expo. Several hunting pavilions were planned alongside the winery but never built. The winery itself went up between 1895 and 1897, with Gaudí's assistant Francesc Berenguer directing the work. From the front it reads as a triangle, its near-vertical roofs clad in steep stone slabs and topped by groups of chimneys. Inside are three levels: vehicle parking below, a flat on the first floor and a domed chapel at the top. Wine production ended in 1936 for lack of commercial success, and there is now a restaurant in it.

The Qatar National Convention Centre in Doha opened officially on 4 December 2011. Arata Isozaki designed it together with RHWL Architects, and it includes water-saving and energy-efficient features that make it roughly 32 percent more efficient than a similar design without them. No building of its kind had been built before to LEED Gold, the US Green Building Council rating, and solar panels covering 3,500 sqm supply 12.5 percent of its energy. The columns along the front stand for the Sidrat al-Muntaha, a sacred tree in Islam held to mark where the seventh heaven ends. Inside are a conference hall seating 4,000, a 2,300-seat theatre, three auditoria and 52 flexible meeting rooms. Venue space totals 200,000 square metres, 40,000 of them for exhibitions across nine halls, and up to 10,000 people can be seated for a conference or banquet.

Once among the largest and oldest groups of orphanage and hospital buildings in the Americas, the Hospicio Cabañas in Guadalajara is also known as the Cabañas Museum. The Bishop of Guadalajara founded it in 1810 to serve at once as workhouse, hospital, orphanage and almshouse. It is named after Juan Ruiz de Cabañas, appointed to the see in 1796, who hired the Mexico City architect Manuel Tolsá; Tolsá based the plan on classic examples such as Les Invalides and El Escorial. Single-storey ranges 7.5 metres high form a rectangle of 164 by 145 metres, kept on one level so the sick, elderly and children could move easily. The chapel is twice as tall, its dome reaching 32.5 metres. José Clemente Orozco painted monumental frescoes inside, among them The Man of Fire (1936–39). It became a World Heritage Site in 1997.

This Buddhist temple in Bagan, Myanmar, dates from 1105 AD, in the reign of King Kyansittha of the Pagan Dynasty. Its plan is a cross, with terraces stepping up to a small pagoda crowned by a hti, the umbrella ornament found on nearly all of Myanmar's pagodas. Four standing Buddha statues inside face the four cardinal directions. The design has been described as a fusion of Mon architecture with an adopted Indian style. Built of brick and plaster, it carries stone images and glazed terracotta plaques meant to teach Theravada Buddhism. The central square is 53 metres a side, gabled porches project 17 metres from each face, and the terraced superstructure rises 51 metres. Jataka scenes of the Buddha's life cover 554 terracotta tiles on the base, sides and terraces. Damaged in the 1975 earthquake, it is now fully restored.

Officially named the Alisher Navoi State Academic Grand Theatre, this national opera house in central Tashkent was among the region's first modern theatres. Alexey Shchusev designed it, and it went up between 1942 and 1947, partly by forced labour.
