Between 1945 and 1947 the Soviet Union made Japanese prisoners of war work on it; a plaque honouring them was put up at the theatre in 1996, when Islam Karimov was President of Uzbekistan. It opened its doors to the public in November 1947, to celebrate 500 years since the birth of Alisher Navoi, regarded as the greatest figure of Chagatai literature. The hall holds 1,400 people, and the main stage measures 540 square metres.

Gottfried Böhm (d. 2021) designed the pilgrimage church of Maria, Königin des Friedens in Neviges (Velbert, Germany), built from 1966 and consecrated in 1968. Devotion to a wonder-working image of the Immaculate Conception there goes back to 1681. The church is regarded as the most influential and widely recognised of Böhm's works. On 23 September 1978 Cardinal Karol Wojtyła came to the "Mariendom" together with German and Polish bishops, led by Primate Cardinal Wyszyński and Cardinal Höffner. Twenty-three days later Wojtyła was elected Pope John Paul II.

Villa Méditerranée stands in Marseille's 2nd arrondissement, in the La Joliette neighbourhood next to MuCEM. Stefano Boeri designed it within Euroméditerranée, an urban renewal scheme. It opened in 2013, the year Marseille was European Capital of Culture, at first as a conference venue: a 9,000 sqm centre for exhibitions and research looking over the port, intended for cultural and research events on Mediterranean subjects. Boeri imagined it as a place where the region's many identities could meet and blend, with the sea as its point of reference. An artificial dock lets the 36-metre-high conference space look down onto a broad square of water. Since 2022 it has been home to Cosquer Méditerranée, a museum built around a replica of the Cosquer Cave.

Aspire Tower, also called The Torch Doha, is a skyscraper hotel 300 metres tall in Doha's Aspire Zone. Architect Hadi Simaan and AREP designed it with the engineers Ove Arup and Partners, and it was the focal point of the 15th Asian Games, which Qatar hosted in December 2006. Its structure is a reinforced-concrete cylinder core, 1 to 1.8 metres thick and 12 to 18 metres across, ringed on every floor by radiating cantilevered steel beams. An energy-efficient glass skin helps keep temperatures comfortable in the desert climate. Midmac and Six Construct, a BESIX subsidiary, finished it in November 2007 for €133,395,000. Inside are a five-star hotel, a health club, a museum of sport, a revolving restaurant and an observation deck. The pool sits 80 metres above the ground, cantilevered from the core and reaching 12 metres beyond the facade.

Charles Correa designed the British Council's headquarters in India, a New Delhi building that took him five years, from 1987 to 1992. It brings together a library, an auditorium, an art gallery and the Council's offices. Correa set these out over several floors as layers, meant to recall three centuries of contact between India and Britain. Walking through, one moves from a spiral that stands for Bindu, the cosmic centre of energy, past a traditional Islamic Char Bagh, to a European emblem inlaid in marble and granite that represents the Age of Reason. Across the front, the British artist Howard Hodgkin made a mural of a banyan tree whose branches spread over the walls, worked in black Kadappa stone and Makrana marble.

Barcelona's Dispensario Central Antituberculoso was planned as a centre to coordinate the fight against tuberculosis across the country. Designed in 1934, it was finished in 1938, in the middle of the Spanish Civil War. Josep Lluís Sert, Josep Torres Clavé and Joan Baptista Subirana designed it with other members of GATCPAC. To meet its functional needs, the building takes in as much fresh air and sunlight as possible throughout. Two linked wings form an L, with the caretakers' quarters standing apart, and a courtyard garden ties the parts together, acting both as the entrance and as a buffer against the surrounding city. Each part has a steel and concrete structure, faced with light panels in a range of materials. It is now recognised as heritage architecture for its history in Spain and its design.

The Apollo Pavilion, also called the Pasmore Pavilion, is a public artwork in Peterlee, a County Durham new town. It was designed by Victor Pasmore, a British artist and architect, and completed in 1969. The town was designed around this central abstract artwork and pavilion, named after the Apollo space programme to echo that programme's optimism. Cast in place in reinforced concrete, it is made of broad geometric planes of white concrete, with two oval murals as its only decoration. It spans a small lake that frames a large geometric sculpture by Pasmore, first serving as a footbridge between the estate's two halves. It remains a rare British attempt to fuse art and architecture at large scale. After a £400,000 restoration it was formally unveiled on 11 July 2009; Grade II* listing came in December 2011.

Denys Lasdun's building for the Institute of Education, now part of UCL, was designed for the University of London and dates from 1970 to 1976. Plans for new premises on Bedford Way had been drawn up in 1960, but only part of Lasdun's first scheme was completed. The building proved controversial for the way it was set into the existing pattern of squares and terraces; Lasdun argued that it respected that plan, even if its language was more Brutalist. Its fire escape stairs are expressed on the outside, nodding to Louis Kahn and Wells Coates, while Lasdun's masterplan laid a new, partly public square over car parking. The library finally moved into an extension in 1992, taking the name Newsam Library after Peter Newsam, the Director who oversaw the new construction. The building is listed Grade II*.

The terminal at Beijing Daxing International Airport is nicknamed "the starfish" for its shape: six curving spokes radiating from a central hub. Zaha Hadid Architects designed it with ADPI, a French planning firm, and partners, and BIAD, the Beijing Institute of Architectural Design, carried it out; it was still being built when Zaha Hadid died. Work on the airport started on 26 December 2014 under chief engineer Guo Yanchi, and the terminal's concrete structure was capped by March 2017. Nearly five years and CN¥80 billion (US$11.4 billion) later, the project had a 700,000 m2 terminal, the largest airport terminal in a single building anywhere, on 47 km2 of land. Opening day came on 25 September 2019, six days before the People's Republic of China turned 70, at a ceremony attended by Xi Jinping.

Eun Young Yi won the international competition for Stuttgart's new city library in 1999. Work ran from 2010 to 24 October 2011 and cost about 80 million euros, 4 million of them for the interiors. Yi designed a plain cube on a square plan, 44 metres long and 40 metres tall, with nine floors above ground and two below. The frame is precast concrete, with glass brick panels set into it. At the centre is the "heart", an archaic four-storey space with no specific library function. Behind the outer glass front sits a second, membrane-like glass skin, with a walkable gap between them that ventilates the building. Plan, elevation and section all keep to a 0.97-metre grid. Inspirations included the Pantheon, a 1785 proposal for the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Noah's ark and Kubrick's A Space Odyssey.

Blues Point Tower stands in McMahons Point near North Sydney: 83 metres tall, with 144 apartments on 24 levels. Harry Seidler received the commission in 1958 from Dick Dusseldorp, through Dusseldorp's company Civil & Civic. Because planning rules then counted balconies toward the floor-space ratio, the design was changed in 1959 to French balconies, and that is how it was built. Completed in 1962, when its first residents moved in, it was the first high-rise apartment block to be strata titled and stayed Australia's tallest residential building until 1970. Following Albers, Seidler avoided static symmetry and plain grids, offsetting elements to create "visual tension", which shows in the tower's window pattern. Its heritage listing calls it a "conspicuous, though unpopular" example of the Internationalist style, and North Sydney Council added it to its local heritage register in 1993.

Miles Warren designed the Dorset Street Flats in Christchurch in 1956, a year after starting his own practice. On a 771-square-metre site, the original scheme held eight one-bedroom flats with built-in furniture and fittings, a ninth made from an old stable block, four garages, courtyards and a shared laundry. Warren drew on modernism and on New Brutalism, which he had met in Britain in the 1950s. The flats are credited as an early work of the Christchurch School and one of New Zealand's first attempts at building in load-bearing concrete block. Critics and fellow architects praised the work, but public reception was cooler: the flats were compared to a prison and nicknamed "Fort Dorset". Heritage New Zealand listed them in Category 1 in 2010, and a restoration by Young Architects' Greg Young won a 2023 New Zealand Architecture Award.

The Adam Art Gallery, Te Pātaka Toi in Māori, is a purpose-built gallery at Victoria University of Wellington, on its Kelburn Campus. Ian Athfield designed it. It sits between three university buildings, Old Kirk, Hunter and the Student Union, and over the "Culliford stair", which was already in place. New Zealand's Governor General, Sir Michael Hardie Boys, formally opened it on 21 September 1999. That year Athfield Architects received two NZIA Resene awards for the building, both in the Community & Cultural category: a branch architecture award and a colour award. In 2025 the gallery received the Enduring Architecture Award at the NZIA's Wellington Architecture Awards.

1 Bligh Street is a 30-storey office tower in Sydney's central business district, looking out over Circular Quay, the harbour and the Harbour Bridge. Germany's Ingenhoven Architects designed it with Australia's Architectus. The Green Building Council of Australia gave it a six-star green rating. A sewage plant in the basement recycles 90 percent of its waste water, the roof carries solar panels, and chilled beams handle the air conditioning. It was the first major Australian high-rise with a full double-skin facade and external louvres. On the south side, a naturally ventilated atrium runs the full 120-metre height, bringing daylight to every office floor. In 2012 the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat named it Best Tall Building in Asia & Australasia, and it also won the International Highrise Award and the Harry Seidler Award for Commercial Architecture.

The Centro per l'arte contemporanea Luigi Pecci in Prato was founded in 1988 by the curator Amnon Barzel and the industrialist Enrico Pecci, in memory of Pecci's son Luigi. Since it first opened that year it has staged more than 250 exhibitions, events and learning programmes for students and adults. Italo Gamberini designed the original building. In 2016 Maurice Nio enlarged it with a U-shaped wing wrapped around an open-air amphitheatre for 800 people. The new wing holds 3,000 square metres of galleries, an archive, a library, an auditorium that doubles as a cinema, a bookshop and a restaurant. Besides its permanent collection of contemporary art, the centre has a sculpture garden and an area set aside for temporary shows.

Dudley Zoo is credited to Berthold Lubetkin and the Tecton partnership; it was an entirely new zoo, commissioned from Tecton by London Zoo alongside Tecton's buildings for London Zoo's reserve park at Whipsnade. The engineer Ove Arup acted as Tecton's structural consultant on it, as he did on the Penguin Pool at Regent's Park Zoo in London. The zoo was made up of twelve animal enclosures and was an early example of Modernism in Britain. Every original enclosure still stands apart from the penguin pool, which was pulled down in 1979. The Twentieth Century Society sees in these playful pavilions a reminder that architecture should answer more than material needs, and should also set out to inspire and delight.

In central Cardiff, St David's Hall (Neuadd Dewi Sant in Welsh) serves officially as the national venue for concerts and conferences in Wales, hosting the Welsh Proms every year and the BBC Cardiff Singer of the World every two years. Seymour Harris Partnership had to fit a 2,000-seat auditorium, with all its foyers, bars, offices and backstage rooms, onto a tight city-centre plot. Space was so short that it had to be built into and over the St David's Shopping Centre, then planned and partly built, which explains its unusual form. Angular grey concrete covers nearly all of the exterior; Building Design called the style "complex late brutalism". The first concert was held on 11 September 1982. Cadw gives it interim Grade II protection. It closed in September 2023 when RAAC was found in the roof.

Alex Gordon, who went on to become a prominent south Wales architect, designed Cyncoed Methodist Church in Cardiff. Its foundation stone went down in November 1965; the church dates from 1966, the year it was dedicated, in September. It follows the International Modern style that Mies van der Rohe pioneered, with a rectilinear form built of glass and buff brick. A large extension went up at the back in 1992. The church was listed in 2001; the listing praises it as an individually accomplished design that helps to set the architectural benchmark for Welsh religious buildings after the war.

Henry Hobson Richardson designed the Converse Memorial Library (or Building) in Malden, Massachusetts. Elisha S. and Mary D. Converse gave it in memory of their son Frank Eugene Converse, killed in what is described as the first bank robbery and murder in North America. Built from 1883 to 1885, it forms an L, faced in brown Longmeadow sandstone, with a tower at the inner corner and a deeply arched entrance porch in the short arm. The main library room measures 50 by 36 feet, lined in richly carved white oak beneath a high vaulted ceiling. Richardson also designed the furniture, made by A. H. Davenport and Company of Boston. It was his last library and is often ranked among his finest works. It housed Malden Public Library until 1996 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1987.

Built to show widescreen Cinerama films, the Cinerama Dome in Los Angeles opened on November 7, 1963. The French architect Pierre Cabrol, lead designer at Welton Becket and Associates, proposed the design; as a student at MIT he had worked with R. Buckminster Fuller. Crews worked around the clock, and the whole build took just 16 weeks. It is the world's only geodesic dome in concrete, assembled from 316 hexagonal and pentagonal panels in 16 sizes, each about 12 feet across and weighing around 7,500 pounds. Inside are a loge with stadium seating and floating stairways of architectural note. When it opened, its curved screen, 32 feet high and 86 feet wide, was the largest of its kind anywhere. The dome was made a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument in 1998.

Benaroya Hall fills a whole city block in central Seattle. LMN Architects of Seattle designed it, and it cost $120 million when it opened in September 1998; in 2001 it received the American Institute of Architects' National Honor Award. It has two auditoria: the S. Mark Taper Foundation Auditorium, with 2,500 seats, and the Illsley Ball Nordstrom Recital Hall, seating 536. Cyril Harris designed its acoustics, which draw heavily on technology, and the main hall rests on rubber pads that isolate it from the outer shell. The hall stands right over the Great Northern Tunnel, the city's main rail corridor, and beside the Downtown Seattle Transit Tunnel, whose Symphony station is built into it. The lobby displays glass art, including Crystal Cascade by Dale Chihuly. The hall has helped the Seattle Symphony double its budget and its number of performances.

Toronto Reference Library is the largest public reference library in Canada, holding books, manuscripts, microfilm and more. Raymond Moriyama's design was revised after months of talks with local government and approved in April 1974, slightly reducing its size, height and bulk and switching its cladding to brick. It opened at Yonge Street and Asquith Avenue on 2 November 1977. Upper levels step back from the street to form a pyramid. The structure is steel-reinforced concrete, clad in orange-red brick to match its neighbours, with glazing toward Yonge Street. A heat pump system recovers heat from lights, visitors and sunlight. The curved, skylit atrium lets air move freely, with plants and water inspired by the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. A 2009–2014 renovation added a glass cube with a larger lobby, shop and café, recalling Moriyama's 1973 proposal.

The Cinquantenaire Arcade in Brussels began with the Belgian government's plans, under King Leopold II's patronage, for the 1880 National Exhibition, held 50 years after the Belgian Revolution. Gédéon Bordiau conceived that exhibition's single arch. After his death in 1904, Leopold II chose the French architect Charles Girault to rework it; Girault made it a triple arch but kept Bordiau's quadriga. Leopold II inaugurated the arcade on 27 September 1905, in time for 75 years of Belgian independence. The arch is 30 metres wide and 45 metres high, with three equal bays. On top, Thomas Vinçotte's bronze quadriga, Brabant Raising the National Flag, has horses by Jules Lagae. A wall closed the back of the colonnade in 1905, and from 1912 Jean Delville covered it with a 360 m2 mosaic frieze. Protection followed on 29 June 1984.

Head office of CEC Bank, the CEC Palace stands on Calea Victoriei in Bucharest, facing the country's National Museum of Romanian History. Construction started on 8 June 1897 and ended in 1900, with the bank paying for both the land and the building from its own funds. The site had earlier held the ruins of the Saint John the Great monastery and an inn beside it. The design came from Paul Gottereau, who had studied at the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris, while the Romanian architect Ion Socolescu oversaw construction. Eclectic in style, the palace is crowned by a dome of glass and metal. Its entrance is an arch carried on two pairs of composite columns, and each of the four corners has gables, coats of arms and a Renaissance dome.

At 97 metres, the Administrative Palace in Satu Mare is the tallest building in Transylvania and among the tallest in Romania. Work began in 1972; Nicolae Porumbescu from Iaşi was the main architect, assisted by Ludovic Gyüre of Satu Mare, and more than 1,000 workers took part before it was completed in 1984. Built in the brutalist style, it pairs one large main tower with three smaller ones. The smaller towers were meant to stand for the three ethnic groups of Satu Mare County, Romanians, Germans and Hungarians, and the main tower for the bond between them. Today it houses several public bodies, among them the county council, the prefecture, the city hall and the culture office.

The Haludovo Palace Hotel was the architectural and social heart of Haludovo, a resort at Malinska designed by the Croatian architect Boris Magaš and built from 1969 to 1972, as tourism on the Yugoslav Adriatic boomed. Covering about 25 hectares, Haludovo was planned as a self-contained tourist town rather than one hotel. The Palace held the commanding place of a castle, long blocks of rooms at the edge read as city walls, and clusters of small atrium villas formed a settlement inside. Shared rooms centred on a double-height atrium ringed by a gallery, where tall, thin concrete columns branched into arches. Similar concrete forms recur across the site as pergolas, sunshades and roofs. Guccione set up the Penthouse Adriatic Club in the Palace, with a casino aimed mainly at foreign guests. Historians count Haludovo among Magaš's key works.

Sofia Central Railway Station is the main passenger station of Bulgaria's capital and the largest in the country. Transproekt, with Milko Bechev as lead architect, designed the new terminal. Work began on 23 February 1971 on the plaza and gardens of the 1888 station, so that trains could keep running during construction. The station was picked as one of 30 buildings to be renovated, rebuilt or newly built for the 30th anniversary of the 1944 Bulgarian coup d'état. Spread over two levels below ground and three above, it held 365 rooms and spaces and used white marble extensively. It was inaugurated on 6 September 1974 before the country's elite, with Zhivkov, Bulgaria's de facto ruler, cutting the ribbon. A full renovation followed in 2016.

Kuala Lumpur Railway Station went up between 1910 and 1917 on the site of an earlier station. It was the city's rail hub for the Federated Malay States Railways and then Malayan Railways (KTM), until Kuala Lumpur Sentral largely replaced it in 2001. Its designer, Arthur Benison Hubback, a British assistant to the Director of Public Works, drew on the region's Anglo-Asian architecture. The main block blends Western and Mughal elements in a "Raj" style close to Indo-Saracenic. Horseshoe and ogee arches and large corner chhatris (six, plus two added later) make it comparable to contemporaries such as the Sultan Abdul Samad Building. Unlike similar buildings in bare brick, it is fully plastered and painted in pale colours. Its original glazed roofs were partly open to let out locomotive smoke. It reopened as a railway museum on 31 August 2007.

Mimar Sinan built the Caferağa Medrese in Istanbul in 1559 for Cafer Agha, while Suleiman the Magnificent was sultan. It lies below the forecourt of the Hagia Sophia, in the historic heart of the Sultanahmet district, so it falls inside the UNESCO World Heritage conservation area covering the whole district. Visitors enter through a main gate into an inner courtyard, with the former teaching rooms set around it. In 1989 the Turkish Cultural Service Foundation converted the medrese into a tourist centre, with 15 rooms for classes and exhibitions, a large hall and a garden. Traditional Turkish crafts such as calligraphy and ceramics are taught, made and sold there.

Ben Gurion Airport's Terminal 3 was inaugurated on 28 October 2004, when Prime Minister Ariel Sharon spoke, and opened to passengers a month later, replacing Terminal 1 as Israel's main gateway. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) designed the main building, while Moshe Safdie & Associates and TRA (today Black & Veatch) were responsible for a link building and the airside gates and departure areas. Hamid Kia, SOM's lead architect, aimed to capture the emotion of arriving in and leaving Israel. In Safdie's connector, arriving and departing passengers share one space and see each other through glass, with views to the Judean Hills and a garden of the Seven Species. An inverted dome hangs over the departures rotunda under a white fabric ceiling that softens daylight. Walls are faced in Jerusalem stone, set against white concrete, glass and aluminium.

Bab Al Bahrain, Arabic for "Gateway of Bahrain", stands in Customs Square in Manama's central business district and marks the main way into the Manama Souq. It opened in 1949 to a design by Charles Belgrave, the British adviser to the emir, who saw how much trade mattered and pushed for a gateway at the edge of the market, beside the landing jetties for dhows. It once stood on the shoreline, but heavy land reclamation in the second half of the 20th century has left it several kilometres inland. The square is regarded as the region's first formal public space. A 1986 refurbishment added Islamic architectural features. Today the monument is essentially one large arch with a road running beneath it, flanked by two side arches for people on foot.

Deira's Clock Tower in Dubai dates from 1965. Otto Bullard designed it with Ziki Homsi, a Syrian architect who was a partner in the Architecture Design Construction (ADC) Office. Meant as a symbol for Dubai, it was placed in Deira because, before the Dubai–Abu Dhabi Road existed, the main roads into the city came together there. Its roundabout leads onto the Al Maktoum Bridge, the first land crossing ever built between Deira and Bur Dubai, and the tower is now a well-known landmark of the area. Its form came from Bullard's own ideas and was not meant to show a drill bit or anything else. The Daily Telegraph included it in a list of the 17 most beautiful clock towers in the world.

Moscow Cinema stands on Charles Aznavour Square, on Abovyan Street, in Yerevan, Armenia's capital. Tiran Yerkanyan and Gevorg Kochar designed it, and it opened in 1936 where the Saint Paul and Peter Church had stood until the Soviet authorities demolished it earlier that decade. Kochar came back in 1960 to redesign the building with Telman Gevorkyan. In 1983 the facade was redone with scenes from well-known Soviet-Armenian films such as Sayat Nova, Pepo, Chapayev and David Bek. The Golden Apricot Yerevan International Film Festival, held every year since 2004, uses it as its main venue. Today it has four halls, the red hall (491 seats), the blue hall (350), the small red hall (49) and the gallery (35), plus an open-air theatre on its east side.

The Tbilisi City Assembly Building is a clock-towered building on the south side of Freedom Square in Georgia's capital, and it houses the City Assembly, or sakrebulo. The first building went up in the 1830s under Imperial Russian rule and has been rebuilt several times since, changing its appearance over two centuries. Until 1879 it held the Chancellery of the Chief Policemaster and the police department. In 1878 a competition was held to remodel it as the City Hall, and Paul Stern's entry won. Its exterior follows the Exotic style popular at the time, in a Neo-Moorish manner. A tower was added in 1910, and the building was enlarged again in 1912.

On Cusco's main square the Incas built the temple of Kiswarkancha, palace of Viracocha, who ruled the Kingdom of Cusco about a century before the Spanish arrived. Building the cathedral was entrusted to Juan Miguel de Veramendi in 1560; Juan Correa replaced him a year later and worked until 1564. In 1615 Miguel Gutiérrez Sencio, a follower of Vitruvius and Giacomo Barozzi who admired the sober Herrerian style of El Escorial, took charge with Francisco Becerra, and the cathedral was finished in 1654. It was built of local stone, with red granite blocks reused from Sacsayhuamán. Its three naves share one height, as at Lima and Jaén, and fourteen cruciform pillars set out twenty-four rib vaults. The facade is Renaissance, the interiors Baroque, late Gothic and Plateresque. Since 1983 it has been within Cusco's UNESCO World Heritage centre.
